en: A Painful Admonition by Chan Master Tianmu Zhongfeng Guanghui to His Disciple Chan Master Foyin Yuan, from his *Yushi tu* (Words for Disciples).
Its brief summary states: "A single moment of stilling the mind ultimately leads to the realization of perfect enlightenment. [The frog...]

If one walks without resting, even a lame turtle can travel a thousand li. Instruments may be sharp or dull, and faculties may be shallow or deep; yet when success is achieved, they are one and the same.
It depends solely upon rousing one’s indignation and establishing one’s resolve. I now earnestly exhort both monastics and laypeople:

you should know there are four things that are easy and four things that are difficult. What are the four that are easy? You yourself are the Buddha; there is no need to seek teachers or patrons elsewhere. If you wish to make offerings...

To nourish the Buddha is simply to nourish oneself; this is the first ease. To be non-active is to be the Buddha; there is no need to read scriptures, prostrate before images, perform ritual practices, or practice seated meditation.
When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep; follow conditions and accord with destiny; this is the second ease.

To be without attachment is to be the Buddha; there is no need to mutilate one's body or abandon one's kin. Whether in mountain forests or market towns, one is free everywhere; this is the third ease.
Seeking nothing is Buddhahood. It does not require the accumulation of merit or the diligent practice of asceticism. The two adornments of merit and wisdom have never had any mutual interaction.
This is the fourth ease. What are called the four difficulties? To be able to believe is the first difficulty; to be able to recollect is the second difficulty;

to be able to awaken is the third difficulty; to be able to practice is the fourth difficulty. Now, believing in cause and effect may be considered small faith, but it cannot be considered great faith. However...
Those who harbor doubts are many; those who believe are few. Among those who believe yet remain free of doubt, there are typically only one or two in a thousand or ten thousand.
How much more so for those who suddenly perceive their own nature and directly enter the state of a Tathāgata in a single leap!

Though thousands of sutras and tens of thousands of treatises, along with wondrous traces and extraordinary records, have been left behind in the world, it is only because people lack faith. The compassion of the myriad sages [is directed toward this].
Alas! He extensively employs skillful means to enlighten the deluded masses, leading them to enter through the gateway of faith. For those who possess faith will surely put it into practice;
this is why such faith is so difficult to attain. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, he desires only that [this thought] be kept in mind without forgetfulness:
practicing while walking, contemplating while sitting, whether rising or resting, moving or still, speaking or silent, lying down or arising—at all times.

One should keep them in mind at all times. Whether attending to affairs, interacting with others, or even during times of hardship, distress, calamity, or peril, one should likewise keep them in mind.
One’s body should be like withered wood, like a dull stone, like a corpse, or like an earthen figure; only the mind should dwell upon the Way.
In responding to others, one should appear as if dull-witted or intoxicated; hearing sounds or seeing forms, one should appear as if deaf or blind.
Thus, it is likened to a cat catching a mouse: the mind and eyes must be focused intently on the gaze; even a slight lapse results in losing the mouse.
It is like a hen brooding over her eggs: the warmth must be maintained continuously; if she abandons them, they will not become seeds. This is why this mindfulness is further [emphasized].
It is difficult. To contemplate the Way requires persistence; to awaken to the Way occurs in an instant.

When conditions have not yet ripened and the time has not yet arrived, though the mechanism is repeatedly activated, one encounters nothing. Once conditions have ripened and the time has arrived, even if form and sound do not meet, [the truth] suddenly appears before one.
It is difficult for those who have not awakened to speak of the vision of those who have already awakened, just as it is for one born...
To speak of the clear brightness of the heavenly sun to one who is blind: though they hear it, they cannot discern it.

One who has already attained awakening no longer treads the tracks of the unawakened; like one who has awakened from sleep, even if they were to recall the events of their dream, they cannot pursue them.
A student of the Way must take awakening as the standard. This is why awakening is essential.

Furthermore, this is difficult. Those who have not yet awakened must constantly maintain anxiety and mindfulness; those who have already awakened must all the more maintain and preserve [the realization].

It is like balancing water in a bowl, like holding a supreme treasure, like protecting one's own eyes, and like treading upon a precipice. It is as if one were in the presence of a sovereign or a teacher—this is the way of maintenance and preservation.
To "maintain and preserve" means to cultivate it. One cultivates only after having seen the Way; if the Way is not seen, what need is there for cultivation? Thus it was asked:
Someone said, "I have already attained awakening; why should I still practice? To this, he replied: "The habitual tendencies accumulated over many kalpas have not yet been suddenly eradicated;
one must simply continue to practice. Only when practice reaches the state of non-practice does one become equal to all Buddhas.
This is why practice is so difficult. Therefore, those who do not understand these four 'easies' may be made to do good deeds, but they cannot be made to enter the Way. Not...
"One who understands the four difficulties may be discussed with regarding the Way, but cannot be led forward on the Way" (and so forth).
The Master said: "The discourse on 'contemplating the Way' mentioned in the text is precisely what is meant today by 'investigation' (*chán*).

Regarding those four difficulties, the first states that faith is difficult. What is called 'faith' here refers to the desire for one to believe in the four easinesses preceding and the four difficulties following them."

However, this faith must be treated with utmost care and may not be obtained by mere chance. First, it relies upon the power of the *prajñā* (wisdom) cultivated through many lifetimes within one’s own being;

second, it relies upon the correct mindfulness that regards the great matter of birth and death as a pressing concern in every thought-moment of daily life, penetrating to the very marrow of one's bones without a moment’s interruption.
Furthermore, once faith is established in this manner, the koan one investigates becomes more urgent than the hunger of a starving man.
Those who are hungry shall obtain food; those who are cold shall obtain clothing. Even if one were to force them to abandon their pursuit, they could never be made to do so.
Their resolve to realize the Way is so continuous and dense that there will never be a time when they do not attain awakening. This is like traveling on a road:

advancing by morning and progressing by evening—how could there be any principle by which one would fail to arrive? What is meant by "attaining awakening"? It is simply the realization of the four preceding transformations. These are the four transformations.
If one has not attained awakening and entry, all such views are termed false understandings. People today, relying on their clever and intelligent dispositions, do not wait for awakening and entry;
they hastily grasp the doctrine of the "four easeful practices" within the confines of their conscious intellect and claim it as actual realization.

Consequently, they abandon the two adornments of merit and wisdom, with which it has no connection whatsoever. While their discourse on the ultimate principle is not necessarily incorrect, they fail to realize that they have never attained awakening.
One enters into and falls within the conceptualization of the measure of consciousness; this is like speaking of food all day long without relieving one's hunger.

Furthermore, if awakening is not genuine, it is like a person who has never personally reached their destination, yet wishes to conduct household affairs while still on the road—is this possible or not?
Thus, one knows that as long as the Way is not awakened to, its cultivation is difficult. It must be so.
Thus it is. One purpose is to instruct future students. Only the Venerable Foyin’s discourse on the "Four Easies and Four Difficulties" is profoundly clear and illuminating.
All those bodhisattvas who study Prajñāpāramitā have distanced themselves from all manner of worldly enjoyments and come here to willingly embrace solitude;
there is none among them who does not speak of the great matter of birth-and-death and impermanence. It is empty... [text ends]
To prolong the months and years—how could one bear to do such a thing? In the text it says: "It is like a cat catching a mouse;
if it falters for a moment, it loses the mouse. It is like a hen brooding over her eggs; if she pauses for a moment, they will not become seeds. These words are worthy of trust.

I hope you will all arouse your resolve and strive to awaken early, clarifying your own person and realizing the fundamental source. This summer, I have been bedridden with illness and was unable to engage in discussion with my elder brothers; therefore, I have cited this.
This is told to you: shadows and reflections flow like a stream; do not leave yourself with regret. Thus I speak.
To the assembly:
Dongshan crossing the water, Xuansha crossing the ridge, Taiyuan hearing the horn, and Śākyamuni beholding the morning star at midnight.
At this very same moment, it is present within each and every one of you, lacking not even a hair’s breadth.

In the past, Linji’s fierce shouts and Deshan’s painful blows were such that one could hardly bear to look upon them; yet they were held up directly before one’s face. Now they have fallen into the monastic groves and become mere conventional paths.
Throughout the monasteries of the world, people speak of Chan in great abundance, merely receiving echoes and grasping at shadows, deceiving one another. This is the medicine.
To this day, it has become even less efficacious. For thirty years, my late master stood firm as a wall;

he devoted himself solely to rectifying this matter for his students. He gripped them by the throat, neither wanting you to speak nor wanting you to understand, nor did he want you to give rise to a second thought.
He required you simply to plant your feet firmly upon the very phrase you were investigating, striving with unwavering diligence.
One must investigate with diligent effort, as if encountering a mortal enemy or rescuing one's own burning head. Cut off external conditions and forget internal emotions and consciousness.
Wait until the cold ashes suddenly crackle like beans popping; only then will you have passed through death and been revived anew.
If you have not yet reached this stage, you must never begrudgingly lead others into the weeds with mere superficial words. You must know that birth and death are impermanent.
This is a matter of great significance; how could it be something that those with shallow roots and limited capacity are able to transcend?
People today do not embody the teachings established by the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity; instead, they pursue their own wild emotions and deluded consciousness.

With every opening of their mouths, they claim to surpass the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Yet, when one observes their resolve toward the Way, there is not even a trace of genuine mastery. In a mere instant—

When one has grasped this "head-word" (*huatou*) for even a brief moment, one feels a private sense of celebration within; yet, as soon as one is disturbed and seized by dullness and distraction, one thinks only of how one's roots of the Way are dull and one's karmic afflictions are deep.
When encountering even a slight circumstance before one’s eyes that goes against one’s wishes, the heart immediately gives rise to resentment, malice, and hatred.
Grinding one's teeth and gnashing them, one’s thoughts continue without ceasing;

or, with perverse reflections and strange imaginings, myriad variations arise and perish while remaining unaware that one is maddened and intoxicated, falsely believing that such is how those who discern the Way ought to be.
Having played this game for three or five years without any resonance, a single thought of retreat suddenly arises, and one enters the armor of "nothingness," content to endure it.
Thus it is that those caught in the cycle of saṃsāra are as numerous as the waters of a rushing torrent.

If one does not act in this way, one will instead use the conscious mind to fish and hunt through antiquity and the present, swallowing the drool of foxes, deceiving the worthy and misleading the sages. Amidst myriad fabrications, there is but a single flavor of hollow pretension;
having fallen into that other realm, one remains unaware of it oneself. Yet if one seeks a state of true stability, thirty or twenty years may pass without [attaining it].

Transformation is not different [from the original]. In the previous inquiry, one who does not involve themselves with the objects of consciousness and takes awakening as the standard is like sifting through sand to select gold.
Yet, in these days, the Dharma-way of the monasteries has gradually become diluted and superficial.

Do you still know that today, opening wide both eyes, one receives the offerings of those who possess faith atop a solitary peak? How much more so for one who personally bears the burden of practicing the Way?
Even with such a human name, one still remains so deluded, arrogant, and indolent as to fail to exercise self-restraint.

How can one know that at another time one might flow into other realms and not be devoured by others, thereby forming karma for the Avīci Hell? The ancients spoke of the three miserable paths and the six destinies;
throughout immeasurable kalpas, it is certain that we have already experienced them all. In this present life, how does one know what past good deeds one has performed?

As they travel, they encounter one another on a narrow path, colliding beneath the seven-fold folds of the *kāṣāya*. Long ago, they were already unable to separate from their emotions or sever their anxieties, losing all sleep and forgetting to eat.
As for this fleeting time that passes like a crack in a wall, upon what can one rely? Since the opening of this mountain, it has been thus.
Encountering the cold of winter, I have set a time limit. I desire that all of you, within this period, must by all means seek a definitive resolution.
This is not a mere expedient device of mine, nor is it a forced exposition; rather, it is the tested method of the former masters for realizing the matter that each of you inherently possesses.
As it is said in the teachings: "I do not cherish my own body or life, but I only regret that [the Dharma]..."
I am instructing you on the Supreme Way. You see only how easy it was for those predecessors to cross the mountain and attain awakening upon hearing the horn;
yet you fail to realize the difficulty that existed before they had crossed the mountain or heard the horn. In this regard, they were no different from people today.
If one truly understands that difficulty, what Path would not gather within oneself? Because the Abbot and the Rector perceived that the minds of the assembly were becoming lax, they requested—
I urge you to be vigilant. The discourse of the Venerable Master Mingben is entirely devoid of pretension;

he merely exhorts those who take the true path as their goal toward the great matter of birth, death, impermanence, and reality. If my words are not believed upon being spoken, [they will be proven otherwise].
Leave it entirely for you to inquire of the various quarters.

Today, the fifteenth day of the fourth month, marks the commencement of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) at Shunxin Hermitage. You should know that two thousand years ago, on this very day at Vulture Peak, [the Buddha]...

At these assemblies, there was also the practice of "closing the summer retreat" on the fifteenth day of the fourth month. From that time until the present, this has been maintained throughout all monasteries without deviation from the ancient precedent.
For ninety days, one binds oneself without a rope—this is called "prohibiting the feet" (jinzu) and "summer retreat" (anju).
Yet they do not realize that for a practitioner of true substance, from the very first thought, the priority is to resolve the matter of birth-and-death and impermanence.
At the time of the Great Matter, this foot was bound here; this summer, it was completed through this.
Exhausting the years and months of one’s entire life, they are combined into ninety days—neither more nor less, neither deficient nor redundant.
One must certainly expect to achieve a direct, essential correspondence with this matter; only then is it called the season of the Buddha’s joy and the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*. Thus it is said.

That they do not entrust themselves [to the practice] is merely because they wish to emulate worldly customs in circulation; they adhere strictly to the rules of ritual and music, daring not to overstep them.
This is what is called "sitting out the summer retreat. Not only do they thus betray the Buddhas and Patriarchs, but many also bury their own true selves.
Today, having resided in this hermitage for over ten years, each member of the assembly knows that such a matter exists; none are willing to let themselves go to waste.
One would be buried in failure; how much more so now, at this time when the New Year of the Dharma has just arrived?

Seizing this opportunity, you must rouse yourself with a resolute, non-regressing, fierce, and uninterrupted mind of true body and spirit. You must single-mindedly take up this "meaningless" *huatou* (critical phrase).
From the very first day you establish your footing, you must not move it by even a hair’s breadth, maintaining it closely and continuously.
Proceed with this practice forward. You must see results day by day; you must see verification moment by moment.
From the first person at the head to the last person at the end, let one exhort and spur the other, and let each polish the other.

Do not allow external conditions to intermingle, do not act falsely, do not engage in idle chatter, and do not harbor divergent thoughts. Do not turn according to objects, do not shift following after sensory realms, and do not merely follow ancient patterns.
One does not establish new patterns; one neither loathes the ordinary nor admires the sage.
One does nothing at all, desiring only to clearly understand that single point within one’s own person.
Suddenly, when you are coldly and thoroughly penetrated through, you will know that ninety days are but a single lifetime, and a single lifetime is but ninety days—even up to two thousand years.
The past is no different from today; today is no different from two thousand years ago. Like interlocking hooks and rings, there is no interruption whatsoever.
This is what is called "this is the field for selecting Buddhas," the time of returning home having passed the examination with an empty mind. If it were otherwise, [it would not be so].
This very Shunxin Hermitage is no different from the two Iron Ring Mountains. Do not say that because you are in retreat there is nothing to do;
by observing the course of these nine months, one can foresee that the lifelong aspirations of this hermitage’s master have not been fulfilled.
The master has sent a letter requesting words of admonition for the assembly. To investigate this Great Matter, it is not only for the sake of the multitude, but for the master as well.
Take care of yourself.
Zen is the original face of all people. Apart from this, there is no other Zen to investigate; it is neither something that can be seen nor something that can be heard.
This very seeing and hearing is, in its entirety, Zen. Outside of Zen, there is likewise nothing else that can be seen or heard.
It can be attained. All of you are gathered here together; each of you has a single unresolved koan that is hidden within your very vitals—a matter no small one.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, do not err in your application of mind. An ancient said: "To practice Zen and study the Way is to apply the mind erroneously;
to seek to become a Buddha or an ancestral patriarch is to apply the mind erroneously. Aside from these, what else is there to do?"
This is not called a mistaken application of the mind. Let us set this matter aside for now and not inquire further.
Simply consider that each person has their own copy of the Ancient Rules of Purity within their own breast; do not trample upon its crops.

For instance, when the board sounds at the hall at the fifth watch to signal the time for *can* (meditative inquiry), even if you do not wish to wash your face, you must follow the assembly down to the ground.
Once this is finished, when waiting for the assembly to enter the hall, one ascends to one’s seat and sits upright.

Upon hearing the board signaling the end of silence, one folds the blanket, dons the *kāṣāya*, and proceeds to the bowl-position to eat the gruel. Whenever eating gruel or rice, one must observe the seniority of the assembly;
if they are quick, one is quick, and if they are slow, one is slow. In this way, one avoids disturbing the thoughts of others. This is especially so when rising.
In every state—whether abiding, moving, or remaining still—one must follow the appropriate dignified conduct (*vīrya*).

Do not say, "I am a man of realization; one who has attained great enlightenment is not bound by minor details. Alas, what can you do? You have not yet realized it. As for those among us who do not follow the rules and regulations, there is no other reason than this:

their correct mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) regarding the Way is not earnest. Consequently, their actions become coarse and crude, they violate the monastic precepts (*vinaya*), and they lose themselves.
This very cause gives rise to the contempt of others. Each of you must examine yourselves individually, according to the method of inspecting the hall.

Since the great matter of birth and death has not yet been clearly realized, act as if fearing that time is being wasted in vain; even if struck by another, do not ask whether you yourself are weary or not, but receive it like drinking nectar.
You must rouse courageous vigor and press forward with all your might—how could this be otherwise?
To turn back and harbor resentment, nursing a grudge for vengeance—is this not contrary to reason?
That birth and death are impermanent is but a single segment of evil habit that cannot be severed by the blade for ten thousand kalpas nor cut through by the saw.

Today, having been willing to give rise to this initial true mind, you dwell high atop the peak of poverty and cold; I cannot bear that you should wish for a single day’s passage of time to be extended into ten days.
Settle yourself firmly and go forth. Whenever you see the sun setting behind the mountains, give rise to deep regret and lamentation: "Yet another day has passed;
my spiritual practice remains unaccomplished. When the light of my eyes falls to the ground [at death], with what will I ultimately repay the Buddhas, the Patriarchs, and the donors?"
"You will simply end up with your hands flailing and feet stumbling. Why not, while today’s illness has not yet reached your very bones, seek out a definitive resolution early on?
(Mingben) "The Venerable One’s view is like this; you do not understand how to untangle the entanglements for others.

It is merely this. I have told you from the perspective of ultimate reality. Originally, I intended to listen to everyone’s discourse on the 'Hermitage Way' (Guandao), but just now there was someone from the Western Mountain."
As you depart, I trouble the Abbot once more to convey these words on my behalf: each of you must investigate your own minds with earnestness; do not treat this lightly.

I hope you will carefully compose your spirits and seek liberation at an early date. Furthermore, do not listen to those who suggest crossing waters or traversing mountains to visit one another at random times; such actions provide no benefit for the Way.

To show his fellow students, he stood on one foot to praise the Buddha, cast away his body to seek a verse, and relinquished his royal throne to beg for alms; all these were merely ways the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" (the Buddha) devised as examples for those who would come after.
The various patriarchs of old wore robes of grass and grime upon their faces, drinking from mountain streams and eating from trees, moving...
This person has spent a lifetime without associating with the world, maintaining a sense of awe and diligence to bear this Way upon his shoulders.
Reflect on this: how could it be difficult for us today? Even for the ancients, it was not easy. How fortunate we are to have been born within this Dharma;
our admiration for the ancients increases day by day, doubling with each passing kalpa. How can we remain complacent, eating at leisure, and indulge in wanton emotions and dissipation?
This is a teaching that is of no benefit. It would be a betrayal of the aspirations of our predecessors. Time passes in an instant, yet the law of cause and effect is unmistakably clear.
Each of you must investigate your own mind so as not to leave room for future regret.
I show those dwelling in the mountains that in studying the Way, the only essential is to possess the great resolve of deeply contemplating birth, death, and impermanence, without ever retreating.
If this mind does not retreat, there will be no one who fails to clarify the Great Matter. This very non-retreat regarding the great matter of birth and death—this itself is [the Way].
This is the foremost skillful means; there is no skillful means that surpasses this. The Way exists in all places, yet the Way does not exist in any place.
It is simply that you do not retreat from the great matter of birth and death.

Whether in cities or mountain forests, whether dwelling alone or amidst a multitude, these are all times for advancing on the Way. As long as you possess this single mind directed toward the great matter of birth and death—
If one is earnest yet lacks steadfastness and rigor, then in the city one will be plundered by the clamor, and in the mountains and forests one will be obstructed by stillness.
Living alone, one’s mouth and stomach will press upon one another; gathering in a crowd, one is beset by the conditions of right and wrong. In such mutual entanglement, neither state is harmonious.
Therefore, the ancients said: "There is no secret formula for practicing Chan; it simply requires that the matter of birth and death be urgent. This refers to the great matter of birth and death.

Be sincere and earnest; remain steadfast for a long time without retreating. Even if you spend your entire life begging for food at the crossroads, it will all be the moment of attaining the "degree" through the emptiness of mind.
Now that you three are dwelling in the mountains, simply do not engage in any artificial fabrication.
Eat rice when there is rice; eat congee when there is no rice. Whether your practice succeeds or fails, your Way-work will be accomplished.
Success or failure is not determined by anything else; it depends solely on your own mind. Ultimately, it cannot be obtained from another.
To the assembly who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta:
"Bodhicitta" is a Sanskrit term; in this language, it means "the mind of the Way. If you all lack the mind directed toward the Way, today—

They are utterly unwilling to come here to this high, towering mountain peak, where they must wear out their trousers and pants through diligent toil day and night to investigate the mystery of life and death.
You should know that this path-seeking mind has already been awakened since many kalpas past;

it is only because the mind has been largely indolent and the will has pursued external conditions that one has not yet attained realization. Now that you have reached this juncture, you should properly sever all [entanglements].
Relying on this condition, rest all worldly concerns and single-mindedly raise the koan you have been assigned. Exhaust your very life beneath the three rafters;
to resolve it in a single lifetime is not considered beyond your capacity.

If you cannot maintain this right mindfulness with firmness, density, and diligent perseverance, yet instead allow deluded thoughts to arise even for a moment, wishing to generate the bodhicitta once more, this is called "vain delusion."
This is perversion. Forgetting right mindfulness and seeking outwardly, one turns one's back on the true mind and becomes utterly estranged from the Way.

Do not speak of merely generating the bodhicitta once; even if one were to generate it a thousand or ten thousand times a day, it would not equal a single moment of maintaining the very right mindfulness of what you are investigating.
Furthermore, any desire to recite sutras, prostrate, or perform elaborate confessions is entirely a pursuit of...
To follow delusions and deviant paths—is this not what the teachings say? "If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
You should know that even the true mark is without thought. This is simply because you believe in the great matter of birth and death;

throughout the twelve periods of the day, you must maintain the phrase you are investigating as if your head were on fire. As for the shadow of one who contemplates the true mark, it is like having someone... [who is] illusory.
The signs of these characters are deceptive; one will willingly fall forever into the Hell of the Severed Tongue. I request that you inform the assembly of the guest hall:
those who wish to resolve to attain Bodhicitta should each relinquish [their attachments] and focus their minds exclusively on discerning the Way. This is my humble submission. Respectfully.
A Teaching to the Disciples on Winter Retreat:
Early this morning, I was unexpectedly visited by the Head Seat (Shouzuo), who informed me that the long-term retreat is about to conclude as the winter solstice approaches.

This serves as a timely exhortation to inspire the assembly, for their hearts are filled with longing and aspiration. Indeed, the seasonal proclamations of the various quarters possess great scope and scale; yet, [the approach of] our own Abbot...
My own practice and understanding are entirely deficient; moreover, I have never before assumed such a stance.
Ordinarily, when fellow practitioners have not yet clarified the great matter of birth and death, they compare their respective views with one another, which is nothing more than mutual exhortation.
Today, I cannot help but add further annotations. I reflect deeply upon how our late Master, the Old Monk, for...
For twenty or thirty years, he has remained deeply immersed in this great matter within remote mountains, offering nothing but a "meaningless" *hwadu* for others to chew upon.
He resolutely refuses to follow the various quarters [of the Chan school] by teaching people to grasp understanding through conventional, ready-made, or superficial language.
One should know that this matter of life and death is a singular instance of self-delusion and self-entanglement throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Delusive habits—past and present—along with the eight consciousnesses and five aggregates, shift and flow from moment to moment. They arise as love and hatred;
they move as subject and object. Adhering to the bones and stitching through the marrow, they persist to the very end of the future, never having a time of self-realization.
If one does not rouse a single piece of resolute, true faith to awaken beneath the heels, all other efforts will fall into the heterodox.
Consequently, students were unable to avoid falling into dullness and drifting into distraction.

Therefore, eighty days were established as a long-term period, with the aim that practitioners would eliminate mental discursive thoughts, cleanse external conditions, sever deluded attachments, and remain pure and unmixed, single-mindedly investigating this very matter.
The term "period" (*ki*) here carries the sense of a mutual agreement; it signifies that one must certainly achieve completion within this time.
To take the Buddha as one’s ancestor, one must resolve to pass the imperial examination; to empty the mind, one must resolve to transcend birth and death;
to continue the Buddha’s wisdom-life, one must resolve to do so. If one does not correspond to these resolutions, it means one has failed within this period of eighty days.
Yet, one will not begrudgingly or dejectedly give up; one must achieve a decisive breakthrough once and for all, lest one’s coming here from the world in solitude be rendered fruitless.
At the summit of this peak, people shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel guard against this desolate cold. Tracing its origins, how could it have begun only today?

Two thousand years ago, during the time when the Great Dharma Wheel was turned at Vulture Peak across more than three hundred assemblies, the entire assembly present heard and received [the teachings] clearly from the lips of the Elder Śākyamuni.
This continued even through the four groups of seven patriarchs in India and the two... in this land.
When the various great patriarchs sang and recited to one another, everyone was invariably present.
Perhaps you lack this profound and fundamental basis; today you certainly cannot cultivate a great mind or harbor a vast resolve.
To resolve the causal conditions of this great matter of birth and death, you must seize favorable opportunities from this day forward. Otherwise, you will merely remain idle and indolent.

Day after day, having lingered until this moment without yet attaining transcendental awakening, how could one have known that today was the time to encounter this opportunity for realization through fixed commitment?
One must no longer merely apply forceful attention to the kōan one has been investigating, but must exhaust one's entire physical being to investigate it thoroughly.
It is like a single person facing ten thousand enemies; one must seek liberation early. Yet, one is further obstructed by long-standing habits of indolence and laziness.

Just as one might run back to a meditation cushion, tucking both feet into one's trousers, drawing both fists into the chest, and wrapping the entire body in a paper quilt—knowing only comfort and failing to realize that exhaustion has arrived. Its...
The hall monitors have alerted and admonished you three or five times, yet you are utterly unwilling to apply even a slight degree of diligence.

If you practice Zen in this manner, claiming you wish to clarify the mind-ground, confront birth and death, cast off the dust of worldly emotions, and eradicate habitual patterns—do not speak of eighty days;
even if it were eighty years or eighty kalpas, you would only increase your karmic consciousness and deepen your delusion.
To retreat while seeking to advance—how could one ever reach the distant goal? Is this how those who aspire to overcome a single person or ten thousand adversaries should act?

Is it not rather like one whose head is on fire? From this, it can be verified that the spiritual practice (*dharma-karma*) of such people will certainly not be accomplished. Why is this? This place is the solitary peak, the very summit.
There is not a single external condition [to rely upon]. Furthermore, each and every one of us has given rise to a mind that seeks the great matter of birth and death with sincerity.
If one cannot exert oneself at this very moment, when will there ever be another time to do so?
Unless one truly investigates and truly awakens to this matter, everything else is merely empty flattery. Nowadays, there are many such people who cite...
The *Song of Realizing the Way* and the *Inscription on Faith* represent the ultimate discourse on principle by the ancients.
For those who have not yet attained realization, when they hear such words as "Right now, who is it that moves the mouth?

they immediately attempt to grasp them with their conscious intellect and harbor them in their minds, identifying these external objects (*pratyaya*) as their original face. Furthermore, they are told to remain entirely ordinary and without affairs.

To depart from this is called "preservation" and "practice. To speak of "examining the critical phrase" (*kōan*) as a method of cultivation is to hastily cite the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on the Mind of Faith), which states:
"If one grasps it with excessive rigidity, one will surely enter a deviant path. Yet you insist that the "Direct Pointing" and "Single Transmission" involve no such thing.
You fail to consider that those of inferior capacity and faculties must have their emotional delusions dried up and their hidden thefts of the mind exhausted before they can proceed.

With the mind directed toward a precipice ten thousand fathoms high, one casts off one's hands into the void. Yet, this is merely intended to cause one to remain mired in dregs and water, identifying with existence and identifying with emptiness;
it is entirely self-deception and is certainly not ultimate. This venerable Abbot has, throughout his life, never even dreamt of this Way.
However, he has always believed that the great matter of birth and death is no small cause or condition. Today, on this narrow path, we have met.
Feng, unaware of his own prolixity, has here spoken what is beyond compare; I hope all will take note.
Addressing the assembly:
Last evening, the Head Seat and the Rector came to the hermitage and said, "The summer retreat is approaching; we request that you preach for the sake of the community."
I have long intended to find a moment’s leisure in the next two or three days to invite you to my hut for a cup of tea and to converse for a short while, so that we might mutually exhort one another.
I did not expect that we would encounter continuous rain and slippery roads, making it inconvenient;
thus twelve days have passed, and now the affairs of both mountains are again entangled with one another, preventing me from fulfilling this intention.
The illusory person harbors a mind of distant avoidance. Consider this: the great assembly gathered here in the hall are all practitioners who have reached the end of their studies.

On ordinary occasions when they come to the hermitage, there is never a time when the matters upon the meditation cushion are not mutually engaged. How could there be a distinction between the beginning and conclusion of the summer retreat as a specific period for discerning the Way?
If one speaks from the perspective of ultimate truth, at the very moment one first resolved to turn toward the Way, this summer had already been entered.
It is understood. Throughout the twelve hours of the day, one contemplates a koan—a phrase devoid of meaning—that has not yet been resolved;

this is precisely the time of "sitting out the summer retreat. After thirty or twenty years of pushing against it until spirit is exhausted and consciousness is spent, one suddenly attains a sharp awakening in a state of cold clarity;
this is the time of "breaking the summer" and the day of *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence). How could it be based on such trivialities?
Let ninety days be the limit. Generally speaking, when one's practice of the Way lacks efficacy, it is usually because the "thieving mind" has not yet died out;
thus, one merely wastes time and months without any other underlying ailment. If the thieving mind dies today, then this very day you will attain resonance.
If it dies tomorrow, then tomorrow you will attain resonance. What is meant by the "thieving mind"?
To see a "self" apart from the very place where one has set aside the fundamental matter—that is a stolen mind.
To see a person or a self apart from the self that is being perceived—that is a stolen mind. When one’s practice becomes proficient, to know it as proficiency is a stolen mind.
When one’s practice is not yet proficient, to know it as lack of proficiency is a stolen mind. Face-to-face...
When one previously perceives the presence of dullness or distraction, this is a "thieving mind.
When one does not perceive dullness or distraction, but only when the phrase under investigation (*huatou*) and the state of doubt are intertwined without interruption, this too is a "thieving mind.
However, if at the moment of observing the *huatou* even a single thought arises—regardless of whether it is ordinary or sagely, genuine or spurious—it is all termed [a thieving mind].

All of these are but thieving minds. Suddenly, there may be a clever person who says that none of what I have said matters at all, and seeks another path for themselves as their Way, their principle, their view, or their learning. This, too, is the "thieving mind within a thieving mind."
Even the Buddha cannot provide a cure for this. You have merely exhausted yourself pursuing so many thieving minds;
you simply must rely on your own fundamental nature and take up the koan you are investigating.
Be like a person carved from clay or wood—a living corpse—neither seeing the great assembly outside nor seeing a self within. Remain cold and still, cutting off all sight and sound. Guard it thus.
After a long time, you will surely attain the "Passing of the Heart" (the highest degree). I have written this at random to serve as the topic for tea-discourse in the hermitage.
Layman Ben, please go to the mountain for a few days to avoid worldly affairs; there is no need to search for the traces of illusion to see where they reside.
Even if you were to find them, I would not speak with you. I trust that the Head Seat and the Rector will convey this to him.
The *Nichi-shi shuchū* (Daily Essentials for Knowing) states that within the teachings there are the first watch of the day, the middle watch of the day, and the last watch of the day;

furthermore, there are the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, and the last watch of the night—this is what the ancient masters referred to as "three periods by day and three by night. It further says: "When the day is insufficient, it is followed by the night. This is the fundamental [principle].
The stream of the Path of Form flows on; not a single moment of time is wasted, nor is one ever separated from it for even an instant.
Throughout the six periods of day and night, how could there be no support? That which is called "daily support" refers generally to the standard practice during the twelve periods (two sets of six).

Whenever one sits in meditation four times throughout a single day and night, one should each time withdraw the mind, sever all discursive thoughts, forget external conditions, and still the mindfulness, deeply investigating the nature of birth and death until the power of the Way is exhausted.

Regarding duties: apart from the necessity of attending to the calls of nature, it is not permitted to converse, nor to wash clothes, nor to mend them, nor to read or study, nor to engage in any other worldly affairs;
even communal labor for the public domain is not permitted.

In all matters—whether ascending or descending from the bed, leaving the hall or entering a room—one must act as if walking on thin ice or standing by a deep precipice, ensuring that one does not disturb or alert those in neighboring quarters.
Regarding his mind of the Way, it spontaneously accorded with both internal and external conditions; body and mind were silent and still.

Once, while Jingxiao was passing by his door with a fellow practitioner, they sat together through the night until dawn. Jingxiao suddenly said, "I have traveled from afar across thousands of li beyond my native land..."
My parents have reached the twilight of their years, yet it has been twelve years since I last beheld their voices or countenances.
While reading the twenty chapters of Master Mingjiao’s *Treatise on Filial Piety*, I could not help but feel a sense of regret regarding their boundless toil; how can I ever repay them?

I said: "In the world, parents toward their children both nourish them and love them; therefore, the sages and worthies instruct them in filial piety (*xiao*). Now, *xiao* means 'to emulate' (*xiao*).
One emulates what they were nourished with and repays them by nourishing them; one emulates what they were loved with and repays them by loving them.
Thus, there is nothing more profound in filial piety than nourishment, and nothing more ultimate than love. However, as for the manner of nourishing them—"
The Way has two aspects, and the Way of Affection likewise has two. To feed with rich delicacies and clothe with furs and hemp is to nourish the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
To regulate by pure prohibitions and cultivate through merit and goodness is to nourish the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Nourishing the physical body accords with human relations; nourishing the Dharma-nature accords with the principles of Heaven. Although these two, though [practiced by] sages and worthies...

These two cannot be practiced simultaneously; this is because of the difference between the householder and the renunciant. Furthermore, for a householder not to provide for the nourishment of the physical body would be unfilial;
for a renunciant not to provide for the nourishment of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) would likewise be unfilial. Thus, it is said that there are two ways of providing nourishment.
To be attentive at dusk and to inspect oneself at dawn, never daring to leave [one’s parents] by their side for even a moment—this refers to that which has form.
This is love. Walking, one practices it; sitting, one investigates it. One vows to exhaust one’s physical form and complete one’s life to realize the Way.
Yet, that which one wishes to repay as a debt of gratitude is this formless love. Formed love is near and easy to become familiar with;
formless love is distant and difficult to approach. If one cannot take this love as the foundation, then even that which is near will remain merely so.
If one cannot even reach this, how much less so for that which is distant and difficult to approach? These two conditions—the easy and the difficult—cannot be attained simultaneously;
this is the distinction between the worldly and the world-transcending. To fail to exhaust the love for that which has form in the world is unfilial;
to fail to exhaust the love for that which is formless in the world-transcending realm is likewise unfilial. This is called the Way of Love.
Secondly, there is a distinction between emulating the worldly forms of nourishment and affection, and emulating the world-transcending forms of nourishment and affection.
Why is this? That which is called "having a distinction" means that one practices while one's parents are alive, but there is a lapse once they have passed away.
That which is called "having no distinction" does not mean that the survival or death of those parents creates a duality in my resolve to study the Way. For the parents are merely the physical form.
This is the fundamental basis of birth. Furthermore, does my physical form exist only in this present life?
Reflecting on the accumulation of kalpas up to the present, as I transmigrate through the three realms, the number of times I have received a body is as incalculable as dust motes and grains of sand.

As for what is called the fundamental basis of the birth of the body, it fills the universe and pervades the entire realm; when one encounters it through sight or hearing, how can one know that it is not the fundamental basis of my past lives?
When one calculates their toil and labor, it is truly beyond reckoning.

That I have failed to consider how to repay them and have instead burdened my parents—causing them to enter the various realms and undergo the full cycle of saṃsāra—is something I have largely remained unaware of until now.

Therefore, our Sage, through the gate of great compassion, crossed the royal city at night and dwelt on high amidst the snow-clad peaks, in order to clarify and proclaim the nourishment of the Dharma-nature.

This formless love is displayed for the sake of instructing people. Although the answers and questions spanning forty-nine years are vast and boundless in their flow, there is no word therein that does not originate from this.
Thus it is said: "While wandering through the three realms, one cannot abandon affectionate love;
to cast aside such affection and enter into non-action is truly the way of one who repays kindness. This is indeed true.
That is deception. The Way is filial piety; filial piety is the Way.
To wish to study the Way without knowing how to practice filial piety is like seeking water by turning one's back to a damp place. Someone might say, "I am unable to participate in this Way;
can I simply be called filial if I provide for my physical body and care for that which has form? I replied, "This is merely [the practice] of those living at home..."

This is filial piety. As for the filial piety of the world, those of our school do not participate in it, because we have cast our tracks at the gate of empty stillness and covered our forms beneath square-cut robes.
Yet even regarding the filial piety of the Great Sage appearing in the world on the Snowy Mountains, we are still unable to approximate even a ten-thousandth part of it.
If there is an interruption of even a single thought-moment, both self-benefit and benefit for others are lost. This is what is meant by "not..."
There is no filial piety greater than this; therefore, the purpose for which the *Mingjiao* (Clarifying the Teachings) was composed is to manifest our Sage’s supramundane filial piety to the world.
This is so that those of external teachings cannot disparage our followers, and also so that those among our own ranks who have not yet understood may cherish these teachings and incline toward them.
The Way must not be forgotten for even a moment. Some may say that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) blends self and other so thoroughly that no distinction ever exists;

how then can there be what is called filial piety? I replied: "You merely know that mirror-wisdom is non-dual, yet you do not realize that filial piety and the Way, as well as love and nourishment, are likewise both non-dual.
Unless one possesses a divine mind that has attained expansive awakening and penetrates through to the very depths..."
The source from which the Sages bestowed their teachings is not to be subject to private speculation.
If one chooses [to understand] by means of these words, one may perhaps see that my participation in this study is not in vain.
At Mount Tianmu, the Buddha’s radiance was revealed as a sacred rite,
and the great assembly beheld once more the Pure Jewel-Eye of the Great Ocean of our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Together with the Bodhisattvas,
Mahā-Ārhatas, and the Adamantine True Eye, their interlacing lights formed a lattice like a net of jade threads, stretching continuously through antiquity.
Is the continuity now unbroken? If you have not yet understood, the Venerable Mingben is revealing it today.
At Lion’s Rock, when the sun reaches its zenith at midday, the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand forms all rise in dance;

the halls and pavilions of the True Lineage open leaning against the heavens, and this single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa shines through ancient and modern times. Long ago, within the sky-reaching thorns and brambles, the Buddha-Sun established [the Dharma].
In this field of movement, the various patrons have opened up the most numinous treasury within these newly established regulations. The golden image requires no plastering;

the white jade hair does not need the labor of the axe. The clouds, forests, springs, and rocks of the Tianmu Mountains, stretching over three thousand *zhang*, and the red cliffs and green ridges, suddenly gain renewed spirit.
From the four quarters and ten thousand *li* away, the dragon-like elephants now possess iron-strong backs.
The beam and the meditation board or grass mat serve as host and guest to one another; within the Great Luminous Treasury, not even a speck of dust stands apart.
The body of the pure Dharma-realm seeks no companion. Now, how can a single phrase that reveals this truth be fully expressed?
"The Sage Ruler’s merit and longevity fill the heavens and earth; the radiance of the ancient Buddhas pervades the universe."
Cease immediately; the Way-person’s cessation is immediate. It does not wait for morning or evening, nor for spring or autumn. This cessation does not allow a second thought to intervene;
it fully gathers the faculty within this very thought. Someone asks: "By what means can the Way-person cease so swiftly? [How to end] the wheel of birth and death?"
It revolves like the hub of a wheel. I regret from the past my refusal to rest; I have been needlessly bound and constrained by the sufferings of worldly toil. Even now, I am still unwilling to rest;
the horse of the mind and the monkey of emotion cannot be penned. Chasing sounds and pursuing forms like leaping pellets, the pivot of the mechanism turns in an instant, leaving no trace to be found.
If I do not rest now, when will I ever rest? Vigorous youth does not stay, flowing away like water.
Throughout past and present, how many have not yet found rest? Skulls pile up like mountain ranges. Rest! Rest again! Rest once more!

Even if one were in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, who would care for the southern continent of Jambudvīpa? Simply by taking up this single word "Great Rest," one becomes a peer for ten thousand ages.
Have you not seen how two thousand years ago, the descendant of the sugarcane clan entered the Snowy Mountains?
Unable to drag it along, he regards wealth and honor as mere ice flowers; he no longer strikes at the clamor of the three realms.
From that time until now, he has been in a state of total rest. Gold wraps his face and adorns his body; a thousand-petaled red lotus supports his two feet.
Unstained by the dust of worldly afflictions, one should rest immediately; yet to come back from there is not early enough.
If one does not rest right now, it is all in vain and leads only to vexation. When both the mundane and supramundane are simultaneously brought to rest, only then does one reach the path of Bodhi.
When even the path of Bodhi is fully exhausted, it too is empty—white clouds crush the peaks of Mount Sumeru. In the end, one need not even become a Buddha; let the four seas [wash away all traces].
He raises the true wind to awaken those who are mired in the confusion of their cognitive nature;
he surely intends for them to attain awakening regarding the afflictions of body and mind, and he surely intends for them to attain joy.
In a state of stupor, the twelve classes of beings arise from it; through afflictions, eighty thousand kalpas continue because of it.
When awakening reaches its zenith, it is like the sun shining in the midst of the sky: the Dharma-realm is illuminated not by expectation, yet it is illuminated.
When joy arrives, it is like spring returning to a cold valley: grasses and trees sprout not by expectation, yet they sprout. People know only that awakening and joy are divine gifts.
They follow inferior paths and compete to seek them, not realizing that confusion and delusion (*mūḍha*) are the source of awakening, and that afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root of joy.

If one can reach this source and strike its root, then upon arriving at the state where afflictions, confusion, awakening, and joy all abide nowhere, one attains great awakening and great joy within that state of non-abiding.
It is perfectly encompassing without exterior and fills all things without limit.
Furthermore, it is like a spring emerging from the earth and coming to rest in a pond: it is clear without being settled, pure without being filtered;
it mirrors the myriad phenomena and receives the ten directions of space in its entirety. When touched by the wind, it ripples; when met with a breach, it flows.
Yet the essence of its tranquil depth fundamentally abides nowhere, yet there is nowhere it does not abide. Thus spoke Chief Seat Yishan, who had cleared away the brush to establish his hermitage.
In the midst of a secluded valley, he was just then distressed by the lack of water. Soon thereafter, a spring gushed forth from the earth.
He then named the spring "Awakening Joy" (Juexi). I, therefore, presented my previous argument and further told him:

"If those who are defiled may wash here, those who are thirsty may drink here, and those who approach may gaze into it as a mirror, then there shall be none who do not obtain this Awakening Joy. The guest said:
Your argument understands that [the spring] but does not understand this [principle]. Why is this? For awakening is self-delight, and delight is self-awakening.
If my spring truly possessed even a hair’s breadth of intention to cause that awakening and delight, it would be slandering my spring.
"To say that I, the Well, have no intention of awakening to joy is also to slander me. Yet, who in the world can discern this? I said:
'If that is so, then is such a speaker slandering me or not? After a long while, we drew water from the well to brew tea; sitting together, we forgot all words.
The moon filled the empty window, its light penetrating to the bottom of the ripples. At that moment, I experienced joy."
As for these matters, it is no longer possible to deliberate upon their merits or faults.

To exhort the recollection of Amitābha Buddha is to realize that this very mind is the Buddha and this very mind creates the Buddha; the Buddhas of the three periods of time have all testified to this mind-Buddha.
The sentient beings of the six realms are originally Buddhas; It is only because of delusion and ignorance that they refuse to believe in the Buddha.
The wise awaken and realize their nature to become Buddhas. The World-Honored One Śākyamuni taught the recitation of the name of Amitābha, who has the vow to welcome and guide those who recite it.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva bears the Buddha upon the crown of his head.
The Bodhisattva Śrīkṣetra embraces those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha; the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude all do so because of mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Buddhas of the six directions collectively praise mindfulness of the Buddha; the Patriarchs who established the teachings exhort people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The shortcut dharma-gate exists only in mindfulness of the Buddha; every one of the lineage masters of a single era practices mindfulness of the Buddha.
The famous sages of all times, each and every one, recited the Buddha’s name. Now that I have the karmic affinity to encounter this practice, I shall recite the Buddha’s name;

I shall recite the Buddha’s name with mindfulness, and with mindfulness of the mind, I shall recite the Buddha’s name. My mouth shall constantly recite the Buddha’s name; my mind shall constantly revere the Buddha; my eyes shall constantly contemplate the Buddha;
my ears shall constantly listen for the Buddha; my body shall constantly prostrate to the Buddha; and my nose shall constantly count the Buddha’s names.
Constantly make offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, and candles to the Buddha; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, do not depart from mindfulness of the Buddha.
In suffering or joy, in adversity or favor, do not forget mindfulness of the Buddha. Whether putting on clothes or eating food, there is nothing that is not the Buddha;
in every place and at every moment, the Buddha is present. Movement is the Buddha, and stillness is the Buddha.
Busyness is Buddha, leisure is Buddha; horizontal is Buddha, vertical is Buddha;
good is Buddha, evil is Buddha; birth is Buddha, death is Buddha.
Every thought is Buddha, every mind is Buddha. When impermanence arrives, it is precisely the right time to recite the Buddha’s name.
Casting off all attachments, one proceeds directly home to see the Buddha; this single circle of light is the Buddha of the emptiness of nature.
To realize this single thought-moment is what is called "Buddha. The Buddha of Infinite Life is eternally abiding and indestructible;
the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Transformation-body are of one and the same essence. Ten thousand Buddhas and a thousand Buddhas are all one and the same Buddha.
I universally exhort all who have the karmic affinity to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. If the Buddha does not contemplate the Buddha, one loses the Original Buddha;
greed, anger, and jealousy cause one to lose their own Buddha. Alcohol, lust, wealth, and arrogance defile the Celestial True Buddha;
the six thieves of self, others, right, and wrong plunder the Buddha. When this single breath departs, where will you seek the Buddha?
Those in the hells and the three miserable paths shall never again hear of the Buddha; Through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, they will regret not having recited the Buddha’s name.
I earnestly exhort you all to recite the Buddha within yourselves; Hasten to turn the light back within, and cease seeking the Buddha elsewhere.
If every thought is unclouded, who is not the Buddha? May all people take refuge in the Buddha themselves.
Dedicate merit toward the Western Land and make vows to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; at the time of death,
personally behold the transformation Buddhas and the lotus pedestals of the nine grades, pay homage to Amitābha Buddha, attain unimpeded vision to see the Buddhas of the ten directions,
and dwell in the Pure Land.
Seven layers of tree shadows cover the azure clouds; nine grades of lotus wombs nurture white blossoms.
Even iron walls and silver mountains cannot block them—why do sentient beings seek the boundless elsewhere?
Vast and boundless, the triple world rolls in dust; a single thought of craving for life is the cause of suffering. The Unsurpassed Dharma King’s compassionate vow is urgent;
he still extends his golden arm far and wide.
Throughout the entire morning, one joins the palms and recollects Amitābha; yet in the mere interval of a single thought, one has already missed the mark.
Cast this very thought away entirely, and with total spontaneity and singular liberation, leave the suffering of Saṃsāra behind.
The waters of the forty-eight vows merge with water; the skies of over a hundred thousand leagues unite with sky. Only the sounds and forms before one's eyes stand as a barrier;
when will the two lands, East and West, truly be joined?
A fine man, complete in the six arts; throughout the hall, they call out to one another in all-day intoxication.
If you wish to know how not to fall into the pit of saṃsāra, do not fail this golden body sixteen feet tall.
In twelve periods of time, the opportunity has not yet dawned; through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, suffering remains difficult to escape.
Although one’s body dwells within the same Sahā world, who would be willing to bow their head and pay homage to the jade-like radiance?
Layer upon layer, towering golden pavilions excel; tier upon tier, magnificent white jade ponds are adorned. How many sentient beings fail to dream of reaching them?
Yet they remain bound by the cauldrons, boiling water, and burning coals.
Śrī-Ābhāsvara constantly says, "Mother, do not forget your child; we are like form and shadow, never separated.
Yet, pitying himself, he alone is Amitābha Buddha, yet he instead casts a golden mask over his face.
I look up and knock upon the realm of my future parents; the Teacher points afar toward the West. It is not for lack of money that I cannot buy straw sandals;
I only regret that the path to my hometown is so easy to forget.
A single ancient Buddha, vast as the heavens; four-colored flower-pools, as expansive as the sea. It is simply that sentient beings lack the power of vision;
yet when the occasion arises, there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation.
Birth, Old Age, Sickness, and Death (Five Summary Verses) Enmeshed by the bonds of love and affection, one thus comes;
The three conditions harmonize and unite to dwell within the womb. The primordial chaos is pierced open, leaving the entire body riddled with flaws;
Empty space is trampled through, filling the face with dust. Life is like a dangling thread as mother and child are parted; The physical form is like a floating bubble, revealing its true nature.
As an infant, I suddenly forgot the suffering amidst the heaps of red and white; drawn back by worldly ties, I once again wore a smile upon my cheeks.
Now that I am old, I sigh to myself all day long, suddenly realizing that my karmic conditions have grown remote from the world. When people speak nearby, I do not hear—their ears are deaf;
at night, there is no sleep, and my solitary heart is lonely. My spirit is secretly depleted as my skin first begins to wrinkle, and my physical strength is imperceptibly dissipated within my bones.
All withered and dry. I recall again how in my youth my wildness had not yet ceased; who would have known that today I would expend such effort?
Having momentarily failed in self-cultivation, the conditions of illness have invaded me; having not yet consulted a skilled physician, the ailment grows deeper by the day.

As the lamp’s shadow sinks into the void, loneliness increases; the sound of rain beating upon the pillow aids my moaning. When meeting people, my only words are requests for medicine; facing the world, I am listless and alone.
Clutching the quilt, this mass of suffering conceals the Dharma of peace and joy;
it is only fit for lamentation and cannot be endured. Fire, wind, earth, and water suddenly part ways. This is precisely the time when the year ends and the age concludes.

Within the mouth, the three-inch breath has abruptly vanished; before one's eyes, there remain but myriad wonders. Karma arises from the transformations of consciousness and is not bestowed by others; the soul follows conditions as it flies away.
I know this for myself: having cast off the skin-bag of the empty aggregates, where in the vast three realms shall I go?

What causes birth, death, old age, and sickness to arise? This physical form, entangled in shame, has persisted from antiquity to the present. When encountering objects, I am unable to give rise to thoughts of existence;
when meeting with conditions, I refuse to settle into a state of non-mind. Karma is accumulated within ultimate emptiness; suffering, from the very beginning, is not real.
Abiding in the deep, a blink of an eye sinks one into ten million kalpas; how could you allow such precious time to pass in vain?

Resolve your will single-mindedly upon the path of "blind" Chan alone; let your liver and intestines wither until they are as firm as iron, sitting firmly to cut off both sages and ordinary beings and walking the right path.
Decree: One must clearly understand that before one’s parents were born, a thousand pieces of gold could not buy the leisure of a single life.
Who would be willing to cast their body into the noisy basket? I send this message to all the officials throughout the city.
The iron yoke is naturally carried by those who love it;

Entrusted to the wild cocks of the forest, they cry out at every fifth watch. Their cries grow hoarse until the sun sinks in the west; In their old homeland, there is a home, yet they have not yet returned.
It is attained. Even infinite hatred and love still entangle and delude one.
To the King of Goryeo, [the Master] showed that human life is like a phantom within a phantom; in this dusty world, who is truly who? Before parents were born, who was there?
I—when a single breath does not come, who am I?
Serenely, within this very reality, the reflections of waves on a pond soak the mountain light. Amidst it, a Zen monk forgets all myriad concerns; at midnight, pine seeds fall upon the roof.
It falls away. The profound ground of the mind is utterly beyond acceptance.
In sickness, I send this to a friend:
all is but three inches of breath being drawn out; if you wish to sever it, let it simply cease. How many times have we known birth and death as dreams and illusions?
Granted. I do not have it dwelling on my mind at all.

Regarding the ascetic practices shown by the ancient *dhūta* practitioners who practiced austerities in the Snowy Mountains: why did he cross the royal city at night? Because the bright star was hidden from his eyes.
It is so. Beyond two thousand years, errors will surely arise.
*Dhūta* is simply another name for a *bhikṣu*. When can ascetic practice be paused?
Wearing dyed robes mended with lotus leaves, one has wandered alone since the days after the frost.
Dhūta alone yielded to the elder Kāśyapa; his two eyes came empty, penetrating to the very bone.
Having transmitted a single tattered *kāṣāya*, he sits withered to this day upon Chicken Peak.
Which bhikṣu is willing to practice the dhūta austerities? Having barely begun these ascetic practices, they do not persist for long. They clear away their means of livelihood until nothing remains;
what can the world do against such a person?
Disheveled short hair covers the eyebrows; his dwelling is one of solitary contentment.
Having cast off his old black cotton robe, he stands bare-chested with arms outstretched.

In leisure or toil, motion or stillness, suffering within suffering; hearing, seeing, sensing, and knowing exhaust the external. There is no ground where a锥 (chui) can be planted, for even the chui itself is spent.
Only when meeting people is it fitting to display one’s family style.
The transformative power extends toward the homes of the wealthy; with a smile, he points out that gold is a venomous serpent. This is transformed into the application of the *dāna-pāramitā*;
like a fragrant breeze, it causes the flowers of the field of merit to bloom.
The broken alms bowl is a bottomless boat; the livelihood of the dhūta practitioner proclaims itself.
Dwelling in a thatched hut at the foot of a thousand crags, snow fills the wooden bed, yet he does not sleep at night.
I have practiced asceticism throughout my entire life; beyond the dhūta practices, I seek nothing else.
Having bound my waist with three strips of bamboo, let the Buddha-dharma rot away as it may.
In this world, only the dhūta practitioner is truly excellent. What else remains after such ascetic toil? With the eyes of the triple world empty, he has forgotten both grasping and abandoning;
having departed in this manner, who else could there be?
To the Chan practitioner Xiji:
In practicing Chan and studying the Way, do not be complacent. Turn back that natural, iron-like face.
Whether saint or ordinary person, drive them all away with a shout, and claim sovereignty directly where there is no Buddha.

To practice Chan and study the Way, one must possess a sincere heart; Risking life and death, disregarding the body, One perseveres until reaching the very edge of empty space, Where the ten directions of the world become but a single mote of dust.
Studying the Way through Zen is a matter already present; to attempt to pluck your eyebrows is a journey of eight thousand miles.
Even if you could grasp it by opening your chest, the pivot of the teaching remains as incomplete as ever.
Practicing Chan and studying the Way is for the sake of birth and death. If birth and death are not yet clarified, one must practice with urgency.
If even a single koan is absent from one's mind, the boundless cycle of birth and death will once again encompass you.
Practicing Zen and studying the Way to attain Buddhahood—how can this be compared to the ordinary play of children? Today, I shall risk my very life;
compared to the predecessors, I am not too late.
In the practice of Zen and the study of the Way, it is vital to forget all artifice. One must by all means avoid using the mind to discriminate between right and wrong.
Constantly recall the excellent words of Nanquan; those who are as deluded and dull as this are truly rare.
Studying the Way through Zen is transmitted in the mind; the entire Tripitaka has never been able to explain it. If one relies on what is heard and seen, one cannot transcend the realm of forms;
once the mouth opens, one falls back into the domain of words and language.
Studying the Way through Zen meditation accords with the profound mystery; how could all the people in the great earth know it?
Were one not a true kind of grass from within this [tradition], a casual step would immediately lead to divergence.
Those who practice Chan and study the Way have been many throughout ancient and modern times; yet most find their niche in dozing upon a single meditation cushion.
Those who do not understand how to bind the body beyond words have already encountered demons before their buttocks even touch the ground.
Studying the Way through Zen meditation is as numerous as hemp seeds; every movement is obscured by the dust of worldly passions.
So long as not even a single speck of dust remains unbroken within the mind, one’s diligent practice merely adds flowers before the eyes.
In practicing Chan and studying the Way, cease all seeking; let only this single doubt remain until it is resolved. When you encounter the adversary, break through like a bursting dam;
then both sagehood and ordinariness, delusion and awakening, are gathered up at once.
In practicing Chan and studying the Way, there is joy within joy. May I venture to ask the Acharya, what is it that you find joyful?
Last night, a tiny gnat opened its mouth and sucked dry the Chan-rivers of thousands of miles.
Shanzhou (Ten Poems) The ancients said: "Use the unrefined to preserve my Way.
For what reason should my Way use the unrefined to survive? Throughout thirty thousand kalpas, I have only struck at myself;
Beyond two thousand years, I do not claim to be honored. The ancient path is buried in snow—who has reached it intimately? When the thunder shakes the profound gate, I...
Alone in darkness, how could one cherish boasting to others of being muddled? The more alert and discerning one is, the more one falls into the gate of right and wrong.
Why must one laboriously boast of one's own skill or clumsiness? The heavens and earth of all time cannot obstruct it.

Raise the mind and immediately the weeds of ignorance grow long; sever thought and frequently the flowers of Prajñā bloom. The sword-traps grow daily larger, yet they are entirely within me; in the subtle breeze of the lotus pond, how could they [trouble me]?
Dependent on others, forty-nine years were spent preaching at Vulture Peak; not a single word can now be added. Whose hands and feet bear these marks?
These illusory traces have no peer; my clumsiness serves as my kin. For two summers we contemplated the same sages by the pagoda lamp;
for three autumns we were willing to share our affairs in the crags. After the rain, the fragrant trees possess a new air; after the snow, the cold plum blossoms reveal their ancient character.
Spirit! The man of the Way has long since forgotten both hatred and love; yet when conversation reaches this point, it still enters his dreams frequently.
Returning from afar, he boards my boat dwelling in the mountains; day by day, with Vimalakīrti, they speak of their old travels. At night, the six windows are closed, yet it is as bright as day;
in summer, a single mat is spread out, yet it is as cool as autumn. The pine waves roll across the earth, yet they are not in motion; the cloud-waves overturn the void—what depth is there?
It does not flow. It is no wonder that the boatman frequently whispers in my ear as we shift our oars past Cangzhou.

Having returned from afar, I wished to cease my practice; the Master detained me at Jingshu Hermitage. Within the crevices of his eyebrows, blue peaks are piled; beneath the tips of his toes, emerald mists gather.

That there is frost in the sixth month, people do not yet understand; that for ninety days he has had no dreams, I— (Note: The final line is incomplete in the source text, but the translation reflects the available characters.)
Fully conversant with all things, why such fuss over empty flowers and shadows? Stirring up trouble, one labors day and night in greed.
At the Secluded Hermitage, the scenery is sparse and the people are sparse; constantly turning the Vajra wheel without ceasing. When there is thought, one seeks conditions to form a pair;
when there is no mind, one dwells as a neighbor to the Way. To mend the worn meditation cushion with tortoise hair, and to take a broken bamboo staff as a rabbit’s whisker—how much toil!
Jiǎo Shēn does not harbor idle dreams of the human world, but spends his twelve hours of the day in constant practice.
He once composed an inscription for Jǐng Shū’ān; now he comes beneath the hermitage to express his profound sentiments. The two mountains ring their bells as he listens by his bedside;
ten thousand miles of clouds arise beyond the railing. The courtyard cypresses hold the frost as cold flames float upward; the stone pond contains the moon and the dew.
Clear and Bright Festival. A guest from Yunnan arrived at my gate, offering me a *kundikā* water jar for drawing water.
In the dwelling of a wayfarer, there is no elaborate arrangement; during the day, I am too lazy to open the closed door. The wind draws the sound of the bamboo through the broken wall;
the rain drags the shadows of clouds across the mountains. Leaning against the pine and stone, for whom do they provide support? The flowers spread upon the ground must surely be for themselves.
Jiālěi said to Chan Master Jǐngshū Ānzhǔ: "When you reach the state where emotions are forgotten, simply let go of your attachments.
I am ashamed of my own meager lot and lowly conditions; I have already forced myself to build this thatched cottage. The Buddha-dharma is harmoniously integrated—there is no day it does not shine.
Space expands and contracts, yet when will it ever cease? A beak three feet long is but idle chatter; a body as fragile as a bubble—who can rely upon it?"
All know it; they have surrendered their intelligence to the village shrine. Who would think today to support those in peril? The power of the Way has never been fully intact;
dust covers his face as he lies by the forest springs. His words lack efficacy, and he is too weary to write characters;
he sees the ultimate mystery and is too indolent to preach Chan. Tattered rags hang down past his neck, and his disheveled hair grows wild.
Shoulders aligned. Cease for now the frequent company of worldly affairs; today, dwelling in the mountains, our conversation reaches its fulfillment.
At the Four Seasons Peak (Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter), dwelling deeply within the depths of Tianmu, the resonance of the Way is extraordinary.
The intent of the Patriarchs merges with every dust mote; body and mind are forgotten in every thought-moment.
