Who adorns the *Avataṃsaka*? The myriad trees naturally exude their fragrance. All things transform according to the seasons; in spring, the waters are likewise fragrant.
Dwelling deep at the base of Tianmu, secluded and remote, beyond all encounter—once this single koan is shattered, the dream-eyes of a thousand lifetimes are awakened.
Bamboo smoke clings to the cold wool; pine dew drips, making the gate pure. Together we loathe the summer heat of the human world, yet our ascetic reflections remain unfulfilled.
Dwelling deep at the foot of Tianmu, we have only the ten thousand mountains as neighbors. Beyond meditation lies a true delight; within our gaze, there is no vulgar dust.
The new frost heralds the seasonal change; ancient seal-script marks the passing hours. Among those who know autumn by the falling leaves, how many are there within the forest?

Dwelling deep at the foot of Tianmu, this practitioner has naturally forgotten artifice. With thoughts exhausted, the mind of meditation is profound; with emotions fled, the essence of the precepts grows full.
Frosty clouds encroach upon the stone steps; cold snow protects the mossy garments. I imagine that those who investigate the profound will not return to me before the end of winter.
Presented to Master Jing of Mount Jing:
At Lingyuan of Caoxi, drop by drop it flows down to Caoxi. How can this matter be compared to anything else? When asked, he said: "It is already perfected, ten thousand miles away."

Separated. To speak further of their distinctions creates a hundredfold delusion. Fierce thunder drives the rain back toward the north of the mountains; the bright moon drags its clouds past the west of the house.
Before sounds and forms have even manifested, one must intuitively grasp it; otherwise, you will needlessly add eyebrows upon your eyes.

A Gift to Yungu (While Guesting at Donglin): Ten thousand layers of Mount Kuang’s green peaks enter my sight; Gently drifting clouds of compassion cover the secluded valley. The spray of the waterfall drenches the mountain monk’s robe;
Lying at the foot of the pines, I listen to the wailing of the cold monkeys. Upon the pond, lotus flowers are a thousand shards of jade; Beneath the cottage, the sound of the stream has ceased.
It continues. The entire Great Canon of Teachings cannot fully describe it; eighty-four thousand discourses are insufficient to express it. I have come to Yanmen when the autumn is at its height;
the clear frost freezes the old chrysanthemums by the deep pool. Turning my head toward the human world, how many true men are there? Wild horses gallop in vain through the six windows of the senses.
Taking hold of a seven-foot rattan cane and snapping it in my hand, I intend to grow a white mold upon my lips—how could this compare [to worldly pursuits]?
Together with you, I carry a broken-legged cauldron in hand; by the hearth, I stir the fire to bake the yellow tubers.
Sent to Lu Quan-zhi (who was avoiding the invitation to Dajue Temple).
I laugh at myself for these twenty years of no cause: teaching people to seek the blue sky upon level ground. There is truly no one left to entrust me with before the wind.
A verse: At that time, there was a letter urging me to board a boat under the moon. It sent me away to repay my debt for the axe;
who would be left to provide the funds to purchase this mountain? Having chewed through the iron pastry whole, I remember only the mountainsides and the watersides.
Presented to the Daoist Zhang Youmei:
If you do not understand the practice of Chan meditation, it is like failing to save one's hair while it is on fire. You have missed countless opportunities for spiritual cultivation.

The cat catching the mouse is no true metaphor; the man riding the ox is a mistaken tradition. Though the four oceans are devoid of drops, the sea still remains; though ten thousand miles are cloudless, the sky still persists.
There is a deity. One should contemplate that all things together may be overturned and transformed; every single thing is a condition for transcending the world.

A monk of leisure beyond the mundane, inheriting the three matters of the family lineage while dwelling in secluded seclusion: silently upholding the yellow scrolls, he gazes in vast stillness upon the blue peaks.
Earthworms bore through withered leaves; mountain mice shake dry vines. Laughing as I observe the world of men, when will I forget love and hate?

At Tiger Creek, we shared a night’s conversation by the bank with our guests; our friendship was as deep as the water. When the talk ended under tonight’s moon, we fully verified the hearts of the ancients.
Chan discourse has nothing to do with study; lofty poetry does not lie in mere recitation. Mount Kuanglu abounds with members of the White Lotus Society; surely there must be those who understand.

Staying overnight at Jixiang Ancient Temple on Tianchi Mountain: A single pagoda rises towering and majestic. The path ascends from the very edge of heaven; People pass through from beyond the clouds.

The sacred lamp hangs at the tip of the tree; the thundering waterfall descends from the mountain cleft. I alone cherish the moon over the icy pool; with no thought of my own, I emerge from the thicket of vines.
Within the mountains—spring has arrived in the midst of the mountains, truly wondrous.
Shallow and deep reds and purples adorn the flowering branches; the Lord of Spring takes no heed of this thatched hut.
Narrow and constricted, the Yang-huo energy is confined throughout the twelve hours.

Living in the mountains during summer, the flavor of life grows even longer. Verdant pines and lush bamboos encircle my thatched bed. From the southern heavens, the rain-bearing breeze arrives at the celestial shore;
all day long, I hear only the fragrance of the white snows.
The mountain hermitage of the Wayman is well-suited for autumn; the whistling west wind rustles through the treetops. The moon is cold over a thousand ridges as clear dew drips down;
one knows not that the deep night has soaked his black robe.

In these deep mountains, thatch-roofed huts fear the winter cold; snow withers and ice dries up as I gaze upon them alone. Digging a fire-pit right on the ground, it reaches all the way to the bottom;
at nightfall, who is there to share the stirring of the remaining embers?

In spring, I visit the Dragon Pond, where forest flowers mingle red with green. The rain has cleared and the season is truly harmonious. In ten thousand ravines, snow tumbles from the valleys; In the three ponds, water reflects the void.
Brocade-colored clouds obscure the medicinal paths; Fragrant mists lock the jade palace. I laugh, however, at those who came before me, Who asked whether the way was passable or not.
In summer, he hides among the emerald peaks of Lotus Peak;
the world of burning afflictions cannot invade him. Myriad monks embrace the azure cliffs; a single flower blooms at Shaolin.
Listening to the pines, I forget my painted fan; hearing the waterfall, I recognize it as a jade zither. Gazing afar at the summer heat of the human realm, I wonder who might come to visit him there.

Ascending the summit in autumn, three thousand nine hundred *zhang* high; the path ends and suddenly one encounters the peak. Wooden planks and stone enclosures form a pearl-like curtain, while the golden breeze withers the green hairpins of the pines.
Myriad dragons stretch across the vast wilderness; ten thousand horses gallop over the level plains. Looking out freely toward the four horizons, both high and low are entirely heaven.
In winter, I leaned against Shiyi Rock on the path before Shizi Rock;
the crumbling peaks surged down, pressing halfway up the mountain. An old Chan monk stood amidst the snow, his solitary robe trailing clouds as he returned.
The icy steps hung a thousand fathoms high; the frost-chilled bell shook the two worlds. Embracing the brazier, I contemplate the Buddha-sun, which once shared a boundary with death.
By the spring pond, the fine grasses grow lush and tender; beyond the railing, the young peach blossoms blaze with crimson.
If one were to try to open two eyes before these colors, there would be no place within them for the spring breeze to lodge.
In summer, ten thousand willow trees resound with cicadas crying in the wind; fiercely, a fire burns through the sky, filling all directions.
If one can forget this heat and affliction right where they are, there is no need to seek out a lotus-leaf boat once more.
In autumn, jade dew hangs down as the moon sinks low; a single patch of clear light shines upon the ancient mind. This is a place where nothing can be concealed:
amidst the chirping of crickets, one faces the cold sound of the wooden mortar.
In winter, several flakes of frozen cloud cling to the broken stones; half the sky, bright with snow, sprinkles the window gauze. Leaning on the railing alone, I fold my double sleeves;
looking up at the plum branch, I see it has blossomed again.
**The Illusory Sea (Five Poems)** The illusory dharma flows vast and deep like the sea;
from of old there has been neither past nor present. A great leviathan spits forth waves that cling to the heavens;
rolled into a single bubble, where can it be sought?
The great illusion has no root and is as deep as the sea; a hundred rivers and ten thousand streams are gathered therein all at once. Look before even a single bubble has arisen:
ultimately, where has there ever been any substantial reality?
The illusion is as deep as the sea; how can it be known? Behold the time when the hero swallows ten thousand streams. When investigated with earnestness, not a single drop remains.
Before the wind, the old Persian is driven to despair.
Flowers in the sky and images in a mirror; wooden horses, straw men, and the city of Gandharva. Bottomless and shoreless, deep and vast;
throughout the years and all day long, the surging waves crash down.
Truly non-existent yet appearing—what thing is this? A vast expanse of surging waves flooding the sun. A thousand-foot tiered pavilion clings to the snowy billows;
gazing at the precipice, whose hair does not stand on end with cold?
Inscribed on Yunhai Ting (Four Poems) Clouds meet the sky, and the sea meets the sky;
casting my gaze far out, where is the horizon? Its vast proportions admit no further carving;
its majesty has always emerged from the natural. Cold plum blossoms hold the snow of a thousand ages; the roots of the cypress clearly exude their fragrance.
Incense smoke from the burner; when a guest comes to inquire after news of spring, the secluded birds outside the gate speak with the most perfect clarity.

The clouds dissolve into the sky and the sea lies deep below; since the beginning of heaven and earth, it has remained thus until now. Seeing this, there is no need to seek the meaning of the Patriarchs;

when emotions are forgotten, what use is there to search for a "Chan mind"? Pine blossoms fill the broom and stock the empty granary; the melody of the waterfall floats through the void, pressing against the heavens.
The ancient zither: those in the city suffer amidst the dust and fire; who would have known that in this mountain retreat, snow fills the breast?

Clouds high and seas vast in the midst of autumn, the Chan-seal beyond all things allows for both going and staying. Since one knows that both the living and the Buddha lack any fundamental basis, how could awakening or delusion have any origin?
The azure crags purely hold the moon of the third watch; the wild ravines deeply conceal ten thousand autumns.

A small boat on the river—who cares if the clear breeze shears the forest slopes? The mountain-clad practitioner wraps his head in his own robe; the clouds and sea reach the heavens, vast and boundless.
The six gates of perception are empty, containing but a single body. Pine needles fill the hearth as he roasts old yams;

bamboo smoke gathers upon his coarse woolen garment as he welcomes the spring. Standing in the courtyard snow at night, his worldly emotions have finally vanished; striking the ice in the ancient ravine, his intent is pure.
Truly unique. Of those who have sworn this bond through the cold of winter, how many remain? Most lose their true nature amidst the bustle of worldly affairs.
To a Zen practitioner (Five Verses): Meeting in leisure, parting in the clamor;
At the prow of the boat, there was once a promise to meet again. A sudden shift in the spiritual mechanism—seeking the traces.
On the road, unaware, one’s entire body falls into the Iron Ring Mountains.
Seeing the face and hearing the name, there is no intimacy at all. Where one attempts to deliberate, the true source is obscured.
As for those who cross the river and beckon with their hands, who from ancient times to the present has been able to follow in their footsteps?
My coming back to you again has no other purpose than to inquire together about the "entanglement Chan" (ge-teng chan). Though space has a mouth, it cannot speak;
iron walls and silver mountains are pierced through face-to-face.
This gāthā is sent from afar; do not harbor doubt or suspicion. The sturdy gate of birth and death must be opened. Raise your two eyebrows and look for yourself:
who says that this illusory dwelling will not be visited again?
Remove the one and set aside the seven; birth and death, life and death, are truly without end.
If a man has not yet attained the eye that transcends the mundane, do not deceive yourself throughout the twelve hours of the day.
At the request of the Venerable Ōnkei, I spoke this verse for the consecration of his robe:
"The Great Hero of our school once donned this garment; though not a single thread remained, he draped it over one shoulder. There, a single branch of the *utpala* flower blossomed."
For the sake of the Zen practitioner Lye, this robe is empowered and named "Formless Field of Merit.
It is worn as the lingering radiance of the ancestral Buddhas' legacy; it is as pure as ice and snow.
"Wait and behold: one flower blooms and five petals unfold.

The Zen practitioner Lie requested that I empower a hooded robe (*kaṣāya*) he had fashioned from coarse cloth, praying that he might never lose this garment through successive lifetimes and thereby continue the life-force of the Buddha's wisdom.
You should know that while this robe is without marks (*animitta*), it is that which is to be investigated.

The saying, too, is without marks. Nevertheless, don this robe and investigate this saying; if you do so for a long time without interruption, it is called the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom—how could it be an external matter?
You should exert yourself in this.

This Way is manifest without concealment, utterly free from covering; the myriad phenomena of the universe stand revealed in their majestic dignity. The western wind fills the courtyard—who shares it with anyone?
Only Master Shangu hears the fragrance of the cassia.
A single stroke of pale mist over the distant mountains paints the clear sky; it is as if Mount Sumeru has revealed half its peak.
Having traveled nearly to the end of ten-thousand-li Yazhou, the towering mountain still stands amidst the white clouds.
In the snowy valley, a thousand crags and ten thousand peaks form a jade sphere. Who can discern the sound that follows every knock? Within lies a spirit that never dies;
I have personally reached it, and my very bones and hair turn cold.
The springtime of Plum Valley reached the cold cliffs last night; amidst them, the five-petaled flower blooms. A single sheet of white cloud cannot block it out;
the celestial wind blows forth its hidden fragrance.

The foolish old man spends his whole day not departing from the source of conditions; his inability to do much is merely the theft of a dead mind. From the beginning, great skill has always been like clumsiness;
until one reaches old age, who knows its depths?
Zhu’an’s attempt at cleverness turns instead into error; he exerts himself only to fall headlong into a patch of weeds. He does not even know how to put on his robes or eat his meals.
Yet that one who raises his fist continues the ancestral wind.
Non-characteristic:

whatever exists at any time is all delusion; from the beginning, the place of severance has never been entirely real. If one possesses the eye that transcends the mundane within the crown of the head, then every blade of grass and the finest hair are all the Dharmakāya.
Ancient trees have weathered wind and frost for countless years; their dense, cool shade provides shelter for many.
Observe how they remain untouched by the cycles of prosperity and decay, for their roots are nourished by the springtime beyond the kalpas.
Plowing the sea, a single breath dries the blue depths to their very bottom; he refuses to leave so much as a drop to sustain fish and dragons. The fields have been divided and all plowed over;
the ox rests in idleness while the man is already at his window.
The mist of the vast blue sea is boundless, and the waters stretch on endlessly. The rolling tide submerges the eight directions. At midnight, the old dragon sleeps and does not yet rise;
at dawn, the clouds push the sun up over Mount Fusang.

Before the Elder had opened his mouth, [the meaning] was already grasped; as soon as he raised his eyes, the destination was known. In old age, the turning wheel of the mechanism becomes even more lively;
preaching the Dharma is like a flash of lightning.
The pomegranate has long been nestled within the grove at Zīlūdu; for many years it was buffeted by the autumn winds. Now that the season has arrived, it smiles with open mouth;
its entire interior is filled with mani-jewels.

Entrusted to Zhu Gaogang: Loyalty and forbearance are his nature; a single inch of luminous clarity encompasses the great thousand-fold world. The whole world turns to benevolence as he realizes the cessation of study;
all things are complete within me as I recognize that there is no transmission. The phoenix cries atop the high ridge of the moon; the crow and the hare push open the azure sky.
Falling from heaven—when one gazes to the limits with a mind as vast as space and remains unobscured, what need is there to seek external conditions?
To the Venerable Hudu I say:
the Way does not belong to the realm of knowing or not knowing; it is the perfected samādhi, utterly transcending the subtle and the minute. How could mercury and lead be the elixir of immortality?

The Medicine: Departing from *kaṇa*, he emerges through the upward-moving mechanism; having leaped over the jade luan, he returns to the phoenix palace. He turns back the stone horse to the celestial courtyard;
had he been led to enter the empty royal chamber, he would have raised his brush-tip and parted the Iron Ring Mountains.
A Gift for Layman Jing: Layman Jing’an resides in Jinling. His reputation for the Way resounds throughout the rivers and lakes. A lotus flower emerging from the water has three white petals;
a pine trunk bearing frost is half green after a lifetime. Pushing aside the elephant carriage, he returns to Mount E; riding the ox-cart backward, he departs.
The Fire City: Waiting for those who cross over until their human aspirations are fulfilled, they return to knock at my door to discuss birthlessness.
Sending off a monk: How magnificent! The August tide of the Qiantang River; ten thousand heaps of raging snow rub against the azure heavens. A seven-foot black staff, a black rattle.
The Vinaya: Trustingly, it is plucked from the hand; heaven stretches far and wide. Before Mount Wulong lies the Mirror Lake, its cold waters soaking the light of heaven as if washed clean.
One passes through the Three Rivers and Nine Weirs; the Great White Jade Table rises majestic and clear. Twenty li of pines screen the moon from the sky;
atop the Ten-Thousand-Labor Ponds stand three-tiered pavilions. Layer upon layer, the shadows of the pavilions float upon the clear waves. Chao-yin Cave.

The inner essence of Avalokiteśvara: a blink of an eye and white clouds stretch for thousands of miles. The five hundred elder śrāvakas at Shiliang Bridge cry out like partridges amidst the deep flowers.
At the Flower-Crested Peak, eighteen thousand *zhang* high, green creepers hang a thousand feet beside ancient pines.
To recognize Dongzhou, this alone is it; why need one don sandals once more? When the moment of realization strikes, do not treat it as a mere description of a scene.
One must also act with resolve from beginning to end.

Plucking a branch of plum blossoms, I have broken it off and inserted it obliquely into a chalice-flask. A few buds, half-opened, exude the essence of spring; sparse shadows slant across the window as the night light leaks through.
The moon; its dark fragrance drifts on the breeze entering the door. Having no root or foundation, how can it be real? Its outward form exists in vain; it is entirely empty.
Do not wait for the time when passions are cast aside; right now, assume the appearance of withered decay.
Cloud-sea pavilions atop Mount Huazang overlook the wild plains;
half the sky, bright snow rolls across the distant heavens. Dragons drag their coils as they stand tall, green shells glistening with moisture;
whales spit forth the cold moon, its jade mirror perfect and round. Thirty thousand acres lie submerged where the sword of the Lord of Wu sank; two thousand years of resentment remain for Yue.
The King’s boat; the man of the Way pays no heed to matters of rise and fall. Having listened to the distant bell, he sleeps upon his stone pillow.

Paying homage at the stupa of Great Master Huizhao, the Patriarchal Seal is fully upheld as a guiding compass. Amidst the mass of white clouds, the udumbara flower appears; its pearl-like radiance flows with flames across three thousand worlds.
A village where jade carvings and ornate patterns fill five hundred cases. Ancient frost blankets the stone steps all around; hoary snow encircles the pine huts beneath the eaves.
I have come to this place and can only snap my fingers in emptiness—how many of its descendants wish to cease their practice?

Seeking a recluse in the mountains, half a lifetime’s thoughts are entrusted to the mist and clouds. With staff in hand, I idly pass the recluse’s dwelling. Woodpeckers call out, their cries echoing through the distant and near hills.
The woodcutters’ voices murmur as they traverse the winding paths. A gusty wind blows down the seeds of the green pines; a fine rain steams open the white [mushrooms].
Bean blossoms. Not a guest from beneath the Shaolin gate, how could one sustain such a life?

Walking through the mountains, pear blossoms fall and bean-plum trees turn green; with two sleeves filled by the spring breeze, staff and sandals are light. By the bamboo fence, the sound of a dog is heard.

Hei! Beneath the purple wisteria flowers, I see people passing by. The mist has cleared from the distant ridges as the mountain mists grow dim; the rain has ceased in the village ahead and the river waters have become level.
The traveler’s road is long and he has not yet returned; he cannot bear to listen to the cries of the cuckoo at such a time.

Dwelling in the mountains, I cast no shadow upon the human world; carefree, I have naturally preserved my youthful countenance. My pure dreams ripen upon half the bed; the white clouds are idle against the four walls.
Wild deer come and go without departing; mad monkeys leave and then return. Only the guests of the capital and the marketplace would surely long for me as I dwell in these deep mountains.

A single mountain hamlet hides white clouds within its stone steps; A half-ruined thatched cottage hangs amidst the wisteria vines. The secluded birds, carrying flowers in their beaks, know not where they go;
The gate is closed against the setting sun, yet spring thoughts abound.
Congratulating Lingyin on the Incense Offering:
The ancient incense burner spews purple sandalwood smoke; A fragrant breeze stirs the curtains with a touch of morning chill. On Mount Lingjiu, the people have not yet risen;
The golden cock crows atop the jade balustrade.
A Gift to Master Chuan (Regarding His Mother’s Remains):
The stupa shadow hangs from the ten-thousand-fathom peak; The golden bones grow cold as the evening sun fades. The old mother’s countenance remains clearly present;
Tears fall in the east wind—whom can this grief attach itself to?
Seeing Yunxi depart for the Ninth Grade Contemplation Hall:
Layered evening clouds lock the cold of the stream; The waters are sluggish, and the lotus incense burner has run dry. Master Jiupin rises from his meditative concentration;
The night tide pushes the moon up onto the balustrade.
The "upside-down black staff" of the Lu Shan dharma-friend emerged from Yanymen; his sky-reaching eyes cover heaven and earth. What has that old venerable master of Jiangxi?
With eyebrows raised, he swallows it all in one gulp.
Presenting a recitation of the Lotus Sutra:
daily proclaiming one scroll of the Wondrous Lotus. A fragrant breeze wafts through the teeth; outside the window the sun slants as the door is half-closed.
A lotus fiber tugs at the white ox-cart.

Presenting this blood-written Lotus Sutra, a single needle-point reveals great merit. Where the blood flows, the wind awakens and fans it. Deep in the night, it blows upon the moon over the jeweled pond;
white lotus flowers bloom, their petals crimson.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* written in blood reveals the true body of Vairocana pervading as many lands as grains of sand; the spring winds of the second month are stained with blood.
Beyond the mists and waters of one hundred and ten cities, the youth Sudhana has not returned home.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written in blood asks:
"How does one subdue [the mind]? How does one abide? When he questioned Gautama, his mouth was like a drill-bit; though the printing block remained, the patterns were revealed.
The cuckoo cries until its throat bleeds upon the flowering branches.
Entrusting this meaning to Yuan Duanya, the conditions for transformation have caused my father’s gateway to lean entirely askew. Looking up, who among those people does not move with emotion?
Extending the hand of transformation at the crossroads of the street, one must still repay me, your elder brother.
Entrusting this to Elder Tianzhu:
Ancient winds fail to stir, worldly waves destroy all. Ten thousand li of rivers and lakes roll with raging thunder. On Mount Tianzhu, the man of lofty character rises from meditation;
he picks wild yams and stirs the cold ashes.

At the mountain cottage of Longchi Hermitage, the azure dragon roars as it breaks through the moonlit ice pool. The mountain elder stands alone facing the snow upon the cold cliff. A great dream of the human world is suddenly awakened;
rustling at the treetops, the yellow leaves are blown away.

In Master Lang’s bamboo chamber, dense green jade stalks stand in rows against the eaves; their whistling, pure sounds wind around the secluded room. The patch-robed monk sits with a single-minded heart of meditation;
his faculty of hearing is unimpeded as sensory dust enters.
Moored my boat before Mount Miaoxi;
the waters fill the clear stream, the moon fills the heavens. A single path back home is as straight as a string. I know not when this traveler will find rest;
the old cuckoo cries itself to death in the empty mountains.

In my village dwelling during summer, the grassy marshes are fanned by a gentle breeze from the water. After the cool rains have first cleared, the bean leaves are lush and thick. Amidst the wild trees, the disordered cries of cicadas have not yet ceased;
amidst the sound of unrolling bamboo flutes, the cowherd returns home.
On the road through Jinling, the splendor of the Six Dynasties flows away with the current; the sedges on the banks and the grasses on the marshes are a vast, lingering green.
Leaning my slender cane against the eastern fence, I smile and ask the chrysanthemums: how many autumns have passed?
Presented to a monk on his pilgrimage:
a seven-foot black staff cast from wrought iron. Casually picked up, it cannot be held back; the frosty sky, the setting moon, the vast expanse of heaven.
With every step, he kicks forth mountains beyond number.
In the practice of the Way, one diminishes daily;
yet before reaching the point of perfect completion, how many times have I leaned upon the railing in particular sorrow? Today is the third, tomorrow the fourth;
snow and frost easily take their toll upon the human head.
Inscription for the Miaozhan Wuwei Pagoda:
The essence of non-action accords with the natural state; How could such wondrous clarity admit even a speck of dust? The thousand-fathom plain of Shu rises abruptly and high;
The livelihood of Mount Moshan is renewed once more.

To the Long-Term Fellow Practitioner Tianmu, who resides on Mount Bie: We have stayed together at Mount Lu as well; among all these places, there is but one thing that differs—both of us are thirty-six years old this year.
I have a zither without strings; as we part, I shall play a single melody for you. It is not of the Yang [world].
Spring is not white snow; it is like ten-thousand-foot cliff cascades pouring down after the rain, or like a thousand mountain bamboos bending under the weight of heavy snow.
It startles the crimson-tailed brocade carp, stirring the waves at the bottom of Poyang Lake;
it drives forth the golden-maned lion, swallowing the moon upon the coral branches. A-he-he! How marvelous and extraordinary! Grasses, trees, and the myriad phenomena all rejoice.

Delightful! This sound does not enter the ears of the people of this age. Do not join with these people in distinguishing between self and other. Roll up your robes, embrace your lute, and go home; enough!
Your own mountain range—let it be as you wish to leave or stay. Should we suddenly meet again after thirty years, this melody must not be lightly answered in return.

Preface and Verse for Establishing the Jade Pavilion (Liyuting) I have humbly heard that Mount Tiantai possesses the Huading Peak and the Stone Bridge; Mount Konglu possesses the Heavenly Lake and the Embroidered Valley;

the Shili Rock at Beitai is comparable to Mount Qingliang; and the Zhurong Peak at Nanyue is comparable to Mount Heng. These sites extract the finest excellence of clouds, forests, springs, and rocks; they are indeed—
This is no ordinary human world. To my east and west lie the two Tianmu Mountains. Their long ridges and distant peaks lean against the void and enter the clouds;

I have already witnessed their majestic forms, like dancing phoenixes and soaring dragons. My late teacher, Master Gaofeng, stayed his staff at Shizi Rock during the Jīmǎo year of the Zhìyuán era (1279).
Not long after, he sat in meditation within the "Gate of Death. He established two sites for the Dharma and... [four]... 4.
At that time, practitioners of the Way who had attained mastery in emptiness and stillness were as numerous as those whose shoulders brushed and heels followed one another.
All said that while this mountain was vast, open, lofty, and cold, it lacked a site of supreme excellence.

On the thirty-seventh day of the month, in the year of Yanyou (Yimao), the gate of the monastery was being constructed at the summit of Longgang. Suddenly, while descending through the air for some dozen paces, clouds appeared.

The springs, pines, and rocks there presented ten thousand strange and marvelous forms. Those who beheld them at the time were so astonished that they told one another, "Is it not as if the Creator has guarded these treasures with care, awaiting this very day?
Otherwise, this mountain has existed alongside heaven and earth since their inception;
yet why have the men of old who sought out the extraordinary and gazed upon the beautiful never once cast their eyes here, such that only now has this structure been built?"
A small pavilion stands atop a precarious rock, its plaque inscribed with the words "Liyu Pavilion" (Pavilion of Standing Jade).

This was likely taken from the lines of the scholar Haishu’s *Fu on Tianmu*, which describe looking down upon the various peaks as they stand like jade. It is like a person of ultimate attainment who harbors something within;
though they do not wish for it to be heard or known, once the conditions of time have arrived, it cannot be concealed, and thus its fame spreads.
The phrase "the patterns of its fragrance and color are revealed" is somewhat similar [to this]. Some say that the mountain has no intention of seeking an encounter;

yet how could the person of realization have any intention of receiving one? It is simply because the principle (li) so ordains it. Formerly, when a monk asked Jia Shan about the nature of his realm, he replied:
"A monkey carries its young back into the green peaks; a bird picks up a flower and drops it upon the emerald cliff."
Previously, there was also the dialogue between Layman Wujin and Chan Master Ji regarding the scene of Cuiyan. The Master replied: "The gate is near Hongya’s Thousand-Fathom Well;

a stone bridge flows with water winding around pines and cypresses. Second, the Master placed brush and ink upon the tip of his three-inch tongue, portraying the scene with such vividness that it leaves nothing to the imagination.
Among those of past and present, there are few who have not taken this as their own meditative object (*kōan*).

Regarding that which is confined within the enclosure: since it does not function as an object of perception, suppose someone were suddenly to ask, "How would you respond if asked about the Jade Pavilion?
I have never been able to answer such questions; thus, I have composed this long verse as a mere approximation.
Mountain flowers cluster in profusion across eight hundred li; they paint the heavens and earth as a true masterpiece. The lion’s tail lashes out from mid-air;
the flying monkeys’ feet find no rest upon the precipices. On Dragon Ridge, a jade-green pagoda appears by illusion; its crystal *śarīra* radiates light across the forest slopes.
Turning his body, he suddenly reveals what was hidden by heaven; even the sacred grottoes of Xianchi seem mundane by comparison. Ancient pines and wondrous rocks—
The eye has not yet seen it: a low pavilion where walls stand a thousand fathoms high like jade. Thunder-chariots overturn, raining down torrents of water;
thousands of *li* of precious pearls are crushed to pieces. Great Spirit whips up the iron Kunlun mountains; ten-thousand-fathom tusks churn the void and line the deep valleys.
In ancient caverns, a hidden spring blooms beyond the kalpas; creeping vines slowly accumulate a cold green. In the scorching heat, there is no wind, yet ice fills the breast; at night—

In Chan, where even spirits and ghosts weep at the immovability of the mind, the boundless universe resides upon the tip of a single hair. In vain do you debate the ripening of the mind and its objects;
you have never yet come here to lean against this railing. Do not say you have traveled to Mount Xitianmu.

At Shōmyō-in on Mount Tōtenmoku, four scrolls were erected as temple plaques for Shōmyō, causing people to remember the Liang dynasty; how can this compare to merely maintaining one's ordinary routine?

The flower of the mind blooms within the Buddha’s hall; the resonance of the Way opens the Chan chamber. Were one not to ascend Mount Dongtianmu, it would be difficult to cause self and other to be forgotten.
Radiance is the very substance of clarity; when there is clarity, radiance is not obscured. Principle is attained beyond words; awakening is dissolved while sitting.

I recall from afar how Ma filled his belly; I turn my thoughts back to how Shi’s waist was crushed by a falling rock. Do not toy with the fleeting flow of time; life and death leave no room for indulgence.
The western peak rises steep and lofty; the eastern hall stands even more majestic. A fawn with white spots lies in its rocky cave; flowering birds peck at the *bìluó* vines.
The frost-bitten bamboo by the railing grows old; the rain-moss upon the steps is thick. You have not yet been willing to forget the mind-ground—what can this petty striving possibly achieve?
The Way-mind is luminous and clear; what need is there for bitter debate and evaluation? Sitting in stillness, there is no idle day; dwelling in cold, all alien feelings are severed.
Clouds cling to the jagged rocks; trees lean against the perilous cliffs in the clear weather. Reaching the summit of East Tianmu, the external world is exceptionally pure.
A *dhūta* practitioner sings of the true practice of *dhūta*:
"To practice asceticism is *dhūta*; not practicing asceticism is not *dhūta*. If one possesses a sincere heart for the Way..."
Listen now to this song of the ascetic *dhūta* practitioner: The ascetic’s practice is without measure: His tattered robe of many years weighs a thousand pounds;
Ice and snow reach his waist and pile upon his shoulders. In summer, when it is time to wash, he hangs it from the rafters with a rope.

Ascetic practitioner! His face is never washed. At the third watch of the night, he rises first; Blindly and without hesitation, he straightens his iron backbone. Who cares for the dust and grime that pass over him?

Both ears. Enduring the ascetic practice of *dhūta*, he abandoned home and family. Beneath trees and among graves, he forgot day and night; with heaven as his canopy and earth as his mat, he delighted in solitude.
With bare bones as his ultimate refuge, he practiced the most courageous *dhūta*, forsaking sleep and forgetting food as his mind attained self-conviction.
Holding fast to a single *huatou*, the iron-cast gate of his face was as cold as frost. Enduring the ascetic practice of *dhūta*, a hundred [times].
This is how it is done. Who cares about pulling the plow or hauling the mill? Sunk in lowly service, the heart accepts it of its own accord; let the natural skin-sack wear out as it may.
The ascetic who endures suffering is most worthy of pity. At all times, he is bare-boned and skeletal; when moving, even iron and stone would wear through by his friction.
In stillness, for years on end, he does nothing but face the wall. This ascetic who endures suffering knows no hesitation, even when met with the insults and humiliations of others.

Like floating playfulness, throughout one's entire life one dwells only as a neighbor to the Way. No matter who comes to deceive you, even if you enter the earth, the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) and austerities are difficult to compare;
they neither startle others nor are they long-lasting. The ascetic practices and austerities are difficult to fathom; they consist purely of true mind without artifice.
The ascetic practices and austerities are difficult to comprehend; with a single practice, one enters directly to the limit of the Tathāgata. The ascetic...
The ascetic practices of *dhūta* are difficult to annotate; they are as lofty as Mount Sumeru and as deep as the ocean.

When one fully explains these ascetic practices of *dhūta*, they are inconceivable—truly inconceivable. Yet, if these ascetic practices were suddenly overturned, that would be like a single branch of the *udumbara* flower.
The song of the mendicant on the Way:
truly a life of joy! With a single bowl in hand at ten thousand households and a thousand doors, it is not that there is no food in the monasteries, nor is it that one’s own home lacks provisions.
Rather, it is because of the subduing of the banner of self-conceit, and the desire to sever the greed and attachment of sentient beings.
He severed [his ties]. An ancient Buddha once renounced the dignity of a ten-thousand-chariot sovereign; day after day, he descended upon seven families to bestow salvation.

Whether receiving abuse, being met with shouts, or being trampled under the feet of a drunken elephant, all these were his body of adorned merit. Benefiting others and benefiting himself, he was called a Bodhisattva.
Among the sages and worthies of the three periods and ten directions, none attained realization without passing through this. I hold my bowl, my feet...
From head to tail, heaven and earth are vast; wherever the eye turns, there is nothing but the ancestral fields. Who cares whether it is a pint or a pinch?
Whether they give much or little, go out and clap your hands with a laugh. If they give little, it is simply enough to break open the purse of stinginess.
Some say there is nothing; following conditions with skillful means, they apply themselves to their practice. They serve until the storehouse is emptied and given away entirely;
they overturn the alms bowl and take nothing at all. From the beginning, the intent was only to break your stinginess, not to nourish the body as a master of proselytization.

Wandering through the human world and visiting every village, one is not bound by illusory sounds or empty forms. Entering short alleys and threading through long streets, one moves the body with untrammeled ease.
The mind follows its own course as it goes and comes. Encountering villages and meeting mountain inns, he idly holds up his alms bowl once; he speaks in vain of Tiantai and Wutai.
Whether you have a thatched hut or an official residence, it is all but one whole black alms bowl. Picked up with a trusting hand, there is not the slightest lack.
There is not the slightest lack; there is nothing to be grasped. Returning from begging with the bowl in hand, all matters are forgotten. One.
Twice a day one requires gruel and rice; these are simply procured from within the alms bowl. First, there is no worry about stingy donors;

furthermore, one rejoices that the local authorities do not subject one to interrogation or punishment. Setting out in the morning and returning at dusk, whether there is anything inside or not is known only to oneself.

A lifetime’s journey passes away just like this; why worry that eyebrows are not worn above the eyes? The purse of stinginess is torn, the banner of pride is toppled, and radiance shines from within and without the alms bowl.
Both hands drop from the void; a clear breeze blows through the four walls of the thatched hut.
Sitting upright on the grass mat without companion, one leisurely recounts the twelve months of the year from the beginning. The First Month.
1. The alms bowl does not need to be sought from others. In the second month, the spring wind blows across the great earth;
the alms bowl is adorned above and below with a thousand flowers. In the third month of spring, Lingyun realized the Way; the alms bowl also knows how to laugh and turn over.

In the fourth month, the monasteries all observe the *śīla* of restricted movement; the alms bowl does not allow itself to be bound by others. As time passes in a flash, the Double Fifth arrives; the black-lacquered bowl.

Dancing on the Street of the Alms Bowl. On the sixth day of the sixth month, within the alms bowl there is no third summer heat. In the autumn of the seventh month, the myriad phenomena of the universe are gathered within a single bowl.

On the Mid-Autumn Festival of the eighth month in the human world, people mistakenly take the alms bowl to be the bright moon. When the yellow chrysanthemums cover the ground, they know it is the ninth day of the ninth month;
yet the "black bowl" looks up at the sky and opens its great mouth. On the tenth day of the tenth month, in a single day, the alms bowl is doubled.

Crossing the damp; the moon is established in the month of Zi. The bottomless almsbowl cannot be lifted. As the years reach their end and the winter solstice concludes, there is no need to attach a new handle to the bowl.
The light and shadow of the human world flow as swiftly as a stream; tomorrow, at the start of the New Year, it shall begin once more.
What is it that is being spoken of? Deshan used his staff; Touzi carried his oil; Xiangyan climbed the tree; Xuefeng rolled the ball.

No matter how many tens of thousands of miles the Patriarch traveled from the West, swallowing the Red Land with his light and spreading the Way throughout the Divine Land—how can these compare to my own holding a single bowl, attaining freedom at all times?
The Song of the Wandering Monk:
A seven-foot black staff forged of cast iron, How many times have I snapped it against the mountains, yet it never broke?

Held crosswise or used upside down for twenty years, It has never left a trace wherever it touches. A pair of straw sandals originally have no soles; How much more so when threading through hair from a tortoise?
Two ears deeply enclose ten toes; when stepped upon, wind and clouds rise from all four sides.
I have but a single bowl, neither of clay, nor gold, nor tin. Morning after morning I rest it at the crossroads, yet the discerning monks all fail to recognize it.
Three kinds of requisites accompany me as well; in heaven and on earth, there is no separation from the mundane dust. Thus he grants—
Where shall I go? I shall travel on foot; the four seas are empty before my eyes, with no neighbors near. Traveling on foot, I come; traveling on foot, I go;
the karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no foundation to rely upon. Traveling east, traveling west—the path lies within the breast; who knows it together with me?
If someone calls me a "traveler," I laugh until I fall over in the wind before Huang Fanche. I do not emulate the old Zhaozhou; I run!
The superior man seeks out the gate of play and jest; casting his gaze, he knows not the breadth of the lakes and seas. Taking a step, he only complains that heaven and earth are narrow.
He flaps his arms to brush away the clouds beyond the heavens; he turns his body to pierce through the colors of a thousand mountains. Sometimes traveling on foot, it is yet otherwise:
gazing at mountains and gazing at waters, he simply follows conditions. He does not linger in this land, nor does he go to the Western Heaven; he has no need for Mount Wutai.
Visit Śrīparvata; do not seek Mañjuśrī on Mount Emei. Realize that the Great Way is as straight as a bowstring;
the road to Chang’an is free of thorns. Having feet, one must travel—what can be done? From the Buddhas and Patriarchs down to the present day, they have been drifting and hurried.
If you wish to know where the "phantom-dwelling" traveler has arrived, the mechanism was already revealed before you even stepped through the door. If you ask me further when [this will happen]...
Returning to Western Zhejiang, he saw that I had once moved my feet;

he realized for himself that the songs of the Buddha-dharma are interpenetrating and without interval, such that the four sages and the six classes of beings share a single pulse. This is truly because delusion and enlightenment are but a fleeting moment.
Arising! Both rising and sinking are accomplished by oneself. The ancients were as straightforward as a taut string;
they leaped forth before the trigger, without discrimination. Observe where they land—beyond all deliberation. "What is the Buddha? This is accomplished by oneself; do not suffer needlessly.
The white tuft of hair between the brows fills the universe. Since ancient times, none have been willing to turn their heads back to look; for what reason do you merely follow after others?
It is accomplished by oneself; it is most direct. Every movement is governed by that eighth consciousness, which lightly transforms into the radiance of the perfect mirror.
Not even a hair’s breadth of effort is required to seek it from others. It is accomplished by oneself; it is difficult to evade. One may fall into the trap of the sword or the pit of fire.
Only now do I know that karma does not come from without; it is entirely because one has turned one's back on one’s own numinous light.
It is created by oneself and cannot be undone. For generations, ignorance has accumulated like a deep ocean; with the jaws of a donkey and the chin of a horse, they know no shame.

Even a Buddha can hardly teach them to change. It is created by oneself, yet I want you to know: quickly recognize and break through greed, anger, and delusion. The three realms have no root and no master.
Master, who is the enemy in this cycle of birth and death? It is you yourself; you must awaken to this quickly. There is neither the West nor this land;
since I first trampled the Iron Ring Mountains, my very heels have been the path of non-arising. It is you yourself; you should believe with vigor.

Face-to-face, there is no need to discuss distance or proximity. If even a hair’s breadth of sentiment regarding ordinary or sage remains undissolved, you will roll back into the realm of demons as before.
The military formation is something one makes for oneself; it is the true principle. Bodhidharma has no teeth in his mouth; when he opens his mouth, he reveals his iron heart and liver.
If you intend to accept this, it is still not it. It is something one makes for oneself. What is it? When encountering circumstances and meeting conditions, there is nothing that is not possible.
Since when have there ever been ghosts or gods under heaven? Calamity and fortune, gain and loss—all lie within me; I, too, make them myself.
It is attained. Man also attains it for himself. Longevity or early death, poverty or success, movement or stillness, speech or silence—all these are attained by oneself alone.

It is attained by oneself; yet even when one understands that it is attained by oneself, there is no "attaining by oneself. To claim it is attained when one has not attained it is called "not attaining by oneself.
As for attainment, when has it ever been truly attained? It is attained by oneself; it is attained by oneself. My repeated exhortations are only for the sake of clarity.
Ultimate! A man who has finished his business knows nothing more. Please wait for the future to ask Maitreya.
This song of the paper-cloak practitioner is a priceless livelihood: from a single sheet of mountain-river paper he cuts a cloak; stripped bare, it is white, pure, and radiant.
Floating. A most transcendent mountain of form, a wish-fulfilling jewel. Sometimes he sits; the piercing winds and frost cannot blow through him.
Sometimes he walks; the rustling spring breeze moves upon the earth. Sometimes he is neither moving nor still; inside and out, empty and luminous, he is a mirror that reflects the mind.
Reed flowers and the bright moon are his closest companions; within a single mass of snow, the warm spring is hidden. What need is there to speak of Qin’s hemp?
Furthermore, the *bingyue* ramie cloth, the Wu brocade, and the Shu brocade are even more laughable. They were made in Qingzhou and weigh seven catties;
how can they compare to me, who am naked without a single thread yet have ten thousand strands spread out? This total functioning is most natural and true.
How could one speak of such wealth and honor to others?

Song of Mastery over Water and Clouds: I love the water and clouds for their constant mastery; They move spontaneously and at ease, without change or alteration. Directly beneath them, a thousand mountains flow on;
Far off they face the setting sun, scattering their colors. The water has no mind, and the clouds have no mind; In this very state, there is simply no "now" to cover.
There is no past. A mere span of growth in the void is neither far nor near; a vast flood in a hoof-print is neither shallow nor deep.

Water and clouds—no one can fathom them. Though the universe is broad, they cannot be confined. Ten-thousand-li whale-waves swell in the eastern sea; a thousand-fathom dragon-light illuminates heaven and earth.
Water and clouds harmonize with the minds of sages and worthies; unfolding and rolling forth, they do not touch the dust of the mundane world. They bring down the great rain.
How could his bestowing of grace ever exclude a single person? Water and clouds are precisely what accord with my Way. Radiant and brilliant is its light; vast and rolling is its sound.
Ghosts and spirits cannot fathom its mechanism; from beginning to end, there is nothing to seek in vain. The practitioner dwells here amidst these waters and clouds.

Sovereign and sovereign, without end or limit; the perfect clarity soaks the void and azure within its reflection. Within the brilliant light, the vast emptiness is concealed. Water merges with clouds, and clouds merge with water;
water and clouds are sovereign, sharing the same principle of Heaven. I see that your mind, O Guest, merges with the water and clouds;
you should know that such sovereignty is beyond compare. When guests arrive, we shall together gaze upon the inscription on the beam above, looking up and down at the water and clouds.
Who does not know? This sovereign mastery has continued until this very day; transmitted for a hundred generations, it knows no end.

Amidst the song of pine blossoms filling my granary, I have dwelt in illusion for half my life at Mount Xitianmu. I have always loved these mountains as if they were my own flesh and bone; yet when the broken cauldron lacked rice, I could not bring myself to eat.
Bedding. A slender waist, bound by three strands of hemp; a neighbor comes knocking at the door in broad daylight. Laughter and chatter fill the house as he speaks.
Do you know that the old pine blossoms outside the house are far superior to a farmer’s thousand measures of millet?

They are fit for rice: their jade awns and golden filaments shine with brilliant luster. They are fit for congee: their azure snow and purple mists are richly fragrant. Pressed into cakes, they are like ice.
The snow coils like the shadows of dragons and snakes, kneaded into a single mass; smoke and clouds heave and swell, their jagged teeth cold.
I have heard that the flowers of a thousand-year-old pine turn to stone—who among us, mere commoners with eyes of flesh, could recognize it?

Yet you still intend to seek out its branches and pluck its leaves to examine them; I say you have never tasted this food. Without the labor of the plow or the toil of cultivation, autumn tides sweep across ten thousand miles, driving wind and thunder. I...
Doubting the crow and the hare, they topple the eight-cornered millstone; they exhaustively grind the void to pieces.

Had they not grasped it with a free hand before the pivot of the mechanism, by the time they blinked their eyes, they would have missed it all. Vimalakīrti needlessly sought food from Gṛhapati Gandhottamakūṭa; stretching out his hands to cultivate the field was but a waste of effort.
Who knows that it resides right here under the eaves? For ten thousand kalpas, one must ensure that hunger does not prevail. A-he-he!
Who can discern it? The mossy steps have been swept clean, yet the granary is not empty; the bright moon and spring breeze are once again in disarray.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guanghui of Mount Zhongfeng in Tianmu (Concluded).
The Dharma Words of National Teacher Puying, Master Zhongfeng of Tianmu.
To show the Zen practitioner Zhengwen that one who is a true child of the renunciant path must sit and don the robes before being worthy of receiving offerings from devas and humans:

according to the teachings, "sitting" refers to the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharmas*), and "robes" refer to gentleness and patience (*kṣānti*). According to the Chan school, "sitting" refers to...
This is called "non-retrogression in a single thought. To speak of "clothing" means to have a thorough awakening to one's own mind, free from all branches and leaves.
If this is not the case, then even a thread of silk or a drop of water must certainly be repaid with care; the eyes of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past cannot bear to see such things.
This Dharma-gate of ambrosia is opened not for the sake of seeking ease and comfort, nor for seeking leisure and idleness;
it is not for seeking to exalt one’s affairs to spread a fine reputation, nor for seeking to accumulate great stores to pursue evil profit.

Beyond the three robes and one alms bowl, everything else was regarded by the ancients as superfluous possessions; thus they frequently performed the rite of purification (*śuddhi*) and did not hoard or amass them.
