You should know that a single moment of doubt causes one to fall into the realm of Māra. Precisely when applying oneself to the practice, the mental states become disordered and delusive thoughts proliferate.
Do not inquire whether it is good or evil, real or false; do not concern yourself with these at all.
Simply apply yourself to the *huatou* (critical phrase). Rest firmly upon the very phrase you are investigating.
After a long time, the various distracting thoughts of dullness and agitation will naturally subside. Even if they do not subside, do not forcibly suppress them; you must simply practice.
When the right mindfulness of one's practice is continuous and dense, it is sufficient. When this right mindfulness of one's practice is firm and dense, thoughts will naturally subside.
Once thoughts have subsided, there will be the prospect of a sudden, transcendent awakening. Having awakened, one will naturally possess a point of insight.
One might say that regarding future lives—whether they are illusory or not—and whether there was a great or small awakening with Master Dàhuì, there are many such things and yet many are not;
these are naturally understood within the sphere of one's own mind, without depending on questioning others.
Since you have not yet awakened, do not idly contemplate these miscellaneous matters; it will only serve to increase your dullness and distraction.

Much! To show Zen practitioners that there is something truly vital in practicing Zen and studying the Way: birth and death, impermanence, are no mere child’s play. One must sit and cut off all emotional consciousness.
Polish and refine your resolve; forever sever the taints of attachment and forever forget anger. Do not give rise to a frantic mind or speak recklessly of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Contemplate this *huatou* until it is cold and clear. Exhaust this lifetime without ever abandoning it for a moment. If you seek swift enlightenment, you will instead fall under the influence of demons.
If you simply do not grow lax, what need is there for "fierce intensity"? This matter is fundamentally neither difficult nor easy; it simply...
Maintain right view and remain free from delusion or distraction; what cause for concern is there not to understand the intent of the Western Patriarch?

To instruct practitioners on the practice of *gongfu*, one must simply harbor the great matter of birth and death within one's breast and, seizing the *huatou*, apply oneself with diligent perseverance.
Investigate this with deep, continuous intimacy. Simply ensure that the mind does not falsely follow external conditions and that there are no divergent views.
It matters not whether you are courageous or not, nor whether your practice has become a solid mass or not; proceed with a relaxed and long-term commitment of body and mind.
After a long time, you will naturally awaken to clarity; it is certain that you will not fall into anything else. If you depart from this right mindfulness, regarding the subject and object...
To engage in conceptualization and understanding, for even a fleeting moment in the mind, and to calculate gain and loss or attainment and failure—
all these belong to delusive conditions and are not right mindfulness.
To all you practitioners of Chan in海东 (Haidong):

this morning and tomorrow morning, the new year follows upon the old. Birth and death are impermanent; you merely follow along with the crowd. Pay no heed whatsoever to worldly dharmas or the Buddha-dharma.
Focus single-mindedly on one point: investigate the critical phrase, remaining instantly present upon your meditation cushion and beside your Zen board.
Who cares whether it takes thirty years or twenty? Extinguish body and mind; let go of ambition and spirit.
Add diligence upon diligence; augment valor within valor. Endure until emotions are forgotten and views are exhausted. Then, each and every one will find the heart empty—truly the highest degree.
This was spoken by Huanzhu (幻住), on the fourth day of the new year, for the sake of all Chan practitioners of the Eastern Sea (Haidong).
On the Double Ninth, shown to various Zen practitioners of Haidong:

Today is the ninth day of the ninth month; yellow chrysanthemums are found everywhere. As for that single phrase you have investigated, simply devote yourself to guarding it with long-term perseverance.
Guarding until the aperture of the mind opens—there is definitively no before or after. A carp from the Eastern Sea flies up into the heavens;
startled, the Dharmakāya emerges from its hiding place in the Northern Dipper.

To the Chan practitioner Keongnang (who resides at Nancheon-sa in the Capital): *Hae-dong Ko-ung* (Seal of the Eastern Sea) *Chan-jin* (Dharma Disciple) *Jung-gi Nam-cheon-sa* (Residing at Nancheon-sa in the Capital)
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth do not obstruct the eye’s light; brightness, darkness, form, and space dissolve back into one's own self.
Every thought and every movement of the mind is none other than oneself; seeing forms and hearing sounds are originally and spontaneously manifest.

"Since you have not yet returned, when you return you shall attain it. Who can compete for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes? Such words as these—anyone with even a modicum of intelligence will know them upon hearing them. However...
I grant that you may have memorized much and spoken with fluency;
yet, if you wish to achieve a ten-fold liberation from the delusions of birth-and-death beneath your very heels, you are worlds apart from this goal.

Not only on the shore of birth-and-death, but even while the sun shines brightly in a clear blue sky, with eyes wide open, facing sounds and forms, meeting with favor or adversity—the arising and ceasing of a single thought-moment [remains].

To merely dissolve and pass through appearances is not enough. Even if you can digest every instance of right and wrong, favor and adversity, this is still just playing with the spirit—a ghostly livelihood of grasping at a master.
Of what use is it? Nowadays, people everywhere are taught to practice Chan;
for the most part, they practice only this kind of Chan, valuing only the verbal communication while seeking nothing of heart-wisdom. If it were...
This most spiritual mind has never once been awakened within the field of reality.

No matter how many hundreds or thousands of times you allow your clever and brilliant disposition to run through the bellies of Śākyamuni, Bodhidharma, Linji, and Deshan in a single moment—piercing right through to their hearts and lungs—it is merely a state of deluded madness running outside. Reality...
Those who are truly determined to resolve the matter of life and death will resolutely refuse to tread this path;
they rely solely on a single, seemingly meaningless "head-word" (huatou) for investigation, holding it directly before them like one who is as good as dead.
One must possess only a single mind of true inquiry and earnest investigation, never giving rise to even a single thought of delusion that seeks to understand Zen or the Way.
Even if Śākyamuni and Maitreya were to pour forth all their samādhis into your heart and belly while you are in the midst of inquiry, you should spit them out then and there.
I am willing to exhaust my very life without ever fully mastering the Buddha-dharma; I simply will not settle for anything less.
Before awakening, do not recklessly direct your conscious intellect toward the extraordinary manifestations of others to grasp even a single drop.
To do so is to erroneously enter the field of consciousness; this is called the saliva of wild foxes that can cause one’s eyes to see flowers in the air, leading one to wander madly outside.
This is utterly disastrous. If you continue your inquiry until the end of your days, you will attain clear realization within your own person.
He has no destination; he is truly a person of the highest purity.
You need only have faith that does not regress, and in future lives you will certainly be granted a time of true awakening and clarity.
If you are impatient and wish to understand Zen immediately, this very impatience is itself what casts you into the net of saṃsāra.
This is indeed a matter of concern. Old Miaoshan said, "The essence of this school is difficult to grasp; you must apply yourself with meticulous care.
Old Huan spoke thus only because he wished for people to reach a definitive resolution regarding the great matter of life and death.

He did not want people to merely take their mental consciousness and engage in intellectual excavation of past and present on the path of meaning. If you cannot pass through the barrier of birth and death, then when it comes time...
Practice by treading the ground of reality. Even if you merely wish to be proficient in Chan Buddhism, it will not suffice for you.
Nevertheless, as the Venerable One requested words of admonition, I, Old Huan (this humble one), have written them.

Furthermore, it was said of old that "the divine light shines alone, a sublime legacy for all eternity. Upon entering this gate, do not harbor knowledge or understanding. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also states:
"To establish knowledge within seeing and knowing is the very root of ignorance; when there is no seeing within seeing and knowing, this is precisely nirvāṇa. From...
Whether it be the Buddhas above or the Patriarchs, they swept away the intellectual understandings of practitioners; this was not done out of necessity.

For they knew that this Way is a Dharma-gate of uniform equality: as vast as the earth that supports all, and as expansive as the sky that covers all, there is no place for you to harbor a calculating mind.
There is no place for you to pay attention; there is no place for you to exert effort; even there is no place for you to squat or sit.
It is simply a matter of seizing the opportunity and acting before you have even defecated. As soon as you attempt to engage in deliberation or thought, you lose the connection.
People nowadays, seeing such statements, immediately take them up with their conscious intellect and fall into the net of intellectual understanding, failing to seek true and authentic awakening.
If you have not yet achieved a decisive awakening beneath the heels of your feet, then no matter how much you may carry away with your mind,
intellect, and consciousness all the similar phrases from the *Chuan deng lu*, you will merely rely upon them to form intellectual interpretations.
I have spoken of this single flavor: that this matter is inherently complete. Buddhas and sentient beings have from the beginning lacked nothing.

In our daily lives—whether putting on clothes or eating meals—all is the manifest samādhi. If you further intend to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere with your mind, you will merely be gouging a sore into healthy flesh.
What you say is quite plausible, yet alas, you have never attained awakening at the point where emotions are forgotten and consciousness is exhausted.
Ming said: "Because they do not awaken, their verbal explanations become more intimate while their cognitive attachments grow ever more intense.

Those who truly seek to investigate and clarify the great matter of life and death will never, while unawakened, allow themselves to harbor false conceptions or falsely claim to understand the Buddha-dharma."
At all times, rely solely on the phrase you have taken up for investigation—a word devoid of meaning—like biting a raw iron stake.
Bite it incessantly from morning until evening; if you cannot bite through it this year, resolve to bite through it the following year.
Even if you cannot bite through it, strive on without retreating and continue biting without interruption.
Let alone thirty or fifty years—bite until you reach the ultimate point. You will surely find the moment when there is a sudden snapping and a bursting through.
If you simply maintain this essential confidence that must bite through, remaining steadfast and unchanging, what else could there be?
That you have not resolved this great matter is because your right mindfulness in pursuing the Way has been neither firm nor dense;

you have never established a secure footing upon the koan you are investigating. Now, having happened to hear someone speak of "semblance prajñā," you have set about learning it through the intellect.
If you persist in such erroneous views, yet wish to achieve true awakening and clarity, it is like taking a step backward while seeking to advance.
Previously, there was no such principle. The Senior Seat Master Ke’ung possessed the brilliance of a keen intellect and harbored the great resolve to settle the matter of life and death.
For no apparent reason, he had initially become entangled in a certain kind of superficial intellectual understanding.

Only after remaining in the mountains for over three years has he recently come to believe with certainty and is no longer deluded by such intellectual interpretations. Now, suddenly stirred by thoughts of his hometown, he has established a great resolve.
In the latter years of his life, he exerted all his strength to investigate and penetrate the depths, hoping to attain authentic awakening.

He again produced paper to request further admonitions. Consequently, I cited the previous words to tell him: "There is yet another 'final word' at the very end, which I entrust to you with both hands. Do not seek transcendence within the realm of awakening;
do not merely guard at the periphery of what you have heard, clinging to views and knowledge. Take this to heart, take it to heart!"
To Master Ling-sou, Former Head Seat (Residing at Wanshou Monastery in Fengzhou):
The Essential Resolution for Zen Practice is to resolve the doubt regarding birth and death. Once this doubt is resolved, all distinctions of right and wrong are simultaneously resolved.
Having thus reached such resolution, one finally realizes that there has been "not a single thing" from the very beginning; within this state of no-thing, [all is complete].
This is the state of being free from doubt. There is neither birth-and-death nor resolution; there is likewise no one who receives such teachings.
All things are gathered back into oneself. Without thinking of good or evil, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is originally equal.
To reach this point and yet say there is even so much as a speck of dust that is Buddha, Dharma, Chan, or the Way, is to fall into delusive conditions.
Moreover, if even the teachings of Chan and the Buddha-dharma are still delusions, what doubt or lack of doubt could possibly be non-delusory?
If you have not yet truly attained a thorough penetration beneath your own very self and clearly seen the ultimate source,
you will merely indulge in delusive views within a mind of worldly toil and falsehood, interpreting the words "originally there was nothing" through mere intellectual sentiment.
With consciousness, you engage in deliberation and conjecture, saying, "There are no three realms from which to escape; there is no nirvana to be realized.
While what you say sounds plausible, it is merely that both you and your speech have become deluded views.

To attempt to liberate oneself from birth and death by means of such deluded views is no different from carrying firewood to extinguish a fire—it only causes the flames to blaze more fiercely. This is impossible. If you are truly...
One must apply diligent effort. First, place this great matter of birth, death, and impermanence firmly within one’s breast, without a moment’s interval of distraction.
Solely maintain the *huatou* (critical phrase), advancing straight ahead with this present physical existence as the limit.
By all means, do not engage in prior deliberation or subsequent calculation; whether you succeed or fail, practice in this very manner.

Practice. Persist for a long time without changing or wavering. When the work becomes mature, artifice is forgotten; all delusions dissolve. One enters into awakening through this state of neither perceiving nor knowing.
Now, as for being mature or immature, and whether doubt arises or does not arise—the ancients said, "There is no secret formula for practicing Chan;
it simply requires that the matter of birth and death be urgent. You must take this great matter of birth and death as your primary concern.
This mind is most urgent and most authentic. From this very state of urgency and authenticity, there arises a state of total doubt; naturally, no effort is required to dispel it.
Through long-term cultivation, this becomes the most pressing matter of birth and death. If the mind is uninterrupted, then from beginning to end, everything will flow as one.
What other dharma could serve as an obstacle to your progress? It is simply that your right mindfulness regarding birth and death is neither true nor earnest.
You merely persist in forcibly raising the *huatou* and violently arousing the state of doubt; you will certainly not attain awakening.
You may only force yourself for a time and maintain doubt for a time, but once that forceful mind slightly recedes, the doubt will likewise fade.
The fundamental principle [of practice] and one's emotional state will both be lost together. You need only ensure that your cultivation is not inconsistent;
do not force yourself to give rise to doubt. It is sufficient simply to contemplate death and impermanence once and observe it.
When you reach a point of helplessness where there is no other expedient means to break through, there is only one thing to do: suddenly and forcefully bring up the *huatou* once more.

Practice it together with them. Whether you succeed in practicing or not, practice in this very way. When you reach the point of being at your wits' end, that is precisely when your training has matured;
yet even then, do not harbor thoughts of having mastered it. Simply continue practicing, attaching yourself to the head and tail of the matter.
If you practice in this manner, there is no possibility that you will not attain thorough realization. It is said to be difficult.
The *Yījīng* (Book of Changes) all judges people according to their own measure and makes distinctions; in reality, there is absolutely no doctrine of "easy" or "difficult.

Consider, for instance, Deshan seeing the paper candle blown out and immediately realizing how to take it up, or Lingyun seeing the peach blossoms and at that moment attaining realization—such karmic conditions, are they easy or difficult?
One should know that from the perspective of Deshan and Lingyun, they were easy.

Regarding others, however, it is not so easy. If you do not truly take the great matter of birth and death as your own primary responsibility, and instead merely resolve to consult and inquire with the hope of seeking correct enlightenment, then even if one were to provide a word-by-word commentary on each of the seventeen hundred public cases and teach them to you until you understand them, it might be called "easy.
Little do you realize that while understanding the words is easy, penetrating their true meaning is difficult.
When the delusions of birth and death are taken as real, it is difficult indeed—difficult beyond measure.

However, if you can simply take up a single *hwadu* (critical phrase) and investigate it closely and continuously, there is no need to inquire whether it is difficult or easy. After a long time, when the mind is enlightened and the nature is thoroughly penetrated, the distinction between difficulty and ease becomes nothing more than a superfluous burden.
"The word 'Mu' and burning [the paper] away—'Which of these is my nature?'—these are already two."
This is important. If I were to show you another koan, it would only lead to excessive confusion and cause your practice to become fragmented.
Today, simply take whichever of the two previous koans you have mastered;
stand firm upon that which you have mastered and, with total commitment to life and death, remain one with it for ten thousand years in a single thought-moment.
Go ahead and practice. Practice without ceasing until, in one place, you penetrate a thousand places and ten thousand places all at once.

Practice until both delusion and enlightenment are forgotten, and the boundary between the holy and the ordinary is simultaneously obliterated. Looking back then, the seventeen hundred cases of idle talk and long-winded discourse will appear as nothing more than golden dust in the eyes.
Be careful, be careful! For three years I have not written a single character, nor have I spoken with anyone.
Since my elder brother has traveled so far to visit me, I have not realized that this digression has become as tangled as a creeping vine; I shall say no more.

Regarding the instruction given to Chief Seat Hyeon-jeon concerning the cultivation of *kung-an* (meditative work), it begins with the arousal of the "doubt-mind" (*yi-ch'ing*). One should know that this doubt-mind originally has no teacher’s instruction, nor does it have any fixed form or substance.
There is no cognition, nor any handle, nor any direction, nor any expedient, nor any contrived arrangement or such matters.
Furthermore, there is no other principle by which one could dispel it to cause you to give rise to doubt.
That which is called "doubt" is simply that you have not yet [resolved] this great matter of birth and death for yourself.
It is clear and evident. It is simply this doubt regarding the great matter of birth and death: for what reason have we wandered from immeasurable kalpas ago until now?
What is its fundamental nature? Furthermore, for what reason will we continue to flow from today until the end of the future, with no certain time of liberation in sight?
This very point is the locus of doubt for all Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past.

All of this arises from doubt. By doubting without ceasing, the path of the mind naturally becomes severed, emotional delusions dissolve, intellectual understanding vanishes, and subject and object are forgotten.
One does not realize it, but suddenly there is resonance; this is precisely the moment when the essence of doubt is shattered.

The ancients of old never merely looked at the "head" of a phrase or studied public cases (kōan) to put on a show upon their meditation cushions; they simply applied themselves with intense earnestness.
Utterly perplexed regarding the great matter of birth and death, he encountered a person after traveling three or five thousand li;
before even taking off his straw sandals, he went straight to question him: "I am concerned because the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift.
Thousands and tens of thousands of people are all like this—leaving home, traveling on pilgrimage, seeking out a teacher, and studying the Way. At first...
It is not for a second purpose; even if one were to have it, one would not employ it.
Since later generations, there has been an excessive amount of manifest proclamations and entangling vines within the lineage school.

Often, before one has even stepped across the threshold, they are led away by this sort of talk and fall into the nest of such entanglements, calling them "Buddha-dharma" and calling them "Chan and the Way."
They have fallen into the net of intellectual understanding and cannot lift their heads;
they merely increase their erudition, which serves only as a cognitive hindrance (jñeyāvaraṇa) and has truly never had any contact with the Way.

Consequently, the venerable masters of recent times could not bear to see this one malady and corruption within the monastic communities. Before you have even opened your mouths, they simply take up a single "meaningless" koan.

He thrusts the "head" (the critical phrase) before the student. He simply instructs you to relinquish all worldly conditions, mental distractions, and even the language and texts of Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma;
he teaches you only to take up this head-phrase and investigate it with great doubt. When you are investigating in this manner, it is not for the purpose of seeking to understand the Buddha-dharma.
It is not for the sake of attaining mastery in the Way of Chan, nor is it for the sake of seeking all-encompassing knowledge and understanding that one practices.
That which the mind applies itself to in practice is solely this: being unable to bear the great matter of one’s own birth-and-death and impermanence.
Therefore, when the kōan is broken through, the great matter of birth-and-death is simultaneously shattered along with it.
When the great matter of birth and death is clearly understood, then all speech and writing are simultaneously clarified.
Apart from birth and death, there is no other "head phrase" (hua-tou); apart from the head phrase, there is no other birth and death.
Although those of antiquity only doubted birth and death until they attained enlightenment, people today only doubt the head phrase until they attain enlightenment. As for that which they doubt—
While the outward manifestations of these matters may appear to differ, the Way of awakening is in reality neither ancient nor modern, neither mixed nor distinct.
When you are precisely in the midst of doubting the *huatou*, do not seek expedients; you must believe that in the practice of Chan there are no expedients.

Do not seek a direction toward which to proceed; you must know that in the practice of Chan there is no direction. Do not seek a handle by which to grasp it; you must know that in the practice of Chan there is no [handle].
The handle. What is called "expedient means" (upāya) is precisely this *huatou* (critical phrase);
it is the very path toward awakening, and it is the handle. However, one must simply have sufficient faith and a stable reliance.
In this life, one should investigate this *huatou*, determined to achieve a thorough breakthrough (*dache*) upon it. If one has not yet broken through, there is initially no obstruction.
The obstacle lies simply in your own lack of a certain intensity, a certain steadfastness, a certain non-retrogression, and a certain degree of conviction and stability.
You need only be able to maintain the right mindfulness upon the *huatou* you are investigating;
do not concern yourself with dullness or distraction, nor with movement or stillness, speech or silence.

Do not concern yourself with their birth, old age, sickness, or death; do not concern yourself with their suffering or pleasure, or with favorability or adversity; do not concern yourself with their success or failure, and so forth.

Apart from the right mindfulness directed toward this very *huatou* (critical phrase), even if the Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations were to appear before you simultaneously, you would not be moved by them, for they could not overturn the unsurpassed essential dharma of the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If it enters your heart and belly, you must also vomit it out at that very moment; do not concern yourself with it.
For this matter does not reside within Buddhas or patriarchs, nor within external conditions, nor within words and letters, nor within intellectual understanding.
It rests solely upon your own capacity to reach the ultimate point of faith regarding the great matter of birth, death, and impermanence. Therefore, nothing can withstand it.
What is birth and death? It is the very phrase of the ancient masters used for investigation (*huatou*).

Apart from that single thought of investigating the ancient's phrase, if you further intend to seek it out within a second thought, it is much like stirring up waves in search of water. An ancient said, "It is hidden right beside you.
And yet, how could there ever have been a single dharma given to others to be seen or heard, or to be maintained or guarded? Only today—
I shall teach you how to observe a *huatou* (critical phrase). This is already a matter of necessity;

yet, if you were to depart from this *huatou* to engage in further discursive thought or calculation, you would wander further and further away from the essential point. After a long time, when your practice has matured and the right moment arrives, the doubt will be shattered.
You must know that the doubter, the practitioner, and even the *huatou* itself are all struck back into one’s own self, such that not even a single [fragment remains].
The Dharma accords with reality; furthermore, there is not a single dharma that can be characterized as either realized or unrealized.

Therefore, the teachings state that the myriad phenomena of the universe are all stamped by this one dharma, yet even this very one dharma has no place to be sought. How, then, could there be such a thing as a "head of discourse"?

Simply cultivate a heart of resolve; you will certainly not be deceived. The Zen practitioner Hye-don has resided in the Sangha Hall for some time, yet he has not attained penetration regarding the *hwadu*.
He has come forth with paper to request instruction, so I have answered him directly with these words.

The four characters "Show the person practicing meditation how to turn the light back upon themselves" represent the ultimate state of being uniquely liberated from ordinary sentiments and transcending into the realm of great enlightenment.
Since your practice has not yet reached this stage, for the time being, how do you turn the light back? How do you reflect?
If you have not yet reached the state of true awakening and clarity, there remains the principle of returning and turning back; all such states are merely self-deception.
For when one has attained thorough penetration, the light of the mind returns without needing to be turned back, and awakened illumination returns without needing to be brought back.
This is because there is nothing upon which to depend. There is no light to be returned, nor is there any illumination to be brought back.

This is called the Samādhi of the Single Practice. From the Buddhas and Patriarchs above, everyone has taken their stand right here. It is by no means something that can be reached by the delusions of the conscious mind or intellectual thought.
Nowadays, there are certain foolish people who, in quiet and secluded places, withdraw their sight and hearing and cut off all visual and auditory perception, remaining like wood or stone;
they call this "turning the light back to reflect. Even if one were to practice such reflection for thirty years, it would be of no avail.
In every thought-moment, you must resolve to liberate others from birth and death; you may not do otherwise.
Simply take up this "Mu" (無) from Zhaozhou’s case and give it a sharp, vigorous lift. Investigate it by day and examine it by night; harbor doubt while walking and apply pressure while sitting.
When you are looking at it in this very manner, you must by no means entertain the notion of reflecting inwardly. Simply investigate that which cannot be grasped. Precisely...
This is the moment of casting off the body and relinquishing life. After long and thorough cultivation, one suddenly attains awakening;

it occurs without one’s own prior awareness, and the process of turning the light back to reflect upon itself is complete. If you further attempt to conceptualize this as "turning the light back to reflect," you remain as before—never having awakened.
For the practitioner who stands on no ground (Wudi Chanren), I, [Name], have written these words of admonition at his request.
To show you: according to what has been said, the Lord presides throughout the twelve periods of the day; you cannot help but recognize Him.
Apart from the very phrase you are investigating, what else could be called the Lord? You should know that this very phrase is your Lord yourself. Simply keep it so.
This koan one investigates does not depart from the activity of the mind; this is what it means to "be the master. Yet, one must not give rise to the thought that one is the master.
The ancients never spoke of "being the master" in their fundamental intent. When Yangshan said, "Do not forcibly assume mastery;
do not follow worldly sentiments," he was merely using words to inspire diligence at that moment; it was not his ultimate teaching.
Furthermore, there is the claim that drowsiness and distraction are matters of observing the "head-phrase" (huatou) from the perspective of whether they are favorable or adverse.
This teaching has no principle that is difficult to understand at first; it is simply that you do not understand it yourself and thus forcibly produce intellectual views.

For instance, while you are in the midst of observing the head-phrase, if states of drowsiness, distraction, favorability, or adversity should suddenly manifest before you, you must immediately rouse yourself.

Direct your mind toward the states of dullness, distraction, and the favorable or adverse conditions. After practicing for a long time, these dullness, distraction, and deluded attachments to the favorable and adverse will naturally vanish.

When some people see these states of dullness, distraction, and the favorable or adverse manifesting before them, they immediately give rise to a fleeting doubt, wondering what other expedient means there could ultimately be to eliminate these habits of dullness and distraction.
Furthermore, they place the blame upon their own spiritual capacity (*indriya*).
When this mind arises due to past karma and various circumstantial conditions, it merely adds further dullness and distraction upon existing dullness and distraction;

likewise, amidst favorable and adverse circumstances, it simply increases those very conditions. Therefore, when you are subject to dullness or distraction, I instruct you to observe right within that dullness and distraction.
It is not that there is some other thing to be observed, nor is it a matter of observing dullness itself.
What is distraction? I am not instructing you to separately seek out the "nose-ring" of confusion, laxity, favorability, or unfavorability.
I am simply instructing you to take up the *huatou* directly upon states such as confusion and laxity, looking into it yourself, never letting go.

Furthermore, do not falsely give rise to a second thought to discriminate between this being dullness or distraction, or favorable or adverse, nor that this is not dullness or distraction, favorable or adverse.
In general, when practicing *gongfu*, one only needs to awaken to the *huatou*. It does not require you to dispel dullness, distraction, and so forth.
You should simply harbor a deep sense of urgency regarding the great matter of birth, death, and impermanence, single-mindedly holding the *huatou* and giving rise to great doubt.

One seeks correct awakening through sincere application of the mind. It is only when the thought of birth and death is urgent that the *huatou* (critical phrase) will naturally become continuous and dense.
When the *huatou* is thus maintained with density, states such as dullness and distraction will naturally fail to appear.

Whenever you perceive dullness or distraction during the practice of *kung fu*, it is simply because your resolve regarding birth and death is not urgent, and your mindfulness of the *huatou* is not dense.
Furthermore, it is said: "To give rise to doubt regarding the *huatou* (critical phrase) is feared to fall into the trap of discursive thought; this is an error.
The ancients did nothing other than seek a resolution for this great matter of life and death, traveling thirty or twenty years' distance, or three thousand or ten thousand li.
Whenever I meet someone, I ask about the great matter of birth and death. When have I ever looked at a *huatou* (critical phrase) to give rise to doubt?
Although I do not look at a *huatou* to give rise to doubt, this very mind that has not yet resolved the great matter of birth and death is precisely the point of doubt for the ancients.
The students of the present day do not even take birth and death as their primary concern; how much less so, then, the complexities of the Chan school!
Excessive speech has become rampant; even before one has stepped through the door, one’s primary concern is already the memorization of words and phrases.
Consequently, that which serves as the correct mindfulness for life and death is completely severed.

Thus, the venerable masters of recent times have had no choice but to plant this "meaningless" *hwadu* (critical phrase) within your storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), instructing you to cast away all intellectual understanding.
Focus solely on the point where this statement is not understood;

let that which you doubt be like encountering a silver mountain or an iron wall, such that there is not even an inch’s worth of space before you to advance. As soon as a second thought arises, you have fallen into discursive reasoning.
To simply not give rise to a second thought is precisely the state of doubt. Within that very state of doubt—

However, once you have severed all illnesses of intellectual understanding and conceptualization, and suddenly encounter and overturn that which you doubt, you will finally realize that a single word or half-sentence from the ancients is truly a great mass of fire or a hair-piercing sword—something not to be trifled with.
Simply cultivate faith; there is nothing it cannot resolve.
Instruction for the Zen Practitioner Jizu (Residing at Fayun Chan Temple in Changzhou; style name Fuan; Dharma heir of the Master):
Why did Zhaozhou speak of the word "wu"? These eight characters constitute the Eight Gates. Each character must be treated with full intensity and brilliance.
Observe whether you are merely vague and indistinct—half-asleep and half-awake, as if something exists yet nothing is certain—if you practice in this manner.
It would never be realized even in a donkey’s year. Zen practice consists entirely of a single mass of spirit.
If your spirit slackens even slightly, you will be led by the two demons of dullness and distraction into a den of chaotic thoughts and delusions, where you engage in inverted activities.
When you reach the point in your practice where your spirit seems to fail, you will suddenly experience a sharp awakening; only then will you know that even this very spirit does not exist.
At the very moment of attachment, one sees that the self is the school (zong), and the school is simply the self. Outside the school there is no self; outside the self there is no school.
To speak of "only the self" and "only the school" together is merely idle talk.

Since a Chan practitioner seeks words of admonition, I have thus recorded this directly and composed a verse for them: Why did Zhaozhou say "No-Character"? Let neither the self nor the school be discussed.
Exert yourself to the utmost to penetrate to the very bottom. Then, even where there is no Buddha, you may claim the title of Honored One.
To the Zen student Xiong (the Dharma heir of Master Yu), he asked:
"At the moment when the four elements disperse, where will you settle your body and establish your life? If you truly wish to awaken and realize this, [you must do so].
This is for yourself alone. However, throughout the twelve periods of the day, simply raise this very *huatou* (critical phrase).
Adhere to it from beginning to end; without interruption, go straight ahead with it.
While you are practicing, do not at all seek verification through any language, texts, intellectual paths, or principles. When working on the practice, do not seek rest elsewhere.

Rest. Furthermore, do not concern yourself with whether the ancients’ methods of practice are the same or different; as soon as such a thought arises, you fall into intellectual understanding and will never be in accord with the Way.
First, you must completely let go of all prior views, understandings, and interpretations regarding Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma.
Second, you must suddenly [take up] the great matter of birth and death.
Within the breast, moment by moment, be as if saving one's head from fire; if you do not attain sudden enlightenment, do not cease until it is achieved.
Third, you must be able to maintain mastery and stability. Even if you have failed to awaken for a long time, never give rise to a second thought to seek elsewhere.
Whether it be life or death, share in life and share in death. Possessing such a sincere vow, grasp—
Once you have attained meditative concentration, you will surely reach the day when your mind attains the "first place" of emptiness. Zen practitioner Xiong, simply believe this and take it to heart.
Furthermore, this Way has no front or back and is beyond all deliberation; if you attempt to apply your conceptual mind, you will be thousands of miles away and have no connection to it at all. You—
If you do not direct your mind toward it, there will be no place for you to settle.

When you apply yourself to the practice and contemplate the *huatou*, body and mind will be forged with such vigor into a single unity, like a silver mountain or an iron wall. Since body and mind have already become one, [how can there be separation?]
When person and environment are encountered in their essential nature, they are fused and interpenetrated, leaving no room for there to be "knowing.

If one were to know them as "one piece," then they would immediately become two pieces or three pieces; how could there be any principle of fusion then? This is the true practice of the present moment.
Do not ask whether it is one piece or many pieces. Simply have a day’s worth of spirit and investigate for that day.
As years pass and months deepen, you will enter through awakening without even realizing it; this will certainly not deceive you. Rely solely on your own single-minded, resolute faith.
Aside from the question of why Zhaozhou spoke of the word "Wu," when you encounter others speaking of Chan, [do not seek anything else].
Having said this, he spat directly into his face. Life and death, impermanence—these are no small matters.
You must devote twenty or thirty years of solid effort, treading the ground with your feet, and persevere until you have exhausted yourself. Do not fear that the turtle will escape from the jar.
O valiant practitioners of Zen, simply believe in and follow the teachings in this way; let it be as you go toward the eastern mountains or the western waters.
Furthermore, if one has truly attained a state of being "fused into one piece," one does not even perceive it as a silver mountain or an iron wall.
Once one perceives it as a silver mountain or an iron wall, it cannot be called "fused into one piece. For now, do not ask about being fused into one piece.
It does not form a single solid piece. Simply take up the koan you are investigating and persistently follow it from beginning to end, examining it moment by moment.
When you investigate until the reach of the conscious mind is exhausted and all intellectual understanding has vanished, awakening will occur spontaneously, without being noticed or known.
At the very moment of awakening, delusion and enlightenment, gain and loss, right and wrong—all are simultaneously transcended; there is nothing more.
One must question others to seek evidence; then one will naturally be secure and at ease, for there will be no such complications.
Be meticulous, be meticulous. When you reach this stage, you must allow your chest to expand and remain open for many years and months.

Furthermore, to exert one's own strength while harboring thoughts for the peace of others is the mental application of a bodhisattva. If one simply maintains this mind directed toward the Way, then there will be nothing that does not accord with the Way.
As the Master of Old (Laozi) said: "Knowing the masculine, he maintains the feminine. This is what it means.

To be a valley for the world: to be a valley for the world means that one’s constant virtue (*changde*) is never absent from them. To be called "masculine" means to rest oneself while laboring for others;

to be called "feminine" means to rest others while laboring for oneself. It is like water gathering to form a stream; so too does constant virtue abide within the person and cannot be separated from them.

In practicing the Way, there is no distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, the crooked and the straight, or the difficult and the easy; it simply requires that one be mindful of nothing else.
Always be cautious and never be indolent; then every step will be upright and not deviant. Simply believe that one’s own mind becomes a Buddha and do not seek it outwardly.
Naturally, mind after mind will be straightforward and free from crookedness.
It is only when this practice fails to take root, when doubt cannot be aroused, and even when hundreds of thousands of obstructive conditions manifest simultaneously.
If this mind that seeks to investigate and clarify the Great Matter remains concentrated and unwavering, then the principle will be easily understood and not difficult to realize.
However, whenever one encounters any point of difficulty in the course of one's spiritual practice, it is entirely due to obstructions created by one’s own mind.
If this mind is willing to be exhausted [of its habitual tendencies], one will reach the stage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; there is nothing else whatsoever.
As for those who create obstacles, if one’s right mindfulness in training the Way is simply permitted to reach its full completion, who cares whether it takes thirty years or twenty?
One will naturally become steady and secure, without even a trace of doubt.

How could there be external obstacles arising from without once one has attained self-acceptance? Maintain the mind of the "female" (submissiveness) with uninterrupted thought after thought; this is true accumulation.
Through long-standing effort, he ceased all contrived activity. As his cultivation became single-minded and his maintenance of the practice steadfast, the conditions for the Way were fully perfected;

everything he encountered was revealed as true. Proceeding spontaneously without deviation, he attained mastery over all phenomena. He proceeded directly toward the realm of the World Hero (the Buddha) without even realizing it himself.
How magnificent! How magnificent! While the eminent Chan practitioner was staying alone in the mountains, an elder from his hometown...
Having no place to lodge this single sheet, I have yielded it to you. My heart’s sense of righteousness is thus in profound accord with the Way.
I have transcribed these words from paper as a warning and exhortation for all occasions; therefore, I have recorded them directly in my own hand and left them to you.
Written by the old phantom [Name].
To Zen Practitioner Yuan of Japan (residing at Zhenru Chan Temple in the capital; his style name is Guxian; he is a Dharma heir of the Master):
This mind, when deluded, becomes birth-and-death; when awakened, it becomes nirvana.

Yet, while the delusion of birth-and-death is indeed difficult to dispel, you do not realize that the nirvana of awakening is likewise but a speck of gold dust before the eye. You should know that Prajñā is like a great mass of fire.
I do not permit any lingering attachments. Your mind for practicing the Way is not sincere and earnest.
You cannot, at the very first thought of the dawn, sit and cut it off with total blindness. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you must remain stark and rigid like one who is truly dead.
You must sever all reliance on the kōan you are investigating. Yet, whenever you fail to maintain this continuity in sitting, you give rise to conceptual fabrications.
One conceives thoughts of difficulty and thoughts of ease, giving rise to a proliferation of discriminatory emotions and delusions that intermingle within the breast;

unable to sever them at every instance, one establishes ten kinds of solemn vows, desiring to rely on the power of these vows to cut through floating thoughts and illusory fantasies like stones pressing down grass.
Yet, even with the establishment of a thousand kinds of solemn vows, they cannot be suppressed, and one’s resolve instead becomes increasingly lax and distant.
That you do not contemplate the impermanence of birth and death is the single greatest causal condition from time immemorial.
If you truly desire to achieve resonance with this reality, there is no other expedient means whatsoever; there is only one point of inquiry:
directly and immediately discern a single piece of resolute right mindfulness that is non-regressive, unchanging, and immutable—sharing in life and sharing in death.

It is the same regarding death. Even if, while you have not yet attained awakening, a thousand Śākyamunis and ten thousand Maitreyas were to pour forth the Buddha-dharma from the four great oceans until it entered your faculty of hearing, it would all be nothing but false and delusive toil; none of it would be ultimate.
It is simply that your single right mindfulness is not stable enough; thus, your invertedness and recklessness follow a thousand paths and ten thousand tracks without any end in sight.
Be meticulous, be meticulous! Yuan Chanren, exert yourself!
To Zenman Zesheng (who resided at Jing-shi Zhenru Chan-ssu; later styled Ming-sou; he was a successor to the Master):
Long ago, a monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha? Mazu replied, "The mind itself is the Buddha. This single phrase is direct...
These people are all soft-headed and stubborn. They claim that everyone has understood it; yet when you ask them, "Which one is your mind?
they point east and west, identifying form and identifying emptiness, speaking of doctrines and principles—turning further and further away from the essential matter.
Since the mind cannot be pointed out, what then do you call "Buddha"? It is simply non-existent.
Regarding the place where one seeks the head: you must know that this matter can only be attained through genuine awakening.

If you have not yet awakened, no matter how long you spend your life identifying "this very mind as Buddha," when the time comes for your eyes to fall from their sockets, you will not find even a mind to grasp, nor will you find a Buddha to grasp.
You will then endure the cycle of rebirth, and by then it will be too late for regret. This is what is called...
As for those who practice Zen, people like you are as numerous as stars in your own village.
Yet how can they compare to one who takes up the "Mu" (無) koan of Zhaozhou, plants their feet firmly, and with a single breath of total blindness, presses forward in their inquiry?

Unless they personally reach the ground of great penetration and great awakening, they will certainly not rest. If you can establish such a resolve and investigate in this manner, after a long time, you will suddenly—
Upon awakening, one realizes that "the mind itself is Buddha" and this "wordless" (mu-zi) are both merely superfluous words.
This was written by the old deluder [I, so-and-so] for a person of noble lineage and wise Chan practice who seeks words as a stimulus for self-examination.

The attendant Shizi Haiwen reported that from the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs above, he had been earnestly concerned that the matter of the great cause and condition of birth and death could not yet be fully resolved. For kalpas,
he had deeply perfumed and refined himself within the ocean of Bodhi, never abandoning even a moment of time, until finally, within the Dharma of Bodhi, he cast aside [all attachments].
Regarding hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings, one views wealth, status, and affection as no more than flying dust passing before the eyes.
With single-minded diligence, one takes up the "tasteless" kōan of the ancients;
beneath the three-legged pole and before the seven-foot mat, one forgets cold and heat, abandons sleep and food. If one does not reach great illumination and great rest, [it is all in vain].
This ground is inexhaustible. Possessing such a structural integrity, each individual must penetrate to the very top and bottom, with beginning and end forming a single thread.
Only then should one take what has been attained and re-smelt it within the furnace of others, refining it again and again until every speck of dust is purified and one emerges white and clean.
Thus, one may sport with ease upon the shores of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; this is called the mind.
Those who pass the examination on emptiness are not like people of today, whose footing is so superficial that they refuse to die their hearts and minds to turn toward the ground of reality.

They stubbornly plant their feet to seek true liberation, valuing only the memorization of texts and the cultivation of habits through speech and hearing, desiring only to understand Zen and consider it finished.
Little do they realize that the great matter of birth and death lies at one's very heels.
Below, it remains as ever a vast, dark expanse; not only does it provide no benefit, but it actually harms.
At the request of the attendant Wenzhai, I offer these words to serve as an exhortation for his path toward entering the Way.

Furthermore, in practicing the Way, one need only have sufficient faith. From the very first thought of believing in the teachings, one should proceed in this manner for thirty years without ever giving rise to a second thought.
The more one fails to penetrate through inquiry, the more one should increase one's diligence; the more one fails to achieve realization, the more one should press forward.
Exert yourself with even greater vigor. When you encounter that which cannot be grasped or realized through inquiry, do not allow even a single moment of doubt or deluded view to arise.
Do not give rise to various intellectual interpretations, whether regarding ordinary beings or sages; these will cause you to fall entirely into the pit of birth and death.
When you fundamentally fail to realize through Zen inquiry, do not say it is because your faculties are dull, nor do you say it is because your karmic obstructions are heavy.
Do not say it is because the time is late; do not say it is because you have not met the right person.
The essential point is simply that your correct mindfulness regarding birth and death is neither true nor earnest. If this mind were truly earnest, what would thirty years matter?
Even for thirty lifetimes, one would not give rise to fear. One must press forward with utmost urgency and resolve. As the ancients said:
"When the fishing pole is worn away, plant bamboo anew; do not calculate the time or effort, but rest when you have attained it.
If you do not possess such a disposition, your practice of Zen and study of the Way will be nothing but inverted views. This is what those who truly follow the Way ought to maintain. (Text)
The attendant encouraged him. Old Huan spoke thus:
"To Elder Liaoyi of Dinglin, I say:
'If you are truly realized, all matters are finished. But how can you be said to be realized? If you wish to seek a place of realization, [look at] everything.'"
To employ the mind is entirely like wind and waves on level ground; there is no place for you to find understanding.
Simply take this one instance of Zhaozhou’s "Why did he say 'No'? and plant it firmly within your breast. In silence, devote this entire life to it.
With a firm and dense body and mind, endure and persevere with it. Precisely while enduring and persevering, you must not seek intellectual understanding, nor must you...

This is not a matter of understanding. Both understanding and non-understanding are but deluded views. If you dwell within these deluded views, you will wander on and on without finding a point of realization.
Simply take the koan you are investigating and hold it across your chest. Investigate it this way today; investigate it this way tomorrow.
Within that which you are investigating, there will surely arise all manner of extraordinary and wondrous states.

When the realms manifest before you, they are entirely demonic apparitions. You must not, for even a second thought, recognize them or attempt to dispel them; nor should you engage in conceptualizing them as objects to be grasped or rejected.
If you do so, this mind will merely fall into the realm of the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*), making it extremely difficult to liberate yourself from the roots and dust of birth and death.
It is precisely because of this that one fails to attain awakening and clarity after thirty or twenty years; therefore, you must only apply yourself further.
One attains firm and dense realization. Living together with them and dying together with them, one relies upon the single thought-moment of the kōan, remaining steady and secure.
Without moving or wavering, after a long time, divergent thoughts do not arise and delusive thoughts settle into stillness.

At a point where there is no longer any conscious awareness, one suddenly experiences a sharp awakening; only then does one know the Way of Ultimate Oneness. This was [attained] before the time of traveling as a mendicant.
It has already been fully realized; it is simply not a matter of waiting for something else to be realized in order to be realized. This is called "Dinglin" (The Forest of Certainty).
If you have never had such a genuine awakening and clarification once, you cannot call this "realization," nor can you call it "one.
To even attempt to call it "Dinglin" is still far from it. My words are not empty. —Yi Chan.
In the human realm, mindfulness is continuous and dense. Your years are still at their prime; you possess every capacity to transcend the ancestral Way.
Provided you can discern the heart of resolve, you will certainly not be deceived.

Furthermore, two arise from one; even that one must not be clung to. The moment you blink your eyes, you have already fallen into a habitual trap. Where can this matter be found with even a fraction of room for deliberation?
To know where to return directly is already to have traversed the journey. As for Chan practice, it is simply this.
You must be able to strike with total blindness even before the signs of manifestation have yet divided. Furthermore, you must not act in haste or with superficiality;
you should simply resolve to devote your entire life to this matter. If you do not discern it in this life, you must resolve to bring it to fruition in a future life.
This matter is fully present within your very being; even after passing through thirty lifetimes, you need not fear losing even a single hair’s breadth of it.
It is essential that you achieve a sudden, thorough awakening regarding the practice of death; this is precisely the moment of "passing the examination with an empty mind.
If you cannot die away the thieving mind and instead attempt to grasp at the meaning within words and phrases, you will fall into the realm of conceptual thought.
Even if you manage to understand the Way or understand Chan, you do not realize that it is merely madness.
He went outside. A Zen practitioner of vigorous age, possessing the resolve for true inquiry, came once more to the mountains seeking admonition.
As the ancients said, "If you only distinguish a heart of sincerity, you will not be deceived. What further need is there for admonition?
Exert yourself!
Zen practitioner Shiyi, the entire reality of the Buddha-dharma is already fully present within you. As soon as you give rise to even a single thought directed toward the Buddha-dharma—
Once you have fallen into this state, you have already descended into the realm of the conceptual mind; for kalpas on end, you will not be in accord with the Buddha-dharma.
If you truly do not wish to let go of the great matter of birth and death, yet do not don the burden and take it up at the moment before a single thought arises, [you will never succeed].
Simply take up this koan: "When the four limbs are scattered, where does one find a place to settle the body and establish one's life?
No matter where you may dwell or sit, investigate it closely and continuously.

While investigating, do not retain even half a word of any sutras, teachings, principles, or the words of public cases from the ancient and modern traditions of the Zen school that you have previously memorized.
Keep it within your breast; do not let even half a word hang upon the surface of your lips.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, remain steadfast like one who is a great dead man. Simply maintain this single phrase you are investigating, holding it up alone.
If you do not retreat after doing so for a long time, there will naturally come a moment of transcendent, sudden awakening. If you have not yet personally reached this state of true awakening...
At such a time, you merely take your mind, intellect, and consciousness and attempt to reconcile them with similar-sounding words for understanding.

No matter how much Zen, the Way, or Buddha-dharma you may comprehend—carrying it away like a full load—it is called "munching on the drool of wild foxes. For ten thousand kalpas, there will be no point of realization or discernment for you.
Zen practitioners, take this to heart! Take this to heart!
For the practitioner of Zen, simply have faith in the teachings, take up the koan you are investigating, and set aside fixed time limits;
persevere in your practice for a long duration, and there will naturally come a time when awakening occurs. You must not give rise to any doubts or hesitations during formal meditation.
Furthermore, one must not give rise to a mind that seeks sudden awakening. It is like traveling on a road: when one's strength is exhausted, one arrives there naturally.

When practicing by focusing on the *huatou* (critical phrase), any occurrence of extraordinary, superior, or miraculous experiences—whether through seeing, hearing, knowing, or perceiving—is entirely a demonic condition (*māra-pratyaya*).
One should simply not give rise to a mind that pursues them; after a long time...
Then you will understand yourself. If you allow even a single thought of attachment to arise, from that moment you will fall into the realm of demons;
what you call "enlightenment" will instead become madness. Realizing the Way is like a person returning home:

since the objects and environments before you are already your own ancestral home, everything is naturally secure, settled, and clear, without the slightest trace of doubt. If you harbor [any such thought], it is not so.
If you harbor even a slight doubt, it is certain that this is not your original home; you must then exert yourself to seek instruction elsewhere.
Otherwise, you will merely end up forming heterodox views.
Investigate the "No-Character" (Wu). You must simply give rise to a state of doubt regarding this "No-Character. Investigate why Zhaozhou said "No-Character.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day, investigate in this very manner. At the very moment of investigation, do not ask whether there is conceptualization and discrimination or no conceptualization and discrimination;
for both having conceptualization and lacking conceptualization belong to deluded thought. Now, I require only this from you.
Simply give rise to the doubt-mind (*yiqing*) regarding the phrase you are investigating. Do not, at all times, engage in conceptual discrimination regarding any sensory objects or conditions.

However, apart from the phrase you are investigating, if you give rise to even a single thought—whether it be a thought of the Buddha or a thought of the Dharma—it is all incorrect mindfulness (*asamyak-smṛti*) and nothing but the seeds of birth and death. For one who is truly practicing the work of cultivation:
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, every thought-moment must be like saving one's head from fire. It is as if a single person were facing ten thousand enemies;
where could you find the leisure to apply yourself to matters of physical life or worldly conditions? What leisure is there to seek someone to reveal the truth for you?
Furthermore, what leisure is there to ask others for phrases or to seek intellectual understanding? Moreover, there is another point:
People like this, for three days, could not find anyone to enlighten them; their minds were thus left in a state of blank confusion, with no skill they could apply.
This is entirely a case of following after delusions and wandering in transmigration; such people are not those who practice the Way.

Generally speaking, one who practices the Way is like a thief wishing to steal another's gold and silks: when walking, he intends to steal while walking; when sitting, he intends to steal while sitting.
One must steal. When idle, one must steal in idleness; when busy, one must steal in busyness.
Furthermore, how could one be willing to reveal this heart of stealing so that others might see it? The more one desires to steal, the more one must conceal the mechanism with secrecy.
Heart to heart, thought after thought—thus for a long time without retreating, you will surely reach the station of the ancients. How could it be like those twelve hours of the day?
The master is not fixed; it merely follows along with the wandering of delusive thoughts while forcibly assuming the role of sovereign.
One sits upon the meditation cushion putting on a show, yet moment after moment one rushes about in pursuit, refusing to rest. When will there ever be a time of attunement? Take heed, take heed!
Like flowing light and shadow, time passes swiftly; you must quickly examine yourself.
To the practitioner Zenji:
in practicing Chan, simply have faith in a single *huatou* (critical phrase) and then investigate only that one. This is precisely what constitutes "correct investigation.
Beyond Zhaozhou’s “Why did he say the word ‘No’? there is also the phrase: "Where does the one return? which is currently manifest.
"Previously, you simply must not grasp at it. After a long time, it will naturally be forgotten.
For now, you should simply set aside a long-term mind and body to practice *chan*. You must by no means seek rapid attainment.
If you harbor the thought of rapid attainment, in the long run it will lead you into the net of intellectual understanding. In practicing *chan*, maintain only this one [mind]."

Maintain right mindfulness regarding the great matter of birth and death. Guard the phrase you have taken up for inquiry for thirty years, twenty years, or even for a single lifetime, proceeding solely in this manner.
Never, at any time, give rise to a single thought of seeking swift enlightenment.
As soon as this mind arises, it is already a deluded thought; it will never be in accord with the Way. You need only not seek sudden enlightenment.
When your practice matures and the proper time arrives, it is like traveling on a road:

though you do not expect to arrive, if you keep walking without ceasing or interruption, you will naturally get there. However, practitioners of Zen should simply believe in this way; do not harbor [doubts].
Those who study by imitating others in their pursuit of swift enlightenment fall into deviant paths.
You should take these words and speak them to all your fellow countrymen so that they may know them.
To the Zen practitioner Miaoran, I show this:
in practicing Chan, you need only have sufficient faith. Then, simply take up the *huatou* (critical phrase) and investigate it.
Do not use the conscious intellect to speculate upon "one" and "ten thousand. If you were to speculate, asking, "What is 'one'? What is 'ten thousand'? [you would only be lost].
Even if you were able to point it out with perfect clarity, you would still be wandering outside of folly and madness;
for eons you would not accord with the Way. If you can attain true conviction, you need not even ask what the "one" in "what is the one? refers to.
What is this "ten thousand"? It is simply the ten thousand of any given place. You need only take care that "one" is truly one, and "ten thousand" is truly ten thousand.
However, you must first establish a firm footing at the point where you ask, "Where does 'one' return? Then, take up the investigation for a single thought-moment as if it were ten thousand years.

When you reach the time of great awakening, when the mind is emptied and you attain the highest rank, then one is ten thousand and ten thousand is one; yet one is not ten thousand, and ten thousand is not one.
It is not one. This is clearly understood within the breast.

If you have not yet attained awakening, no matter how you may speak flowery rhetoric about "one" and "ten thousand," it will all ultimately amount to nothing more than inverted delusive thoughts. Yet, Master Ran believed this.
To the Zen practitioner Xuan:
Why did Zhaozhou say "No-word"? Simply, throughout the twelve periods of the day, raise this great doubt secretly and investigate it.
Do not at all doubt whether it is the same as the stories of the cypress tree in the courtyard or Mount Sumeru.

No. If you attempt to weigh and compare the mind-consciousness against the *huatou*, you will be led further and further into the net of karmic consciousness, where you will have no opportunity for awakening for kalpas on end.
In Zen practice, one must sever the life-root of birth and death; there is no other expedient.
You need only cut off all various views and intellectual understandings, relying solely upon the specific *huatou* you are investigating, regardless of the years that pass.
The years have been many and the distance long; entrust yourself with all your heart, and you need not fear not attaining enlightenment.
If you cannot rest securely in even a single thought-moment, you will give rise to numerous conceptual interpretations whenever you encounter things that seem inconsistent with the Way.

How could a mind preoccupied with conceptual interpretation ever possess the principle for severing the life-root of birth and death? Among the people of your own region, there has never been anyone who spoke of practicing the "work" (kung-fu).
As for principle (li), most people merely pursue it through intellectual understanding along the path of logic.

Even if you were to understand it so thoroughly as to break open Śākyamuni’s belly, it would still be nothing but a vast expanse of karmic consciousness—utterly devoid of the true point. Guishan said: "The essence of this school is difficult to attain."
You must apply yourself with meticulous care; this is no small matter. Simply discern a long-term, authentic mind and go forth to practice; you will certainly not be deceived.
Zhaozhou said, "It is because he still has the consciousness of karmic activity (*karmavijñāna*). This single phrase is Zhaozhou’s adamantine eye.

He does not say that you, the student, have the consciousness of karmic activity; rather, if you understand it from the standpoint of the consciousness of karmic activity, then together with Zhaozhou—
The adamantine eye is simultaneously blinded. Now, do not ask whether there is karmic consciousness or no karmic consciousness;
simply and solely maintain the previous statement. Do not turn your head; do not give rise to thoughts. After investigating this for a long time, you will naturally awaken.
Do not produce even a single point of intellectual view, nor should you ask about the arising of great or small doubts.
To "not give rise" [to thoughts] while merely maintaining this view is already to have turned one's head and given rise to a thought prematurely.

Their daughter, Lingzhao, said, "Neither difficult nor easy: the meaning of the Patriarch is at the tips of the hundred grasses."
Although the three sages spoke of the difficult as easy, they did not know that its immediacy and directness are like a taut string.
If you attempt to seek it within the categories of difficulty and ease, you will only end up being more crooked than ever.

Thus, the Elder of Vaiśālī said, "A straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), for it is free from all deviousness. If you have not yet been able to penetrate this principle of ultimate directness, [you remain deluded].
Cast aside all else; do not entertain a second thought. Simply take this phrase—"What is that original face of mine before my parents were born?"—and plant it firmly within your breast.
Investigate it in silence; pursue it with diligence; harbor it with persistent doubt; and practice it with solemn earnestness.
Continue until you reach the point where emotions are forgotten and consciousness is exhausted. Suddenly—

Suddenly, a fierce realization dawned. Only then did I believe that when deluded one is straightforward; when awakened one is straightforward; when attaining it one is straightforward; and when losing it one is straightforward.

Whether ascending to heaven or descending to hell, sitting upon a lotus throne or entering a pit of swords, there is not a single moment that does not perfectly merge with the principle of ultimate straightforwardness.
Reaching this point, there is no Buddha to be sought, nor are there any sentient beings.

It may be discarded. To be straightforward and yet more straightforward—this is the way of the Layman Ping of Qinwei, who styled himself Zhigan (The Straight Hall). He presented paper requesting that I provide words of admonition for entering the Way; I have thus responded with direct brushwork and appended a verse. To speak of straightforwardness:

when the conduct is straight and the mind is straight, that is true straightforwardness. To conceive of it through intellectual understanding is already to deviate and become estranged. Take up the *huatou* (critical phrase) in daily life and penetrate the teachings thoroughly.

To say this— [Verse] Straight conduct and a straight mind are what is meant by "straight. To harbor conceptual knowledge is immediately to go astray. Take up the *huatou* in daily use and exhaustively investigate the teachings. To speak of... (Note: The final character "箇" [gè] indicates the end of the verse or the sentence.)
It is like a string that has already traversed its course;

I show this to the Chan practitioner Xun so that he may understand that practicing Chan must seek awakening rather than intellectual understanding. Take these myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images—they are all sealed by a single Dharma.
To take such an explanation and harmonize it with one's own mind, using this interpretation to align with the intent of the ancients—this is understanding (*jie*), not awakening (*wu*).

With such an understanding, even if you were to string together the meanings of the seventeen hundred patriarchs on a single thread, it would simply be a vast expanse of karmic consciousness (*ye-shi*) with gold dust falling into the eyes.
If you wish to resolve the root and dust of birth and death, you will find that this approach is increasingly irrelevant. Only then can it be called... [the true state].
To rely on others for understanding while obstructing one’s own self-awakening—this is what is called "poisoned medicine entering the heart.
It is not what those who truly engage in study expect to find here. You, Master Xun, have traveled across the vast ocean from afar for the sake of the great matter of birth and death;
you must by no means apply your mind in such a mistaken way. My sincerest wishes.
To Layman Guyi of Yuet-am:

All phenomena are like the moon in the sky; fundamentally, they possess no marks of being full or deficient, nor of appearing or disappearing. Yet sentient beings suffer from the delusion of the eye and all claim that [the marks] exist.
Furthermore, there are those who see a second moon. If one wishes to clearly perceive the true moon...
As for the essence: simply take this phrase, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; to what does the One return? and place it within your breast.
Regardless of whether you are idle or busy, quiet or noisy, investigate it with constant, unbroken intimacy.

When your practice has matured through the passage of years and months, and the time arrives, you will suddenly awaken in a flash. Only then will you know that the entire universe and all under heaven are but a single moon.

In this hermitage, the radiance shines forth, pure white and free from dust; one cannot find even a single point of dualistic perception that distinguishes between "this is the moon" and "this is not the moon," or "this is the hermitage" and "this is not the hermitage.
Layman Guīyī, whose style name is Yuèān (Moon Hermitage), requested words of exhortation, and I have thus responded to him.
To show the venerable Shishangren that he is a monk of true substance: if one studies the Way without the diligence of even clipping one's nails, yet moves with the path for transcending the world,
how could one willingly give rise to self-defeat and allow oneself to be swirled by the various defilements on the shore of saṃsāric birth and death, failing to contemplate the way out?
To have one’s arm alone liberated—this is what the ancients meant when they said, "Simply go thus. That already involves traversing a path;
how much more so for one who has failed three times and does not turn back? What is this matter of birth, death, and impermanence? Do not be hasty or careless.
During the twelve periods of the day, at the moment you encounter objects through the senses, you must forcefully bring up the koan you are investigating and examine it closely within yourself.
Be absolutely careful not to turn your head or shift your body. Stand firm on your feet and seek a definitive conclusion right here and now.
If you do not reach this definitive conclusion, then you will simply be able to share in life with others and share in death with others;
what difficulty could there be in studying the Way? If your resolve is not firm and your footing is unstable, then in the blink of an eye, the white clouds [will have drifted away].

It has been ten thousand *li* since we last met. Master Shangren has come forth with paper seeking words on advancing in the Way; therefore, I have written this to answer him. I shall further provide a verse for him:

The patched-robed monk has no need for the labor of clipping his nails. In studying the Way, body and mind must be as swift as the wind. If one were to allow them even a moment’s slight relaxation, [the Way would be lost].
[This is] a mistake. It would still fall back into the duality of existence and non-existence as before.

To demonstrate the way of the dhūta practitioner, one who is determined to become a genuine and authentic seeker of the Way must simply be able to endure diligent toil, find sweetness in austerity, and possess fortitude.

In the cold of winter, you must endure poverty and hardship; you must undertake heavy responsibilities; you must forget fame and profit; you must cast aside affection and attachment; you must uphold the precepts; you must apply diligent effort;
you must resolve the matter of birth and death; you must investigate the Way of Chan; and you must realize the Buddha-dharma.
Having taken all these many tasks upon your own shoulders and brought them to fulfillment, I further require that you do not look for the faults of others nor strive to flaunt your own virtues.

Do not let your views and learning be dazzled by fame and profit, nor your senses by sounds and colors. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, close your two flaps of skin [your mouth] and establish a vow of single-minded resolve for ten thousand years.
Constantly maintain right mindfulness to guard body and mind; do not fall under the sway of external conditions, and give rise to neither hatred nor attachment.
