If you can practice without wavering and maintain this without change, then the single flower held aloft on Mount Ling will be plucked.
It has been long since you should have caused the Elder Kāśyapa to break into a smile before an assembly of a million people.

Only then would you not have made in vain your departure from parents, your severing of worldly ties, your shaving of beard and hair, your donning of ragged robes, and your practice of asceticism as one who seeks the Way.
If you cannot do so, then you are merely eating another’s food with your mouth, wearing another’s clothes upon your body, and sheltering under another’s roof.
Trampling upon the ground of others, they toil in vain without awakening, remaining in a state of dull ignorance. When one retribution suddenly ends, they must repay their past debts;
thus they change their form and transmigrate through the cycle of rebirth. What benefit is there in this for the ultimate principle?

The practitioner Daozhi composed a paper seeking words to serve as a lifelong admonition. I have therefore spoken these verses for him to show him: To study the Way and practice Chan, one must seek its fulfillment.

Walking with deliberate steps upon sword-blades and ice-ridges, one reaches the point where the path ends and turns back the head. Before the hall, the three wooden boards release their sound of meditation.
This is shown to the venerable person Benjing.
That which is currently speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, looking up or down, turning or walking, seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving—this is merely the deluded and inverted spirit;

it is not your own mind. If you wish to realize the true nature of your own mind, you must take the phrase, "Before my parents were born, what was my original face? and investigate it for twenty or thirty years. Directly...
Only upon attaining thorough awakening can one be said to have reached the ultimate truth. People from your region mostly practice Chan without ever reaching awakening;
they merely rely on their cleverness to study and interpret the explanations of Chan, falsely identifying the vivid, discerning awareness before them as their own true nature.
They refuse to apply themselves with the diligent effort required for genuine awakening, remaining entirely deluded and distracted on the outside.
"Run! This is truly a grave matter.
Master Shiyi said to the monk Yongjia:
"The man of the Way who has severed study and is non-active does not eliminate delusive thoughts nor seek for truth. This is what he said.
How many people have been deceived by talk and remain crouching within a state of "nothingness," ultimately unable to transcend it.
You should know that the principle of "absolute learning" (jue-xue) is not merely a matter of resting as one is;

one must reach the point where the mind is empty and passes the imperial examination, severing the very root of life once and for all in a direct encounter—only then is there absolute learning. Once there is absolute learning, then there is nothing.
For this reason, the Way manifests before you in its absolute clarity.
If you now truly wish to become intimately attuned to this Way, simply maintain the single focus throughout the twelve periods of the day: "Why did Zhaozhou say the word 'Mu'?
Resolve to spend thirty years seeking a clear understanding upon this very koan you have been investigating; then you will know that non-action does not require anything else.
It is that which acts spontaneously, such that every step naturally accords with it. Master Yi, simply take this as your realization.
If it were otherwise, it would not be something I know.

In the *Shiyang*, the first patriarch, Zhaozhou, states that the First Patriarch of Shaolin taught: "Directly pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood. Regarding the "directness" of this direct pointing: it is free from verbal expression;
were there verbal expression, it would not be direct. It is beyond thought; were there even the slightest thought, it would not be direct. It is without fabrication.
To engage in contrived fabrication is not direct; to obliterate cultivation and realization while still subtly involving them is not direct.
Thus, it was said that by the time the Sixth Patriarch reached Caoxi, even speaking of "direct pointing" had already become circuitous.
Under such a teaching, what further principle could possibly be admitted? The ancients, having no choice, instructed you to let go and rest.
Furthermore, instructions such as "teach you not to give rise to a single thought" or "do not deliberate upon good or evil at all"—such deliberations are entirely without merit.
You have received the title *Yangzhi* (Nurturing Rectitude) from the Head Seat.
If you are determined to nurture the rectitude of the direct pointing, simply place Zhaozhou’s “Why did he say ‘No’? within your heart-mind (*fangcun*). Do not question it.
Regarding the arising and non-arising of a single thought-moment, the principle is direct yet not direct.
Planting your feet firmly like a "T" shape, resolve to seize a single moment of true body and mind. Establish a resolute will and investigate in this manner alone.

Whether doubt does not depart, when you cannot penetrate the investigation, when you cannot maintain it, or when you cannot rely upon it steadily—on all such occasions, do not give rise to a second thought.
Act where you cannot act; walk where you cannot walk. Simply maintain this one true, urgent, and correct mindfulness regarding the great matter of birth and death—unchanging and unvarying.
What need is there to speak of thirty or twenty years? Stand like a wall ten thousand fathoms high and investigate until the end of your life.
Investigate until delusive emotions vanish and intellectual understanding dissolves, reaching a state of neither knowing nor...

Awakening suddenly opened up, like waking from a dream after being intoxicated; breaking into a cold sweat, he immediately saw that the Elder Vimalakīrti taught that the "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) is the direct mind, for it is free from all deviousness.

From the Buddhas above to sentient beings below, from the vastness of empty space to the minuteness of a speck of dust, there is not a single point that does not possess the principle of directness. This is called the name of "Nurturing Directness."
One must reach such a point; if one is straightforward, one is naturally so without waiting for cultivation.
If one does not attain spiritual awakening, then no matter how many things you hear or see, they will only increase your crookedness. You should exert yourself in this.
To the Chan practitioner Wei, [the Master] said:
"Neither think of good nor think of evil. At this very moment, what is your original face?
This very statement leaves you with no place for understanding, no place for comprehension, and no place for any mental application; there is only faith."
It is possible to attain it. One must earnestly take the great matter of birth and death as one’s own primary responsibility, undaunted by a period of thirty or twenty years.
Steadying one’s feet upon the ground, one must diligently seek realization beneath the three rafters.
Indeed, at the time of inquiry, there are no skillful means whatsoever, nor is there any fixed limit; even when dullness or distraction manifests before you, do not [yield].
You must attend to it. Practice in this way whether you can penetrate it or not; practice for a long time without turning back.

One day, when deluded consciousness vanishes and all artful contrivances are exhausted, you will suddenly awaken without even realizing it—this is the moment when your mind attains the "honorary degree" of emptiness.
Only those who regard the great matter of birth and death as urgent will possess true right mindfulness.

I can do so. When people from your hometown teach others to practice Chan, they merely cause them to engage in intellectual speculation within the faculty of thought, taking a superficial understanding of similar-sounding phrases through the consciousness as their realization. Such people will certainly not resolve the matter of birth and death.
You, Master Wei, should believe my words; I shall by no means deceive you.
To the Zen practitioner Sien (who has received the precepts):
Do not kill living beings; for killing cuts off the seed of compassion. Do not steal; for stealing cuts off the seed of joy and relinquishment.
Do not engage in sexual misconduct; sexual misconduct severs the seed of liberation. Do not speak falsely; false speech severs the seed of truth.
Do not drink intoxicants; drinking intoxicants severs the seed of wisdom. Do not harbor anger or engage in strife; anger and strife sever the seed of patience.
Do not let the bodhicitta regress. To lose the bodhicitta is to sever the lineage of the Buddhas. Regarding the above seven precepts:
if they are deficient, omitted, broken, or violated, one severs these seven kinds of pure, supramundane seeds;
yet if they are protected and perfected, one transcends the three realms, manifests the udumbara flower, and continues the lifespan of the Buddha.
This demonstrates the path of the Chan practitioner’s selfless,
reverent, perfectly still, and tranquil voidness— a state as impossible to lightly touch as a great mass of fire, and as impenetrable as the blade of the Great A sword.
Were it not for one who receives this wholeheartedly and merges with it through direct realization, there would be no place for you to apply even a single point of effort.
One may enter [this state] through skillful means; this is why Muzhou spoke of "the ready-made case.

Furthermore, an ancient worthy said that to say "there is nothing directly beneath one" already constitutes being buried. It is like a great mass of fire—how could it ever allow the mind to settle there?
"Before your parents were born, what was that which is your original face? Raise this up with sudden intensity and investigate it in this very way.
While you are thus investigating, if you further give rise to even a single thought of "how to" or "what to do," you will wander further and further away from the point.
When the monk Jing requested a word of exhortation on paper, I have therefore written these words directly to inform him.
When one contemplates non-self and perceives no self within the four great elements, then the sincerity of one’s reverence is complete and without deficiency.
Even when contemplating all phenomena and seeing no self in any of them, one does not need to wait for a separate object of reverence to pay homage; this is what is meant by "a single word."
It is complete. I respectfully urge you, Zen practitioner, to exert yourself. To Zen practitioner Song of Nanxu:
"The pine is straight and the thorn is crooked;

the crane is white and the crow is black. If you deliberate upon this, you will not realize it—there is a distance of one hundred and eight thousand miles. A monk asked Zhaozhou: [The rest of the koan follows].
"Ten thousand dharmas return to the One; to what does the One return? Zhaozhou said, "In Qingzhou, I made a cotton shirt that weighed seven *jin*.
In its manifest essence, there is no place for concealment; at this critical moment, it never lingers in verbal expression.
Here, you may not rely on cleverness, nor on intellectual understanding, nor on mental accommodation, nor on calculating estimation. You must simply be yourself.
The three-inch life-root of the household is suddenly severed from the ground and bursts forth; understanding is cut off, and subject and object are forgotten.
Naturally, at every step one transcends, and every beat is the command.

If you have not yet reached this truly matured and authentic field, you cannot avoid having two masters constantly presiding within the field of the eight consciousnesses throughout the twelve periods of the day. There is one person...
One who contemplates the impermanence of birth and death and seeks to clearly discern the practice of the Way;

and another who, amidst the worldly realms of love and hate, favor and opposition, does not allow them to pass by but resolutely intends to reach the ultimate realization—these two types of persons exist within one's own mind.
When one sees that the work of cultivation cannot be accomplished today, nor can it be accomplished tomorrow;
when one exerts effort this year, and again exerts effort next year—because of this exertion yet failing to achieve results, one gradually becomes discouraged.
Among those who travel the rivers and lakes, such cases of becoming discouraged because they cannot master their practice are found everywhere. Therefore, the former Master said:
I constantly teach practitioners of the Way not to give rise to a second thought. After a long time, they will naturally attain resonance.

But what do you call a "second thought"? It is simply when, while facing the bright sun and clear sky with your eyes wide open, you are unable to rely upon or maintain your grasp of the public case (kung-an), and instead shift from thought to thought toward the realms of the mundane body, mind, emotions, and consciousness.
If, for even a moment, a single thought as small as a mustard seed arises, this itself is precisely the second thought.
This very mustard-seed-sized second thought immediately connects with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of endless births and deaths;
how could this not be a difficult matter? Today, the essential point of studying the Way is precisely to address that which we ourselves possess.

Life and death are impermanent; regretting that one cannot break through in a single breath, how could one be willing to procrastinate through the years, letting time slip away, and remain complacent while following one's nature and emotions, waiting for oneself to sink into ruin? Deshan further said: "A thought tied by even a hair’s breadth..."
The karmic causes for the three miserable realms arise from a mere flicker of emotion, yet they result in shackling for ten thousand kalpas; these words encompass them all.
When Master Song of Nanxu came forth with paper seeking my words, I wrote this to answer him. Furthermore, I shall compose a verse for you.
When the "critical phrase" (*huatou*) penetrates where one turns for refuge, Buddhas and Patriarchs alike must yield to its power. Who would say that the gateway is about to collapse?
One must know that there are tall pines to provide support.
To the Chan practitioner Jiashen of Huichuan:
The great matter of birth and death is not something that ends with mere words, nor does it end with mere understanding.
All that can be said and all that can be understood is nothing but the karmic consciousness of saṃsāra from time immemorial; you must urgently cast it out. Simply and solely maintain the [practice].
Take up the *huatou* at the point where it arises; seize the true body and mind for the duration of this one life.
Sit beneath the three rafters like one who is already a great dead man. Cut off the breath within the breast, forget seeing and hearing, and extinguish all conceptual understanding.
Let there be only the single point of the *huatou* upon which you fix your footing. Just investigate in this manner. Even if you do not attain awakening in this lifetime, its—
The right mindfulness with which you engage shall remain unchanging and immutable. When you emerge in a future life, you will surely attain awakening upon hearing it once;
this is a matter of certainty. As the ancients said, "If you can simply distinguish the heart of resolve, you will certainly not be deceived.
Zen practitioner Jia of Huian requested words for exhortation, so I have shown him this.
Showing No Concealment to Chan Practitioners (Residing at Nanchan Chansi; Dharma heir of Master Yu). Dharma after dharma is not concealed;
from ancient times to the present, it has always been manifest. If you intend to look at it with your eyes, it has already been concealed.
This matter must be realized through awakening before it can be attained. If you have not yet truly awakened and clarified it, to speak of concealment is itself a concealing.
One may not say it is hidden, nor may one say it is not hidden.

If you truly and certainly possess a cause for awakening, then you may say it is hidden and yet not hidden, or you may say it is not hidden and yet hidden. To say it is hidden is not to be constrained by concealment;
to say it is not hidden is not to be obstructed by manifestation. This is what is called "mastery over withholding and granting."

This is what is meant by "meeting the source. If you have never personally reached this state, you must by no means act with haste or superficiality, nor should you fix your footing upon the delusions of the conscious mind and its emotions.
Rather, simply hold up the phrase you are investigating—that which is devoid of meaning—right before your eyes.
Do not give rise to any other secondary thoughts; keep your inner mind constantly cool and clear.
It is like ice and snow; it is as motionless as a withered stump; it is as vast as the great void; it is as firm as metal and stone.

Throughout one's entire life and until the end of time, it does not change, nor is it ever abandoned; it is not sought externally, nor is it interrupted. It proceeds forward without being separated by even a single thought.
Simply by holding fast for a long time, one will surely reach that state where, without knowing or perceiving it, there is a sudden and total illumination. This is it.

This means that when one’s mind attains emptiness and, having once reached such a state of extraordinary independence, one finally does not fail the original vow of leaving home and traveling on pilgrimage.
Nowadays, many students are unwilling to rely on this reality and perform the work of death;

they merely seek to deceive others with empty talk of Chan and the Way, thereby destroying the true cause and becoming the progeny of external paths—this is most certainly not what the Dharma-gate intends.
I look toward this very point. The Chan practitioner Hui bears the name Wuyin (No Concealment). Now tell me: when he is concealing, what is it that he conceals?
And when he is not concealing, what is it that he does not conceal? Unless you have personally severed the life-root, you must strictly avoid recklessly communicating any news of it.
Furthermore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one must never seek to hide it, nor seek to obscure it, nor seek to grasp at it;
even seeking to cast it aside and disregard it is not permitted. All such mental applications are entirely ineffective.
It can be attained. One must simply awaken to clarity by encountering the essence directly, with the whole body penetrating through.
One does not linger in expedient means, does not rely on functional activity, does not maintain cultivation or realization, and does not dwell upon merit or achievement.

Even to the point of not relying on a single thing—like water entering water, or space merging with space—thereafter, even the traces of that entry and that merging have no place to rest. This is called...
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of One Mark and Effortless Function (*anābhoga*):

nowadays, whenever people speak of this "effortless function," they immediately attempt to take it up with their own minds. To speak of effortless function while taking it up with the mind is, in fact, to dwell in effortful function.
One must not apply even a single point of mind; there is only the single, flavorless *huatou*.
Provided that you can believe with certainty, rely with stability, and maintain firm grasp, do not give rise to a second thought in any situation.
Single-mindedly investigate in this very manner alone. Even if you cannot penetrate it, do not give rise to a second thought to seek expedients or find external assistance;
such things will have no connection whatsoever. It simply requires that you believe with certainty and investigate in just this way.
After a long time, one naturally enters through awakening by means of neither knowing nor perceiving.
Once awakened, it is permissible to call darkness "light," and it is also permissible to call the hidden "manifest. All actions and activities are entirely free from fault.

The Chan practitioner Hei has presented this long paper seeking admonition; I have therefore written these lengthy words directly to entrust to him. Simply discern the mind of assent, and you will certainly [attain realization].
A Deceptive Display.
For the Venerable Lin of Zuzuan (residing at Wanshou Monastery in the Capital):
The Venerable Lin has previously studied under Śākyamuni and Maitreya; they were his servants. But tell me, who was he? Now...

People of this time who engage in this inquiry mostly seek to fall into intellectual understanding, falsely identifying with conscious emotions, engaging in inverted discrimination, and giving rise to false views;
thus they lose the Buddha’s wisdom and insight. From now on, simply inquire: "Why did Zhaozhou say the word 'No'?
At all times, throughout the twelve periods of the day, raise this up vigorously and inquire in this way at every place. After a long time, it will naturally become correct.
Awakened! Do not deceive one another; take note, take note!
Furthermore, apart from the single phrase of the *huatou* you are investigating, if there is any further mental activity—whether it be thoughts of the Buddha or anything else—it must be cut off.
Mental attention to phenomena, up to and including all conditions of good and evil, are all the second thought.
If this second thought does not arise for a long time, one will simply remain seated, cutting off everything upon the very koan under investigation.

After a long while, the state of meditative harmony and the koan investigated simultaneously transcend [duality], and one will see that the entirety of the ten directions is a field for the playful exercise of liberation. This should be understood.
This is the *Lao Huanzhu Mingben Shu*.
Furthermore, all the many words you have spoken are merely the provisional expedients of the ancients; they possess no ultimate reality. Within the School of the Patriarchs...
It is only valued that awakening occurs before the movement of the mind. If you do not awaken, then even hundreds or thousands of similar words will all become redundant speech;
they will all result in mere intellectual understanding and have no connection whatsoever with the great matter of your own person. The Buddha-dharma is like a great mass of fire:
if you intend to approach it, you will be consumed by its flames. Out of necessity, the ancients established a *huatou* (critical phrase) to restrain [the mind].
Regarding your point of entry, what room is there for deliberation? Now I require you to investigate why Zhaozhou said "Mu" (No).

If you cannot immediately and fiercely exert yourself in body and mind to sever all deluded thoughts of discursive thinking, and instead merely hold up the word alone, desiring to reach a definitive breakthrough, even though you do so, you are not yet a true follower of the Way.
If you further intend to plant your feet upon the expedient paths of those ancients, it will remain as incongruous as a donkey’s year.
You have come from ten thousand miles away today; I shall by no means deceive you. Do not ask what should be done or how.

Simply, during daily activities, raise the koan you are investigating with fierce intensity and push forward with a single breath. If you continue in this way for twenty or thirty years, a state of awakening will naturally arise.
At that time, when you look upon the words of the ancients, they will finally accord with your own realization. My most sincere wishes to you!
My most sincere wishes!

To the Chan practitioner Yi, I show that throughout all time and across the world, the Buddha-dharma transmitted by the Buddhas has never possessed a distinction between being "within" or "outside" the teachings.

When the Buddhas of antiquity appeared, they could not bear that sentient beings had lost their own nature and were delusively chasing through saṃsāra; thus, from within the realm beyond words and signs, they manifested [the Dharma].
In the Great Canon of the Teachings (*Tripitaka*), there is not a single word that does not serve to shatter birth-and-death for others and cause them to awaken to their own original nature. Alas!

Students of equal standing do not grasp the fundamental intent of the Sages; each is preoccupied solely with what they have studied and understood, claiming for themselves that they have realized the Buddha-dharma.
They speak at will, yet remain unaware that they have never awakened to their own original nature. Consequently, the more they speak, the more they stray.
Their delusion becomes ever more profound. For this reason, the First Patriarch of Shaolin could not bear to see it;

he pointed directly to the realization of one's nature as Buddhahood, stripping away all intellectual understanding. Yet the masters of today’s Chan monasteries again broadly cite Linji’s Three Mysteries and Dongshan’s Five Ranks, once more entering the gateway of intellectual understanding.
Thus they remain separated from the truth. To depart from such understanding, simply take up this—
Idle talk that has no meaning. I have taught you to establish resolute faith and to investigate this throughout your entire life, yet you still lack conviction.
You then desire the old monk to provide instructions on the teachings internal and external to the scriptures to provoke intellectual understanding.
If you apply your mind in such a perverted manner, it will be many years before you even dream of awakening. You, man of idle meditation: from now on, perhaps...
Stand firm with your feet rooted like a withered tree or dead ashes and go forth to practice. If you seek further intellectual understanding, I will certainly not grant you an audience.
My most sincere regards. Written by the old Huan [Name].
He showed Master Jiaojian of Yuxi that the Buddha-dharma is one's own mind.
This mind cannot be refuted by the commentaries of the entire Great Canon; the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot point it out;
the seventeen hundred patriarchs look up at it but cannot see it; and all the people of the great earth pursue it but cannot catch up. From—
From antiquity to the present, there have been hundreds and thousands of profound interpretations; yet all of them simply join their palms behind this very mind.
For this reason, Caoxi said, "To speak of 'direct pointing' is already a detour. Under such an instruction, it is like wrestling in front of a horse:
if you even think of blinking an eye, your life and nature will already be in another's hands. How could one afford to let the mechanism of the mind rest or allow for a moment of deliberation?
Only then can you grasp its essence. Perhaps you have not yet been able to force yourself, body and soul, into it before even beginning;
by all means, do not hastily or superficially attempt to take it up in a piecemeal fashion based on sounds or words.
It is better to give rise to a single piece of sincere and resolute faith, and to maintain a "meaningless phrase" within your own person, exerting the fierce intensity of your entire life.
With body and mind, one should strive diligently and single-mindedly, pressing forward with blind persistence. One need not concern oneself with whether it takes thirty or twenty years;

simply practice for each day as long as there is one day remaining. When one’s long-standing faith is firm and one’s resolve is secret and profound, awakening will suddenly occur without one's knowing or noticing.
Only then will one realize that this Way is not obtained from others, like a mute person having a dream.
From the ancients down to the present, those who have attained a degree of realization through either the teachings or Chan meditation have all achieved a sudden breakthrough right here.
At the very moment of practice, if one harbors even a single thought of external conditions, a single thought of grasping or rejecting, a single thought of love or hate,

or a single thought of self-centered discrimination and deluded emotions that follow the flow of phenomena— and furthermore, if one maintains even a single thought of memorizing, upholding, or intellectual understanding— then [one has not yet transcended].

If one can respond with mindfulness and cut it off instantly, yet still desires the illumination of another’s discernment to destroy it, this is no different from taking a step back while seeking to move forward;

there will certainly never be a moment of true correspondence. For the sake of providing a warning to Master Jian, the lecturer of Yuxi, I have set aside my illness to write these words directly to inform him.
In the "Ancient Teachings" (Gu jiao) of the Layman Wei Gong of Qinjiang, it is said: "There is but a single firm and dense body that manifests within every atom.

As for this manifested body, those who have not personally attained awakening through the mind and possess the expansive, authentic eye do not know it; they merely see it, but do not truly know it."—The Layman Qinjiang.
Lord Wei recites the Lotus Sūtra daily and possesses profound faith in this Way. He once sent a letter from within the mountains;
because I had established a precept against using pens, I was unable to personally write it for him. Now that Meifeng has arrived, he requests that I write out his own hand-copy to bestow upon him.

However, as for the meaning of "solidity and secrecy," even if the thousand Buddhas were to appear and discourse upon it with their mouths or inscribe it with their hands, it would still not be secret.
The ancients said: "It is secretly right beside you. Simply, at all times, single-mindedly uphold this phrase: "When the four great elements disperse, where will you establish your body and life?

If, through long-term and thorough cultivation during moments of speech and silence, movement and stillness, you suddenly awaken, then the meaning of that which is firm and secret will be like ten suns shining together; there will be no further need for anything else.
The second person opens his mouth. Exert yourself, exert yourself!
(I) write this to show the Zen practitioner Bak Se-ting.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou said, "The cypress tree in front of the hall. [End of quotation].
In the past, I did not recognize Zhaozhou’s original intent; I instead provided a commentary, saying: "To clarify the mind through form, and to manifest principle by means of things.

To pick up whatever comes to hand and speak whatever comes to the mouth—any of these may serve as an answer. At that time, it would have been sufficient simply to say, "The stream of water flows long in the ravine."

"The peach blossoms on the road are red, too. If the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West can be annotated in such a manner, then those who possess considerable cleverness may all take up words and language as a single document and pass them by.

The Patriarch’s intent would then merely result in the circulation of mere speech. To seek to resolve birth, death, and impermanence in this way is no different from carrying firewood to extinguish a fire. The Patriarch—
The mind must first attain awakening before this can be achieved.

Otherwise, if one has never truly awakened to the reality beneath the very heels of one's feet, it does not matter how you take your clever demeanor and string together all one thousand seven hundred entanglements of the ancients into a single thread, speaking with such precision that not a drop of water can leak through;
when viewed with the correct eye, what difference is there between this and a madman wandering outside? As for the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past...
Unable to bear seeing sentient beings deluded and self-obscured, I am compelled to utter a word or two.

Like a sharp sword honed on a whetstone, like a wheel of glowing red-hot iron, I brandish it across their faces, seeking to sever the very life-veins of human existence and cause one to transcend sense-bases and objects.
To become a pure, clean, and liberated person—how could I ever be willing to merely teach others to dwell within words?
To swallow this [teaching] superficially only increases delusion, causing one to cast oneself into the bonds of birth and death.
This not only betrays the ancients but also buries one's own potential; how could it be a trivial matter?
A true seeker of the Way devotes their entire life to reaching the depths of practice. If they do not attain enlightenment, they must resolve to sacrifice even their future lives.
One must seek a definitive resolution. How could one be content with merely letting words enter the ears and exit the mouth, like straw wrapped in paper?
Before the parents were yet born, what was that which is my original face?

Those who are determined to settle this great matter must by no means engage in speculative calculation within the realm of the mental faculty (*manas*), nor should they attempt to match it with superficial, conventional language. One must simply exert oneself [in total surrender].

Grasp this for one lifetime, standing firm upon the ground like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms high, and investigate it. Simply let the mind have no other conditions and sever all delusive thoughts.
If you do not regress for a long time, neither worrying nor seeking to understand, you will realize the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.
Layman Xiting, you should strive and strive again; be careful not to rely on your own cleverness and fall into the realm of the conscious mind. Even the Buddha did not...
It can be saved. Written by the old illusionist [Name].

To guard the emotions and restore the nature (*xing*) means that when nature arises, it becomes emotion; when emotion is produced, it becomes karma (*ye*); and when karma is stimulated, it manifests as phenomena (*wu*). Indeed, the myriad things arise from emotion and karma.
The bell arises in one place and perishes in another; prosperity and decay, fortune and calamity, are all equal to a dream or an illusion.
This is what the teaching of our Buddha demonstrates. Although all sentient beings are fundamentally one in their nature, there is a distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.
Mundane study refers to the restraining of emotions; supramundane study refers to the restoration of one's true nature. Restraining...
Emotion is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); returning to one's nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). These two explanations must not be conflated.

In the preface to his commentary on the *Laozi*, Su Gongzi You equates the Sixth Patriarch’s teaching that one should "not think of good and not think of evil" with the meaning of the *Zhongyong* passage:

"The state in which joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been manifested is called the Center. This is the first point. Furthermore, he asserts that this "Center" is precisely what the Buddhists speak of.
This is *xing* (nature). This "harmony" (*he*) is precisely the Buddha’s six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*).

To achieve "central harmony" (*zhonghe*), "Heaven and Earth find their positions and the myriad things are nourished. What else but the Buddha-dharma could be equal to this? This teaching bears a strong resemblance to how Miaoxi answered the question of Zishao’s nephew regarding the statement:
"That which Heaven mandates is called nature; following one's nature is called the Way; cultivating the Way is called education."
This is what is called the discourse on "teaching. It is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) employed at a particular time to shatter the emotional attachments of others;
how could the principle of the three bodies (*trikāya*) be limited to this alone?

I have heard that what the Confucians call the "Middle Way" (*zhongyōng*) necessarily requires that human emotions accord with the ultimate mean, so that the path of constancy and regulation may be transmitted without end. How much less would it be limited to the human mind alone?
This is indeed so. As for heaven, earth, and the myriad things, they all receive their endowment from the *Zhongyong* (The Doctrine of the Mean) and thereby undergo birth and transformation.
Without the *Zhongyong*, even the most minute things would be unable to sustain themselves. Internally, it governs the cultivation of the self; externally, it governs the state.
One must never, for even a moment, neglect or forget the *Zhongyong*. Should the *Zhongyong* be absent, then heaven, earth, and the myriad things—
Seeking it, one finds it undergoes transformation and ceases to be; how, then, could a person alone endure forever?

It is because the *Zhongyong* (The Doctrine of the Mean) is the pivotal mechanism for establishing the processes of generation and transformation that the sages and worthies have raised it up and elucidated it as the foundation of instruction and transformation.

When the *Zhongyong* is applied to parents, it is called filial piety (*xiao*); when extended to the ruler, it is called loyalty (*zhong*); when directed toward all things, it is called benevolence (*ren*); and when spread abroad...
In relation to human beings, this is called "instruction" (jiao); when it is transmitted throughout the world, it is called the "Way" (dao).
This Way refers to the substance of the *Zhongyong* (The Doctrine of the Mean), which is contained within the state before joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have been aroused.

When these emotions are aroused and all hit the mark of moderation, it is called "harmony" (he). To speak of "hitting the mark of moderation" means to accord with the measure of the *Zhongyong*. Only that which is excessive or...

If one does not reach this, one will not hit the mark of the seasonal rhythms. Once one hits the mark of the Mean (Zhongyong), one knows that the myriad things are nurtured without being sought, and Heaven and Earth occupy their positions without being sought.
Therefore, when the flow of emotion and activity is inexhaustible, what end could there be to birth and death?
The worldly teachings reach their limit at this point. But the teachings of our Buddhas and Patriarchs for transcending the world are quite different from this.

Regarding what has been heard: Why is this so? It is because the Sixth Patriarch’s inquiry—“At the moment when one neither thinks of good nor thinks of evil, what is one’s original face?”—is the great principle of restoring the nature.
And the Master Zisi’s teaching—“That which is called the ‘Central’ (Zhong) is the state when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused;
that which is called the ‘Harmonious’ (He) is when they are aroused and all accord with the proper measure”—is the ultimate discourse on guarding the emotions. However...

"Attaining harmony and centrality, one establishes one's place in heaven and earth and nurtures all things"—this is indeed a matter of the influence of emotional activity (*qing*), not something that exists within the principle of nature (*xing*).
Youyou surely has never failed to know this; why then does he circuitously cite this teaching?

Zisi’s statement, "That which is called nature is the mandate of Heaven," points to the substance of the *Zhongyong*. His statement, "That which is called the Way is following nature," points to the function of the *Zhongyong*.
This is its function. Cultivating the Way is what is called "teaching. It is intended that people rely on both essence and function to realize the Middle Way.
As for the Way, it cannot be departed from for even a moment; that which can be departed from is not the Way.

This means one must ensure that every thought and movement of the mind never for a moment exists outside the realm of the Middle Way. The discourse on guarding the emotions reaches its ultimate point here. That pure Dharma-body is...

The nature shared by both the sages and ordinary beings is the *dhātu* (the fundamental source). The *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is the supernatural power and radiance inherent in the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) in its hundreds of thousands of millions of forms is the *dharmakāya* pervading all places.
Now, the *dharmakāya* is like the solar orb; the *saṃbhogakāya* is like the light of the sun; and the *nirmāṇakāya* is the light spreading everywhere. This nature is without...
This is known. Nature (*xing*) is non-action (*wuwei*). Thus, the principle of the doctrine of "returning to nature" reaches its ultimate limit here;

it seems not easily comparable to those who speak of "following nature" and "cultivating the Way. Miaoxi [Huihong] sought to unite the study of returning to nature with the teachings on guarding the emotions, while Ziyou [Zhang Shangying] sought to unite the teachings on guarding the emotions with the study of returning to nature.
One Confucian and one Buddhist each upheld what was good.
I have weighed these matters and harmonized them so that the doctrines of the two schools do not contradict one another.
Had I not clarified this, the ultimate truth would have been overwhelmed by their contradictions. Perhaps some may find my explanation to be correct.

The Dharma Words of National Teacher Puying, Master Zhongfeng of Tianmu (Concluded) The Verses on Rebirth in the Pure Land by Master Zhongfeng of Tianmu (One Hundred and Eight Stanzas) Dust-sand kalpas, and again dust-sand kalpas;
though the number of dust-sand kalpas be exhausted, they do not cease. This is because one’s thoughts are rooted in unextinguished emotion.
Cast aside [all attachments]; one remains bound within the boundless cycle of birth and death.
The four elements aggregate to form the horns of a phantom hare; the six sense organs grasp at the hair of a white tortoise.
Performing somersaults amidst bubbles and flower-reflecting shadows, how many times have you emerged and submerged in this Jambudvīpa?
A single red marble in the Eastern Sea; its flowing light shoots daily toward the western woods. How many extraordinary men are there in this world?
Who among them cherishes every moment before them?
Rubbing one's eyes, flowers falsely appear in the empty sky; delusively, one takes the triple world to be one's home. The great chiliocosm is eternally quiescent, a land of radiant light;
not a speck of dust separates it from us, yet all is obscured.

Dragged by the ropes of craving into this suffering Sahā world, one weeps until the Yellow Springs as tears flow ever more profusely. Who would say that the grief of parting lasts through kalpas of exhaustion?
The entire body is, in truth, the ancient Amitābha.
In delusion there is no awakening, and in awakening there is no delusion. Ultimately, the moment of delusion is the very moment of awakening.
Having cast off both extremes of delusion and awakening, the boiling cauldron is revealed to be a lotus pond.
The waters of the forty-eight vows merge with water; the thousand billion bodies unite with space. The Compassionate Honored One of the Dharma-Treasury has no face or features;
there is no need to seek his purple-golden countenance again.
When I maintain right mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha, the moon lingers long over the reflections of trees in the jeweled ponds;
yet my mind still hastens toward returning to purity and peace—this is once again planting eyebrows upon my eyes.
The turbid waters are completely cleared by the power of the jewel; the chaotic mind remains unmoved by the Buddha’s lack of occasion. Before one's eyes, everything is the path home;
there is no need to seek a guide from others.
Ten thousand kalpas of birth and death are like a grave illness; a single invocation of the Buddha’s name is the skilled physician.
When the medicine and the disease are finally both forgotten, there is no need for further proclamation—mother need not remember her child.
The phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness are the true Pure Land; seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are the ancient Amitābha.
Simply by forgetting birth and death in this very place, father and son shall pull one another out of the river of craving.
A single brazier of ancient seal script, a single branch of lotus; The eyes gaze upon the cold void, and ten thousand anxieties are cast aside.
If one can return to this ancestral home of purity and peace, Who would distinguish between the Eastern Land and the Western Heaven?
Outside of Chan, I have never spoken of the Pure Land; you must know that outside of the Pure Land, there is no Chan.
Cast aside both layers of this public case, and the five-leaf lotus will bloom upon Mount Xionger.

Within the abode of Mahābrahmā, not a single dharma exists; yet within this state of non-existence, a thousand differences arise. Turning back to contemplate one's own nature, one is free from conceptual discrimination;
in every thought-moment, pure white lotus flowers blossom.
A great black viper lurks within the dark chamber; do not greedily indulge in sleep until it has been driven out entirely.
With the skull-crushed pillow of Mount Sumeru, the fragrant winds pervading the earth cause white lotuses to bloom.
In the lotus pond, there is not a day that flowers do not bloom; four-colored radiance reflects upon the jeweled terrace. Your golden arm extends afar as your compassionate concern is profound;
for what reason do sentient beings not think of coming?
When the pool of blood dries up, the lotus pond becomes clear; when the sword-trees wither, the jewel-trees flourish.
If one delights in the primordial absence of abiding marks, one spontaneously perfects oneself within that very state of non-abiding.
In this Land of Bliss, the three evil realms originally do not exist; the cries of birds are entirely the flowing forth of the Buddha’s teaching.
As long as the realm of sentient beings has not been fully exhausted, these calls will continue through the spring breeze without ceasing.
Parrots and kalaviṅkas circle the trees and sing; their beautiful voices are harmonious and refined, truly worthy of listening. Why do they so earnestly and incessantly call out?
It is surely because of the weary cycle of birth that they seek to awaken the obscured spiritual essence.
Within oneself there is one ancient Amitābha; yet one has missed him amidst sounds and forms.
If you do not recognize him when meeting him on the narrow path, who knows when you will leave this Saha world?
The road to one's hometown is easy to find; there is no deviation. The bright sun and clear sky are obscured by external objects. Lift up your two eyebrows and look with your eyes:
even the fiery pit is entirely white lotus flowers.

A journey of over one hundred thousand leagues is not separated by a speck of dust; do not distance yourself from or draw near to delusion and awakening. In a single kṣaṇa, all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are exhausted in thought;
they are all people within the Land of Lotus Flowers.
The Buddha and sentient beings have shared a karmic affinity from time immemorial; the Buddha-nature within sentient beings is without partiality.
Alas, why do you so willingly endure the sufferings of this Sahā world, refusing to turn back and apply yourself to the lash of painful discipline?
The faculty of mindfulness is a string of prayer beads; with pain as the whip and exertion as the goad, one sets forth on the distant journey.
When mindfulness reaches the emptiness of mindfulness and is liberated through mindfulness, one is unaware that the body dwells within a white lotus.
Among humans, in the heavens, and in the hells—how long must I toil through these cycles of ascent and descent?
If the white lotus root is not planted, there will be but the entanglements of birth and death as numerous as motes of dust and grains of sand.
The shadows of seven rows of trees interlace; white lotus flowers bloom day and night. Even the Buddha’s own hand cannot come to shield them from being plucked.
Why do sentient beings seek [their desires] without end?
White jade hairs swallow crimson lotuses; a cluster of purple gold reflects emerald lapis lazuli. This fundamental self-nature has always been thus;
having received this same spiritual essence, we know it together as one.
The Lord’s body is sixteen feet tall and of golden hue; white lotuses perpetually bloom with a spring beyond the kalpas. He regards all sentient beings as his own infants;
for what reason, then, do we not draw near to him?

Ceaselessly raining heavenly flowers throughout the six periods of the day, their fragrance and flavor are so novel that nothing can surpass them. At the clear dawn, she fills her robe-sleeve to the brim;
returning home, she once again offers them as a *kāṣāya* for the Buddha.
The candle dispels the myriad darknesses like the sun’s orb; within its radiance appears a person of purple-gold. With the wondrous mind of contemplation, forget all views;
beholding the essence itself, how could there ever be so much as a speck of dust between?
At first, fix your attention on a single drop; as the power of mindfulness deepens, it reaches the Dragon Gate. Contemplate the hundreds of thousands of fragrant oceans until they are exhausted;
do not lightly let even a hair’s breadth be swallowed.
Sitting alone in a secluded chamber, ten thousand anxieties flee; a single orb of mountain moon rises above the pine needles.
Without using delusion or enlightenment to obstruct the eye of the mind, everything is but the white jade tuft between the eyebrows.
The water of eight virtues reflects golden sands; towers and terraces of a hundred jewels disperse the morning mists. Yet there is yet another extraordinary marvel:
red lotuses in full bloom, as large as chariots.
The Amitābha of self-nature need not be sought through contemplation; the five thousand-plus scrolls are but a compass.
If you do not seek true liberation in this very place, you will fall two or three steps behind by chasing after words and phrases.
For what reason is this world called "Ultimate Bliss"? It is simply because the various sufferings do not invade one another.
If a practitioner wishes to seek the path home, they need only realize their own mind amidst the dust of the world.

How can one understand the non-abiding of one's own mind? Bind your mindfulness to the six-syllable name of the Compassionate Honored One. When mindfulness and thought are harmonized, they are all cast off at once;
the lands of India and this earth do not differ much in this regard.
Within one's own home is a single Amitābha Buddha; throughout kalpas, when has he ever been seen with the eyes? Today, one turns instead toward sounds and forms;
this time, if one wishes to see him, it will be difficult.
Having celebrated the New Year, one gazes upon the Upper Prime Festival; ten thousand households illuminate golden lotuses with silver candles.
When the land of eternal quiescent radiance unfolds, how could the Buddha-dharma not manifest before us?
Manifesting entry into *nirvāṇa* and recording the second month of spring, I lament before the wind for the songs and dances of Pāpīyas.
Who would have known that the Buddha of the intrinsic nature’s golden hue Constantly turns the wheel of Dharma amidst a thousand blossoms?
On this Cold Food Festival, the desolate outskirts resound with universal wailing; who among them will think afar of the Elder Golden Immortal?
Buried at the beginning of the kalpa within the soil of the lotus, he has no need for people to come and offer paper money.
In the clear and harmonious season of early summer, the fourth month, the nine dragons spray water to bathe the infant. The Master who transforms the Land of Bliss is beyond birth and death;
he simply fashions a golden mask for his face.
No hanging of mugwort or tiger effigies to celebrate the Dragon Boat Festival; there is only facing the West toward the ancient site of practice.
With a single incense stick rising from the burner and a single strike of the sounding block, the fragrance of lotus blossoms wafts through the six gates.
In the pure and peaceful hometown, there are no months of the sixth; let the fire-parasols spread themselves across the void.
Upon the ground of golden sand, where one walks to and fro, gusts after gusts of white lotus breeze blow forth.
In the seventh month, the human world’s summer heat gradually wanes; the evening breeze by the pond is even more agreeable.
Gazing afar at the setting sun like a suspended drum, I already find my urging the homeward whip to be too late.
Ascending the tower, we share the Mid-Autumn moon; looking back, who would not think of their parents’ land?
Regardless of whether one has fled or passed away over many lifetimes, the lingering remembrance endures to this day, never forgotten.
Who would have known that the chrysanthemums of the eastern hedge on the ninth day are none other than the four-colored flowers of the Western Land?
Once a single skull is completely dried up, the hundreds of thousands of things heard and seen are naturally without discrepancy.
In the tenth month of the human year, the furnace is opened; one stirs the cold ashes deeply to ask if fire remains.
The Golden Light Vow-King is originally this very fire, capable of burning away the River of Craving for a thousand kalpas until it is parched dry.

The multitude of yin is stripped away and a single yang arrives; the five-petaled heart-flower blooms right where it is. Its branches and twigs pervade the entire world yet find no place of attachment;
the fragrant breeze blows them up onto the jade terraces.
The year’s end and the exhaustion of affairs are truly pitiable; Old Wang from the eastern village burns paper money at night. The very mind is the self-nature Amitābha Buddha;
yet another year passes with my face covered in dust.
A single string of prayer beads, dark and lustrous; the reflections of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, round and complete. Pure mindfulness circulates in constant succession;
letting go and picking up are one and the same.
In the practice of Buddha-recollection, one must directly seek to become a Buddha; if one does not seek to become a Buddha, what is the purpose of recollecting him?
All sentient beings who harbor consciousness and spirit possess, equally, a single stem of the white lotus.

In the practice of Buddha-recollection, one must expect to reach its ultimate end; when every single instance is brought together with recollection, the winds and waves of the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) will subside, and one will sail steadily upon the lotus-red boat to the Land of Bliss.
Four snakes in one basket—peril upon peril; two rats gnawing at a vine—danger upon danger.
If you do not plant the lotus in the pure realm, who knows when this kalpa will end?

The affairs of the five human desires are boundless; the sharp shackles of profit and fame cannot be severed. If you recite the Buddha’s name with a mind free from fame and profit, why must you toil in hardship awaiting the future?
The self-nature Amitābha transcends both realization and cultivation; it requires nothing more than to strike at one's own nature for them to meet.
If you allow even a fleeting thought to harbor subject and object, you will once again be blinded by the flowers in the sky that obscure both eyes.
Reflect deeply upon hell and give rise to bodhicitta; do not remain deluded regarding your parents or your homeland. Lash yourself with the whip of urgency and strive to arrive early;
do not wait until the sun has shifted to the west.
One must form the karmic conditions for the Lotus Assembly; abandon all notions of self and other. At no time should one fail to regard this as a rare encounter;
with joy, ascend together upon the vessel of liberation.
Out of attachment and views, you gave rise to greed and anger, burying the sixteen-foot golden body. Today, by good fortune, you have returned to the Pure Society;
you should not continue as before to stir up dust and wind.
The lotus fiber binds the feet of the golden crow; the fire of karma burns the axle-flower of the carriage. Yet there is another dharma even more difficult to believe:
with the tip of one's toe, one kicks out Buddhas as numerous as hemp seeds.
To plant the nine grades of lotuses of the Western Land throughout the entire trichiliocosm of this defiled world—upon careful reflection, there is no other method;
it requires nothing more than a single mind of steadfast resolve.
Seven layers of dense, covering nets of pearls; three tiers of flat, spread pavements of agate stairs. The Teacher of Peaceful Nurturing’s compassionate vows are earnest;
from afar he extends his golden arm to receive those who come.
I send this word to those upon this Sahā world: if you seek the path home, do not be complacent.
If you can pierce through the silver mountains and iron walls, the thousand-petaled lotus shall be a spring apart.
The great whale takes a single breath and dries up the four oceans; the self-nature Amitābha’s field of vision is vast and wide. The jade-white light between his brows cannot be concealed;
like a coral branch, the full moon hangs there, perfectly round.
Six times a day I knock and ask my golden father: "This stray child, when will he return?
When the conversation reaches the point where saṃsāra is endless, we look at one another and, without realizing it, our tears soak our robes.
I attend the morning court and perform evening rites with diligent devotion; dreams of entering the lotus womb at the Golden Pond recur frequently.
Even if I were to grind my bones and shatter my body for ten million kalpas, I could never easily repay the kindness of my compassionate parents.
As soon as one wishes to return home, one arrives at home. Why needlessly give rise to sighs of lamentation? The great road before the gate is straight as a bowstring;
to entertain conceptual thought is to go astray.
A single hook-shaped crescent moon illuminates the pine hut; outside the gate, no one dwells in the thatched cottage.
The Lord of Transformation, with his billions of purple-gold bodies, does not depart from this very thought—this is true companionship in practice.
All sufferings arise from greed and anger; one does not know that greed arises from nowhere else but the forgetting of one's own nature as Amitābha Buddha.
When divergent thoughts race about in confusion, they are all demons.
In the past, Śrīkṣetra attended upon the Sun and Moon; he was instructed to maintain mindfulness of the West.
Since personally realizing samādhi, he has never been apart from the side of the Compassionate Honored One.
The clay ox plows through the lotus soil; the iron horse tramples over the mountain of merit.
One is utterly unaware of Amitābha within one’s own nature, yet still uses the mirror of the mind to reflect his compassionate countenance.
The Path-farer has a distinct land of Mind-only, which does not belong to the directions of east, west, south, or north. Once the eyes are opened, there is a distance of a thousand li;
it is difficult to take the other shore as a compassionate vessel.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* in one fascicle is a letter from home. In the direction where the sun sets, there is an old dwelling.
Prepare your provisions well and hope to arrive early, lest it cause our compassionate father to sigh in lamentation day after day.
The elder brother calls and the younger responds, reciting the name of Amitābha; they wish to lead their entire family out of the river of craving.
If one can discern this mind as it always is, even the Buddha himself will have no power over them.
To leap out of Saṃsāra is itself home; there is no need to seek a lotus land elsewhere. Saṃsāra is not different from the Lotus Land;
it is only that one's previous way of seeing was mistaken.
Long ago there was a man named Wu Zicai, who knocked upon a coffin day after day, calling out, "Come back!
Although his physical traces had not yet departed from the triple world, he had already sent his spirit to dwell within the womb of the white lotus.
In the Land of Lotus Flowers there are no golden chains; yet within the mounds one hears and sees the Iron Ring Mountains.
Once one penetrates the sounds and forms before one's eyes, hundreds of thousands of worthies and sages return as one.
My livelihood consists solely in rowing a single boat; drifting or stopping, I simply follow conditions as they arise. How many times has the ancient sail been unfurled beneath the bright moon?
Everywhere before my eyes, the lotuses of the Buddha-ocean bloom in full splendor.
Dwelling on the boat reciting the Buddha’s name, the Buddha follows the boat; the eternal light of *saddharmadhātu* (the realm of constant quiescent light) ripples upon the bottom of the water.
Unaffected by either bank or the middle current, the red lotuses bloom branch after branch within the field of the mind.
At dawn, the boat moved straight eastward; the full sails were brushed by the breeze of lotus flowers.
The single Buddha of Self-Nature Amitābha appeared over the rising sun, his light shining red before one’s eyes.
Sailing westward upon the boat, I recall my native land; Above the four-flower pond, the evening breeze is cool. Unable to endure this drifting life, my heart yearns for home;
A single light sail is hoisted against the setting sun.
Spontaneously move the boat across the waters to the south; there is no need to seek fellow practitioners elsewhere. Within one's own home is Amitābha Buddha;
in every thought-moment, the *utpala* flower blooms.
The boat is driven by celestial winds to the south and north; wind, rivers, moon, and islets reflect the light of the mind. Suddenly, a thought shifts toward entry into the Land of Common Dwelling;
before one realizes it, the entire body is within the lotus vessel.
The boat has come to rest in the east, west, south, and north; yet it still does not leave the ancient sandbar. At ease, one turns the rudder of empty space;
fragrance fills the vessel and flowers cover the islet.
If one does not board the boat, one remains within the house; from outside the gate of the teaching, one drags three carts.
Laughing, one gazes upon the depths of the burning house, where on dry land there bloom only water-lilies.

The present realization of the koan is purely a matter of inquiry. The dawn bells strike repeatedly as the wax candles burn long. The sound continues unbroken through the six periods of day and night;
the fragrance of white lotuses wafts through the entire gate.
With Buddha in mind, one contemplates with the mind; when contemplation reaches the emptiness of mind, even Buddha is forgotten. Casting off all and returning, one re-examines:
at night, red and white open amidst the intermingling of green and yellow.
The mindful mind follows the body like a shadow; whether in stillness or clamor, leisure or haste, it never ceases for a moment. When the physical form is shattered, the shadow perishes with it;
in the West, this path has no further journey.
At dawn and at dusk, I perform repentance and prostrations; bowing my head and weeping, I address the Venerable Amitābha: "How many times have I wandered through the six realms of rebirth?
I vow that this time, I shall escape the net."
Supporting him out, he reveals the red *uṣṇīṣa* atop his head; brushing the void, the white tuft of hair between his brows emits light. Amitābha Buddha speaks with a harmonious voice:
"The saṃsāra of kalpas is forgotten in a single thought."
Upon the sands of the golden pool, there are no red lotuses; within this mass of red flesh dwells the Most Honored One. A thousand sages cannot shift a single step from His brow;
in an ordinary moment, He kicks down the gate of Nirvana.
Six donkeys pull the cart around; after the rain, the muddy road is still long. Amitābha Buddha’s compassionate heart is urgent;
He vigorously urges on the whip of return, desiring us to reach home.
To mind Amitābha Buddha, there is no hardship; to enter the holy and transcend the mundane takes but a snap of the fingers. Set aside all else and maintain right mindfulness;
then, among the myriad things heard and seen, none shall interfere.

When right and wrong cannot be distinguished, cease seeking further; even when encountering further difficulties, do not let your heart be distressed. Constantly join your brows in a frown with the King of Vows, and hundreds of thousands of demonic afflictions shall be unable to invade you.
Amitābha dwells in the West, the Patriarchs came from the West; reciting the Buddha’s name and practicing Zen share the same essential form.
Once the mass of doubt accumulated over kalpas is shattered, the flower of the mind blooms as one and the same.
The lecture hall divides the schools of Characteristics and Nature; their mutual affirmation and mutual negation are not the same.
But now that we have come to this flower pond, how could the lotuses ever be two different shades of red?
The lay followers of the Buddha uphold the five precepts; yet the Vinaya says these five precepts have not been fully cultivated.
Who would know that within the True Scripture of Six Words, the eighty thousand modes of dignified conduct are gathered into a single phrase?
The Buddhas of the six directions extend their broad and long tongues, praising only those in the Sahā world who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
One must believe that in the White Lotus World, there is never a time when the kalpas do not spring forth.
The earth trembles and heaven is startled as he diligently recites the Buddha’s name; he knocks at doors and hammers on gates, urging others toward practice.
If you ask why he acts thus, it is because he fears sentient beings will fall into the fiery pit.
He has already attained Buddhahood this very morning; the Master of the Land of Bliss already deems it too late. How much more so for those who still wish to go there?
Take it for granted that their cycle of rebirth will have no end.
Mindfulness of the Buddha never obstructs daily life; it is people who obstruct one another in their daily activities. Who can guarantee this illusory shadow of a hundred-year lifespan?
Do not fail the Great Vow-King from the Western Heaven.

Those who possess wealth and honor should properly practice mindfulness of the Buddha. With gold filling their treasuries and grain overflowing their granaries, and with all worldly enjoyments lacking nothing, they lack only this:
to behold the King of Vows at the moment of death.
When a person of humble means recites the Buddha’s name, they have no household affairs to occupy their thoughts.
Bare and with empty hands, they ascend directly to the lotus pedestal and claim a single branch.
In old age, reciting the Buddha’s name is most appropriate; as the days remaining are few, do not forget for even a moment.
The six characters, "Namo Amitābha Buddha," are a compassionate vessel for crossing the sea of suffering.
The world at large says it is difficult for the young to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; I say that youth is precisely the right time.
Behold the Dragon King’s daughter at eight years of age, who held a divine pearl in her palm and emitted precious light.
Having served as a prime minister and a worthy official at court, his worldly fame and achievements are beyond measure.
If you do not contemplate Amitābha Buddha within your own nature, I know not how you will withstand impermanence.
First-rate masters constantly exhort others, yet their own samādhi is not diligent;
though they dwell in the pure land of white lotuses, they pointlessly move Amitābha’s name upon their lips.
In the universal, impartial realm of Mind-Only, noble and base, wise and foolish, are not divided into two paths. We must teach even the lacquer bucket to be turned inside out, bottom and all;
let everyone apply their diligent effort together.
The spontaneous resonance of the karmic mechanism is simply natural. I speak neither of the Pure Land nor of Chan.
If you can entrust yourself equally to that which lies beyond words, then the hundred-and-eight mani jewels will be strung upon a single thread.

One Hundred and Eight Poems on Yearning for the Pure Land by Master Zhongfeng (The aforementioned "Poems on Yearning for the Pure Land" were composed by Master Zhongfeng; there are one hundred and eight poems in total).
This is a single cycle of his plain-bead rosary. I have previously transcribed his complete draft; now, I have specifically selected its essentials and transcribed them once more.
Out of compassion for the deluded paths of sentient beings, he expounds upon the ultimate bliss of the Buddha-realm;
yet when success is achieved, they are one and the same.
(Recorded on the *wùshēn* day of the third month in the spring of the fifth year of Dàdé [1309] by the disciple Qiáo Mèngfǔ).
(The above few words are the colophon to the stone inscription of the calligraphic postscript written by Zǐ'áng himself).
(The *Fófǎ Jīntāng Biān*, fascicle 16, states: "Mèngfǔ, courtesy name Zǐ'áng, was a native of Xīng... [He] cherished purity... )

The postscript to the *Tushi* (Earthly Verses) also records this in detail. It can be seen that the original manuscript contained the complete collection of one hundred and eight poems, while later he selected the essentials—fifty-eight poems—and transcribed them.
[Included herein: Master Zhongfeng’s One Hundred Odes on Plum Blossoms, in response to Feng Haosu.

Its own fragrance, its own color, its own spirit of life—observing these transformations and discerning the subtle workings, one first awakens to the Truth. Before the Liang and Song dynasties, it was entirely unrecognized;
before the times of Fuxi and Huangdi, there were those who possessed this. From two or three stamens, the patterns of odd and even emerge; from north and south branches, the dust of chaos is divided.
When the fundamental root is scrutinized in its profound mystery, it is a single mass of pure qi, a single mass of spring.
Awakening is not a daze, dreaming is not a spirit-sight; after the snow and before the frost, it is exceptionally true. Sparse shadows silently dissolve as the moon passes three times;
a half-couplet, broken and sad, belongs to the solitary reciter. The seasons have withered, yet the solitary root remains; the river post-station is desolate, the dust of past events settled.
Chewing the subtle fragrance, its purity is exquisite; the Jade Consort shall no longer descend to grace this spring.
I have captured the spirit of your solitary chanting; what need is there for Hua Guang to further transmit your true likeness?
Gazing closely at the ancient path and wind-swept trees, one suspects this is the person from the West Chamber waiting for the moon. Half-drunk and half-awake, like jade beyond the mist;
about to vanish yet still present, like dust amidst the snow. Green-clad maidens dance at dawn on Mount Luofu; who knows how many more springs you shall endure in the world of mortals?
Speaking of the profound fragrance that redoubles the refreshing spirit, I have personally witnessed its true essence once more last year. Heaven and earth opened for a night in the realm of poetry;
wind and snow came halfway up the mountain to meet an old friend. The pure whistling of the breeze is soundless, imbued with the breath of the Way;
the steps treading upon the waves stir fragrant dust. The secret of knowing the heart lies beyond the lute-heart; in the threefold melody, the ten fingers overflow with springtime.

The tinkling of her girdle-bells reveals the Valley Spirit; through many lifetimes she has cultivated the attainment of pure truth. For three thousand years she has held her place within the registers of the Jade Emperor;
she is the foremost among those in the palace of the Green Lord. The pipes of the Qiang people have intent to hasten creation, while the Chu lyrics remain silent, seeking news of her voice.
From now on, she shall no longer be accustomed to the heat of Jambudvīpa; with a cool and distant gaze, she holds ten thousand bushels of spring within her.
Resplendent is Fei-qiong, her subtlety enters the divine; before the breeze, one surely wishes to ask about the "True True. At evening, the poetic inspiration is complete within the eastern pavilion;
the cold seeps through as the solitary mountain crane calls out to man. I cherish the refined aspirations of Yin and He; I loathe the falling dust of coquetry from Xu and Yu.
Facing my own shadow at the jade basin, I restrain my emaciation; fragrance falls upon withered branches, and even the water is springtime.
Ashamed to learn the coquettish makeup of the Goddess of Luo at the time of study; half a stream of clear azure naturally preserves its true essence.

The green willow eyes open, gazing favorably upon the traveler; the yellow bee-threads are plucked, coldly smiling at mankind. The scent of *shen-shui* incense awakens dreams from the *yuan-jing* well; the folding-screened mountains cut off the dust of Maiwei.
This place of pleasure within the brocade nest is a ground for longing; a few spots of subtle sourness herald the late spring.

Immersing oneself in the principles of nature leads naturally to spiritual penetration; having thoroughly mastered the true countenance of the "Walking through Heaven," the branches of the eternal past are ever-unchanging.

Through a single flower, one recognizes the artist who came before. The spirit of Yangming is present at midnight and noon alike; when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, the dawn light shines upon the dust of the morning pavilion.
The vital energy of life resides within the thirty-six palaces, yet the universe remains unopened as spring has not yet arrived.

The jade flute’s notes stir the spirit in secret; its transcendent melody on the warm jade terrace is truly sublime. For how many years have the springs and rocks been cold with clouds, and the cranes?

Across ten thousand li of passes and mountains, the moon grieves for men. Fragrance gathers in the deep snow, refining the flavor of things; shadows fall upon the cold window, where the dust settles in the crevices of the pillow.
The sandalwood boards and golden goblets have long been silent and still; yet this faint chanting does not diminish the springtime of old.

Suddenly, amidst the forest, I beheld a jade-like spirit; at times I doubted whether it was real or not. The ethereal souls of the Nine Heavens possess the will to live; a newly adorned court lady emerges from within the palace.
Slanting light shines upon the window-silk, slanting light reflects on the water; half follows the course of the wind, half follows the dust.
The poet does not merely chant of her former life’s emaciation; he inscribes ten thousand varieties of spring into the river-cane paper.

The fragrance of life arises unceasingly, darkening and bewildering the spirit. Who can summon the essence to manifest what is truly real? The Han River plays with pearls, their cold light reflecting one’s shadow;
the pines’ wind stirs the sleeves, startling the soul in the night. How could it yield three parts of its whiteness to the snow?
How dare it steal a single speck of dust from the wandering void? This vast qi surges upward beyond the heavens; how would it follow flowers and moonlight to pursue the charms of spring?

Dwelling in seclusion among crags and valleys, he alone refines his spirit; the mountain deities have intent to co-create the truth with him. A single branch of lingering snow is his robe within meditative concentration;
a solitary patch of wild cloud is he, a man beyond the mundane world. Contemplating thus, this pure seed illuminates thousands of dust-motes within the formless realm.
The celestial mechanism still desires to harbor its secret message; it has not yet sent forth the wild ape’s cry to shatter the spring.

Slowly drifting, the celestial wind’s essence presses upon the spirit; Beside my chanting, pure thoughts trace a path to the Real. Facing each other at the small window, I first suspected it was snow;
When the bright moon appeared, it was as if someone were there. Manifesting forms in response to objects requires shifting consciousness;
That which is empty is form—all returns to the dust. Who can ask for the meaning within the branches? Every character in the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate is spring.
Watching her depart into the distant empty mountains, my spirit lingers; it seems we have known each other before, and my feelings are all the more sincere.

A bed of plain white covers spread like cold jade; a single piece of raw silk depicts a beautiful woman. Her refreshing aura and crystalline grace outshine the beauty of the palace; yet I lament that she followed mournful melodies into the dark dust of the capital.
While Emperor Xuanzong was still enamored with the *Nichei* dance, she cherished her own springtime within the imperial chambers.
Before the flowers and beneath the moon, he darkly concentrates his spirit. A crane comes from the west to visit Zizhen. His gray hair secretly pities the countenance of Guoyang;
his white robes at night fear the person of Guanghan. The great trichiliocosm is lost in fragrant mists;
the twelve towers and terraces lock away the jade whisk. Within this, do not ask about the profound barrier: how can one conceal so much spring?

A wondrous reflection in the water, the spirit is serene; In solitary purity, the original truth is revealed. Ten thousand acres of jade fields under a heartless night; A single blast from an iron flute—where is the person?
Chanting while biting through the frost, the cold reaches the very bone; Seeking laughter against the wind, his emaciation startles the dust.
Who could summon such splendor in a clear, bright sky? Once again, for the sake of next year, he yields to the "Little Spring."
One night the Wind God made an appointment with the Sea God; Together they bestowed all celestial ingenuity upon this jade-like beauty.
Her solitary traces were hidden deep within mists and clouds; In the light of water and moon, one beheld a figure like a human. The fragrance of the calyx was gathered within her pure morning dreams;
The shadows on the icy branches sketched a cold flight of dust. Fang Long recalls sharing feasts of blossoming splendor; A hundred flagons flowed profusely, filling the house with spring.
Jade serves as the water for requesting bones; the spirit is found in the true intent of the former village.

Planted by Fan Xian, who would lecture upon it? Following Tao Buzhi’s love for it, one truly grieves for the man. Deeply locked away in Yu’s bridge are the traces of the dragon’s bag; after the lingering chants of Shu Xi, the dust of the crane’s grain remains.
Still remembered is the stone screen that once quenched thirst; a portion of the ice offered shared the springtime of a single jar.
A spirit flies at dawn amidst banks of white clouds; his Daoist bones are refined as the One Great Perfected One (*Tai-zhen*).

Upon ancient shores, buried incense is mostly snow; on cold crags, leaning shadows find four walls of solitude. Entrusting my thoughts to the wind for distant lands, my sorrows must have grown old; sitting in the rain, I decline the grain-offering, yet my regrets remain untainted by dust.
I long to travel everywhere and compose verses of reclusion, sharing my inner heart with you to answer the leisurely spring.
