On this snowy day, its spirit is enhanced; it seems to cry out its jade-like purity amidst the cold of the crystal world. A single point of fragrant heart relies upon the messenger from the postal station;

half a branch of clear shadow accompanies the poet. The pleasures of wine have long since vanished throughout antiquity and today; all traces of elegance are buried within the emaciation beyond the dust.
If you possess a lingering affection, there is still hope; do not allow the spring of your old garden to wither in vain.
At the slanting end of the broken bridge, I draw near the spirit of the flowers; I have recognized the true form and demeanor of this floral deity.

She would not deign to seek the moon at twilight, nor would she dare to flirt with the man of Tàibái. Her icy and frosty countenance polishes her steadfast resolve; her heart of iron and stone loathes the soft dust of the world.
As the Dipper turns and the Altar Star rises, my feelings remain bright and clear; I cannot bear the spring breeze blowing through the watchtower.

Who would take this penchant for seclusion and indolence and cultivate the spirit? With white stones and clear springs, one nurtures the true nature. At the foot of the mountain, three feet of snow melt into warmth;
from the treetops, fragrance beckons the person of primordial antiquity. Tender pepper buds burst open with powder to welcome the vanguard;
aged honey coats the yellow blossoms, weary of the later dust. Try seeking it out in leisure within a quiet dwelling: where the six yin extremes reach their limit, spring alone returns.
The road of exile is shrouded in sorrowful confusion, stirring the spirit in its dark depths. Piercing through forests and entering valleys, I seek the Truth for myself.

Tall and upright, a shadow shifts coldly upon the jade-like form; silent and speechless, one stands alone in empty desolation. The dream of the Yangtai Terrace ends amidst half-clouds and rain; at the Cold Mound, how many grains of sand and dust have chilled the tears?
The lingering fragrance has faded as the profusion of splendor arises; by the wild waters and azure mists, the spirit finds its own springtime.
I recall how many times you descended as a spirit from the Jade Pond; Waves surged beyond all things as you manifested your true form.

The Lord of the East took special care to cherish the deep snow; At midnight, the fragrance blew forth, stirring the Jade Woman. Along official roads and rustic bridges, your presence surely stirred the spirit;
Upon snowy steps and moonlit grounds, not a speck of dust arose. Sometimes, idly twirling a green branch in remembrance, Amidst my sorrows, I cried out for the spring that softens weary feet.
In this desolate courtyard, my spirit dwells alone; it seems as if I stand beneath the thatched eaves reciting the True. Amidst the single snowfall, one knows not the trees within the garden;
the myriad ladies are all like immortals in the moon. My sorrowful thoughts linger upon the morning dream, while the pure air separates me from the ethereal dust of the Dark Capital (Xuandu).
Who would say that this life is ashamed of its austerity? Beyond the highest cold, there remains a lingering spring.
I know not which celestial deity presides over this place; from the immortal gate, a truly wondrous countenance is released. The sleeves of the dance naturally evoke the grace of whirling snow;

the horizontal flute surely recalls the woman who washed silk at the river. Like Wang Gong’s crane-feather cloak, one remains pure and untainted; like Yan Hui’s sheepskin robe, one is surely free from worldly dust.
When one beholds this most marvelous state in the cool of night, there is no need for silver candles to illuminate the eternal youth.
Shimmering moss-covered trees conceal a divine spirit; illusory blossoms reveal the true measure of their intent.

A solitary pure friend between heaven and earth, a soul from the Nine Underworlds hidden among lakes and mountains. Who can pour wine and sing the *xiè* dirges? I alone carry my poems to mourn the departed dust.
If we should meet again in the second or third month, even the *tùkuí* and *yànmài* weeds will grieve for spring.
Blurred vision falls into the well as the two spirits grow dizzy; with snowy steps far-reaching, one beholds the reality of desire. A sketch in pale ink reveals the horizontal shadow of jade;

in the twilight courtyard stands one leaning against the railing. One still recognizes the traces upon the window-sill from spitting on the moss; only the powder from weeping remains as dust upon the mirror’s surface.
It would take gold to cast such a dwelling, where year after year, amidst the snow, the fragrant spring is preserved.
Once I made a pact with a tree spirit beneath the Bodhi tree, to investigate the Truth together in the depths of the Washing-Flowers stream.

In the deep snow beneath the forest lies the chamber of Vimalakīrti; by the cold stone on the cliff face sits the man facing the wall. Through seven returns and nine reverts, one contemplates form and appearance; through the three voids and four truths, one awakens to the faculties and their objects.
Every single thing is entirely the realm of Avataṃsaka; in this solitary mountain hut, amidst drifting clouds, there is the freedom of spring.
Whose brushwork in vermilion and green so skillfully conveys the spirit? Though Yan Shou was adept, he did not yet capture the truth. Beyond the sun, the shadows of jade pendants return empty;
at the edge of the clouds, the one in green robes grows old in sorrow. Starving bees risk the snow as they wander among the drifting fluff;
sick cranes sleep upon the moss, their tracks envying the dust. Before the Hall of White Jade there is but a single tree; though the gates are layered and deep, they do not shut out the spring.

The Yangtze is empty and the year draws to a close; my spirit is wounded in secret. Suddenly, I see the true dawn-tree of the Southern Kingdom. Transversely leaning beyond the bamboo, it startles the wood-spirits;
washing its reflection by the water’s edge, it puts the ice-maidens to shame. Ashamed to apply otter-bone paste to brighten her face, it cannot bear for dragon-essence incense to darken its dust.
Cold inspiration has already departed toward the horizon; one must surely push through the snow to seek spring afar.
The breeze is clear and the snow warm; a floating spirit animates the air. Treading upon the mossy traces, yet the Truth remains unseen. A single melody from Xiangshan; half a window of moonlight.

For a thousand years at the Hua-biao pillar, a person of the Nine Heavens. The heart of sandalwood perceives afar that the clouds are thin. Turning back to view the jade-like countenance, rouge and powder are but dust.
A pity that the peerless name of Chaisang (Tao Qian) Still leaves lingering regret through many springs.
Traveling along the river road, coldness assails the spirit at every step. One knows not where one shall awaken to the profound truth.

Is it that there is no bright moon shared across a thousand *li*, or that among those who have once gazed upon this brother, how many remain today? Through all eternity, may our friendship remain firm amidst the chill of winter; may the ice and snow filling the void wash away the dust from our robes.
I, for my part, shall set down my brush to compose the histories; as for fame and integrity, I yield these entirely to you alone, who monopolize the spring.
The mountain colors and stream reflections reveal their spirits at dawn; the icicle supporting the heavens is too lifelike. Clear beside the small bridge, it loathes the falling snow;

frozen solid, it peers half-hidden with a single eye at people. Hairpins are askew and disheveled hair clings to the shadows of clouds; jade-like smoothness and buttery melting leave one intoxicated by the dust of the world.
Where do the nobility set up their pavilions for their outings? They alone disdain pure simplicity and refuse to paint in the spring.
Who sent the Divine Lord Donghuang Taoyi to join the assembly of immortals beneath the flowers? With dark skirts and white sleeves, he is the subject of the "Xuetang Fu";

With jade bones and ice-like grace, he is the person from the Moon Palace. In stillness, one perceives the cold waves entering the gutters with charm; In motion, they are fitting for the fine drifting dust of fragrant mists.
This body has returned to the realm of the green spring; How could I not obtain a smile from my child’s family?
A fairy in the water, a spirit in the mirror; night after night, we truly walk together into dreams. The wild geese of Long mourn the place where jade was buried;
the northern wind blows old upon the man who plays with the moon. Cold adds frost to the two brows on the banks of the Ba River; sorrow tires of the dust beneath several pairs of sandals in Jiangnan.
Within the snow, one does not disdain the bitter flavor; a single branch monopolizes the spring of the Nine Provinces.
The remaining crimson calyx half-cherishes the spirit; at the very limit of exhaustion, one truth is revealed.

A silver ladle stirs fragrance into the wine amidst the dew; beyond the jade-like beauty, the reflection follows the person. With a simple breast, one grasps at the snow—this sentiment is beyond remedy. Cold geese soar across the void, their flow untainted by dust.
Do not say that the year’s end brings only the color of departure; even as the year passes, one still faces the spring of all things.
The falling flakes of snow possess their own spirit; how much more so when Yangzhou’s verse enters the realm of truth? Beside the water, they seem to witness the rite of *xiè*;
flying like scattered jewels, they surely emulate the women who leapt from the towers. Upon the Stone of Three Lives, one is startled by a former dream;
atop the Qunyu Mountains, one emerges from the dust of the world. In vain do I face Wei Zong’s longing for Lu Kai; though broken off, this branch of spring does not endure.
In error, I have compared the passing years to the countenance of a deity; I force myself to harbor doubts, fearing it may not be true. Amidst the snow, moss-covered branches obscure half the tree;

to whom shall the fragrant message be sent by the postal courier? Your son faces the snow in his homeland, his heart trembling with cold; Cai Yan heard the *jia* flute and her resentment entered the dust of the world.
You must surely go to Mount Kunlun to gather the jade elixir, refining your soul and spirit to defy eternal spring.

Once the Recluse of Buzhou departed, the brush lost its divine spirit. How many times have I gazed upon the lakeshore, longing for that pure truth? The reflection of water leans slenderly across the green jade table;

the fragrance of the moon coldly bathes the man in white robes. Frosty birds steal glances as the lingering chill remains; within the paper curtains, I sleep alone amidst the dust of last night’s dreams.
I too am lean and pure, my heart like iron; I drink until intoxicated, chanting new verses to cherish once more the spring.
Heaven has bestowed upon him a spirit of pure integrity; since birth, he has followed only his true nature. In his withered thatch hut, he idly paces his old steps;
in the opulence of the Jade Hall, he is but a man of the past. Pale smoke and slanting moon enshroud his cold jade-like form;

flowing waters and drifting clouds sigh over his distance from the dust. Worn out by this desolate mountain, accustomed to emaciation, he sleeps drunk upon a stone pillow, silently repaying the spring.
For years my spirit has wandered alone across mountain ridges; amidst the jade-like trees, my skeletal form reveals its true nature.

At dawn, I rise to find white mist obscuring my staff beyond the haze; at night’s end, the cold awakens me beside my wine. To whom do the Jade Ring and Feiyan owe their shock at such illusions? Xi Shi and Wang Qiang both wept before the dust.
How can they compare to these withered roots that endure through all time? Wherever the warmth of spring stirs, nature blossoms of itself.

Accustomed to racing my spirit through water-villages and cloud-encircled hamlets, I have found the truth within a life of leisure and simplicity. Amidst the fragrances of the Li clan, I am but a solitary figure;
beyond the cranes of the Lin family, I am a man of integrity. Xianghengxi laughs at me for the bitterness of my poetic heart;
I am ashamed of my drunken eyes, which fall like dust upon the steps. As all manner of flowers and scents wither away, I wander alone through the spring for no other reason than this.

Sighing and weeping by the bamboo-patterned brocade, one’s efforts are in vain; yet how many trees stand in错落 (asymmetrical array), their essence naturally true. Beyond the clouds, they appear far away like those bearing the Han mission;
deep within the mountains, they resemble those who fled the Qin. Half-branches with broken buds still linger in poised expectation;
a single knee reaching into the void is unimpeded by dust. I offer my thanks to the Creator for pitying this solitude; at the end of night, He leaves the moon to accompany this tender spring.
The elegant spirit of the Jasper Forest is half-divine; who says its jade blossoms dare to usurp the True? My aged eyes startle at the road along the river;
my solitary frame grieves as it recalls those on the mountain pass. Cold floats over the peaks as my new oars turn back; purity enters the deep ravines, chasing away the dark dust.
Too thin to bear the weight of clothes, the clouds grow weary in their forms; at the midday moon upon the balustrade, what can be done for this spring?
At midnight, the *nièshāng* robes delight the feathered deities; the cold, bright moon reveals its true nature. Within these mountains, poetic inspiration naturally arises;
beyond the rivers, there have long been no vulgar men. A hundred bushels of pearls in radiant spheres, several branches vying for color amidst the fragrant dust.
Who was it that mistakenly dreamed of pear blossoms, awakening idle sorrows and ushering in the end of spring?

Amidst the flowers, we inquire of the Crane Deity: when shall our bones shed their shells like those of Xi Zhen? Eight thousand warriors possess the spirit that makes their crowns press against their brows;
a million men on precipitous cliffs practice *bigu* (grain-avoidance). In old age, I know only my addiction to clouds and waters; since birth, I have never known the dust of fine silks and brocades.
When will my thoughts become entirely free of affairs, so that I may leave the riverbank idle and pull at the spring in intoxication?

Transverse shadows and slender stalks seem possessed of spirit; in a place half-clear and shallow, they alone reveal their true nature. Several branches embody the refined simplicity of Late Tang verse;

a certain air of solitary loftiness recalls a man of the Eastern Jin. Who in the Imperial Gardens can endure the snow upon the green buds? Would the Jade Gorge of Mount Lu deign to be covered in dust?
Such celestial wonders—how could one possibly know them? Alas, they have been betrayed by the spring breeze.
I recall the deity from years past within my dreams; clearly, it seems to recognize the true likeness of Guangping. A fresh chill first penetrates the medicinal herbs before the winter solstice;
an ancient air threatens to startle those who dwell among the heavens. Who can command the leaden flowers to veil the bright day?

Would they willingly cast their silken bands into the clamor of the dust? In this deep winter, there remains a sense of life; if the powdered butterflies knew, they would surely lament for spring once more.
I inquire of the Lord of Flowers and the Spirit of the Earth: How much of the jade-medicine has been genuine since of old? Fragrance leads the one in white robes as they hoist their sails;
A cold white fan shields the person holding the reins. In its humble simplicity, it alone can repay the pure covenant; It steals moments of leisure, refusing to sink into the yellow dust.
If one knows the Way of Heaven through such wild chanting, One may grow so thin that even the Lord of Heaven fears the spring.

With a chivalrous bone structure so prominent, its spirit calls forth the divine. Before the courtyard, the moon has just been called upon to trace its true form. Moss seals the stones; what tree has grown weary of years?
Amidst the cruelty of snow and the ferocity of wind, it stands as a man of solitary integrity. Its auspicious beauty seems to unfold like the iridescent plumage of a phoenix;

it does not steal grace from the dust of horse hooves. With its radiant jade-like bones, who can share in its laughter? How could one bear to say that the Immortal Consort wishes to lament for spring?

The frost wind rises, stirring the spirits of the mid-air; her graceful immortal robes reveal the truth of the Way. Her brilliance does not fade in the sun, and her cold snow-like beauty remains radiant;

braving the chill, she seeks the mountain man at twilight. Green screens and azure curtains are fit to encircle her jade-like form; upon the purple roads and red towers, how could she dare to let dust settle?
Standing long upon the bridge over the stream, her sorrow stretches far away; yet the subtle fragrance clearly penetrates a whole heart of spring.

Deep within the mountains, the spirit is cold and shrouded; beautiful blossoms cling to branches, revealing the truth beneath illusion. Facing these emaciated forms, I pity their shadows in the chill night;
plucking them to look upon, I bring grief to those in my native land. Water and clouds play with the moon through three transformations; jade-white snow blows coolness across the six sense-fields.
It is laughable that one would plant peach trees to judge the wisdom of ghosts; the Master of Lacquer Gardens (Zhuangzi) must surely feel deep shame for such springtime pretenses.
Reciting by the East Brook, my spirit is doubled; the Immortal of the Exile and I share a single sincere heart. How many times has the lunar essence been brightened and extinguished?

Three washings and three incense offerings for this person of jade-like countenance. The snow would have run rampant, emptying and confusing the eyes; the wind returns to its modest nature, refusing to cling to dust.
Singing the "Apricot" song, one sighs for the feasts of the Kaiyuan era; surely the old garden must regret that spring was seized so early.
Last night I once flew with the deities of the caverns toward the Immortal Capital to face the Nine Perfected Ones.

Their iron faces were colder than the breath of a swordsman; their stony hearts were deeper than the scent of orchids. Branches stretched across the moon-viewing pavilion like jade pendants; fragments fell upon the wind-platform like powdered jade dust.
The dark cranes cried out silently in the empty ravines; with a short song, I became intoxicated by the Great Harmony spring.

The flower alone claims divinity amidst the snow; it punctuates the cold with true, pearl-like droplets. It leads the way for the return of the first yang, and thus follows the nine stages as one who returns home.
Within its fragrance lies a distinct melody that opens a realm of clarity; its lofty sentiment beyond the world becomes the dust of twilight.
Looking back at the traveler by the banks of the Wuling Stream, how many villages of misty waters still remain lost in spring.
A single object has possessed a spirit from its origins; a withered log alone claims the true essence within the wood. Its many reflections have a will to interfere with the moon;
its fragrance, originally devoid of emotion, moves people on its own. Beyond the ridges, frozen clouds obscure the distant view; south of the stream, bright snow conceals the light dust.
The thousand forests awaken from their state of yellowing decay; I entrust this to Yi Qi (the God of Spring) to laughingly receive the spring.
Powdered moon and wind-borne raiment skillfully illuminate the divine; half-revealed dragon-silk reveals a jade-like truth. Cold light naturally reflects the colors before one’s eyes;
a slender silhouette seeks to outwit those beyond the clouds. The phoenix solitary and the crane alone harbor a singular longing;
musk moistens the screen as the warm scene dispels the dust. The sleeping pear tree knows only how to form a wondrous dream; it does not yet recognize this fragment of spring within the mountains.

The cold constrains the flowers, delaying their bloom as one seeks to nourish the spirit; the new Yang has already begun to peer into the truth of the gallbladder. Within the Palace of Eternal Life, the womb of bees and the crescent moon reside;

those who have attained the Way obtain the jade nectar and golden elixir. Their transformations are like clouds emerging from mountain peaks; turning away from the times, they do not share the dust of the mundane world.
Among the red and white blossoms in Luoyang, whose maiden is this? I am reminded once more of Yuan Wei’s spring filling the hall.
At night, by the window, I chant until stillness enters my spirit; guarding against wind and cold, I find the true essence of the Way.
A single breath does not wither the three virtuous friends; yet in ten years, how many fair women have been sent away? The trees are thick with smoke as they welcome the snow;
vast clouds float, and the moon reflects the dust. I beg Xu Xi to paint this new scene; surely the spring upon his brush has not yet reached it.

From this moment on, you are a divine being upon the land of Mount Penglai; with yellow clouds trailing your sleeves, you visit the true man by the stream. Your immortal countenance never ages—this most stirs my inspiration.

Floating upon the water, I have no poem to offer in response to you. In stillness, I cherish Longshu’s insight into the eye of awakening; in sorrow, I pity Jiang Zong as he fell from the heights of song.
At the foot of the Pine Wind Pavilion, where we lingered so long, how heartrending it is that the wild thorns must now endure the arrival of spring.
Whom can these frozen shadows pity? The spirit in the wilds. Sparse and faint, they cultivate their own truthfulness. Several buds of cold white seem half-frozen with tears;
a single breath of fragrant purity is too much for the human heart. Wind and rain stir my nostalgia for the past; mountains and rivers make me regret my old age in the dust of the world.
Gao Jiao is gone and Bo Tao has died; on this day, there is but snow left to face the spring.
In dreams I recall the God Er-lang; the shadows of flowers speak most truly of my sorrow. The moon drenches the courtyard in cold water-jade;
a dream startles me from my lonely pillow as a man with broken entrails. Unable to bear looking back upon past events from the beginning, though I long for new verses, they are but dust.
A woodpecker knocks at the door, spying on my drunkenness; the four mountains are silent, while birds sing out in spring.
I recall how in the past, Lord Ping was a diviner of spirits; his "green-clad" responses must have been truly timely.

Among the clouds, the sorceress has many charming faces; emerging from her bath, Yang Fei is a singular beauty. In the bamboo-leaf cup, there is no moss upon the stone steps; by the moonlight, the bean-stalk ashes warm the dust on the paper window.
Fearing that the times might cause me to fall behind the myriad flowers, I hasten to the famous gardens to pursue the arrival of spring.
After finishing my rhymes by the Jueqi Pavilion, my spirit darkly mourns; Donghun still remembers the truth of the past. Seven Sorrows stir my heart and startle my sorrowful eyes;
A single line flows into the void, pitying this illusory man. My secluded interest wanders far, lost in the snows of the Congling Mountains;
The cold flowers wash clean the dust of Luoyang. I imagine you have already flown away to the immortal capital; To whom shall the jeweled hairpin and golden hair-clasp be sent this spring?

Ten thousand flowers share the same breath yet possess different spirits; standing like jade, your solitary elegance transcends the true. Startled beyond the snow, I behold three or five stamens; among the mountains, how many thousands have known you?
Your fragrance still has its share to contribute to the poet’s materials; your leaning shadow awakens me from sleep as it strikes the illusory dust.
The Eastern Emperor has worn himself out for my sake—I am old now; have you ever felt shame or envy for the springtime of the brocade palace?
Sentiments dispelled, the image of self withers; the spirit seems to sigh as it contemplates the true. At moonrise, I recall drinking together outside the grove;

when the wine is sobered, I grieve for those within the winding path. Walking alone by the desolate stream, the mountains have just become still; cold shadows hold one another, and even the snow is but dust.
Every time I lament the heavy wind and dew upon half the eaves, I rise to don my jade-like fur, accompanying the spring of jade.
A supreme deity within the Purple Microcosm, banished to Penglai and Yingzhou to lead the multitude of Perfected Beings. In the tenth month, he assumes form and distributes the vast vital energy;

the Nine Spirits preside over destiny and record the names of those of jade-like purity. When the precarious roots are inevitably exposed, one must realize they are but delusions; the Perfect Wisdom is luminous and complete, never following after the dust of the world.
His station is pure and lofty, yet too solitary and pristine; when all fragrances have faded, he alone embodies the springtime of the world.

The broad dissemination of his calligraphy has nearly exhausted the divine essence; he wondrously captures the true character and rank among the flowers. A drop of snow half-adheres to traces left by the wind;
light smoke slants across, veiling the person west of the bamboo grove. The cold courtyard cools the eyes of the magistrate; so pure it seems ready to fly into the void and wipe away the miasma-dust.
Recalling the frost-bell as she hastens to wash her makeup, for whom does the spring come—before the year’s end or after?
A divine spirit descends from the Jade Palace into the flowers; a peerless beauty with a celestial air, as pure as fine powder.

She has bathed in the waters of the Milky Way until dawn, yet she brings sorrow to the reed fences and the man in his thatched cottage. Famous beauties and noble steeds are but empty themes for the brush; ruined gardens and wild mosses age amidst the dust of war.
The frozen wilderness is vast and desolate, the heavens mournful on all four sides; two rows of returning geese alone grieve for the spring.
A fleeting scent of incense passes by, as if to stir the spirit; In the distant woods, the breeze is clear and the waters reflect the truth.
From beyond the void, a messenger of flowers and birds suddenly arrives; Amidst the clouds, one surely awaits a person from the Calyx Palace.

Xu Qiong’s jade-like flight and Bo Jia’s sorrowful bearing of verses, Nongyu’s flute-playing that stirs falling motes of dust— Leading the host of immortals to the Emperor’s abode, Spring is born afar upon the Renluo Terrace.

Frost and snow in the gardens—how many times have they exhausted my spirit? Heaven takes pity on this poet facing the void and the truth. A single burner holds the clear water of Hsiung Ling’s incense;
half-applied powder graces the person of Hsü Fei. My grief is absolute, unable to endure the end of the year; my feelings run deep, almost wishing to resent the wind and dust.
The ancient roots have already learned the hibernation of the azure dragon; how strange that spring has already burst forth in the bitter cold.
Huang Hai’s eyes were clouded with drowsiness; he gazed sorrowfully at a few true blossoms amidst the sparse woods. In the southern lands, fragrance mists his drunken dreams;
from the north, the wind is like the clamor of war for the captive traveler. In its full measure of solitude and stillness, it is most suited to late evening;
in its singular freshness, it remains untainted by dust. Emaciated and fallen in the cold outskirts, who shall call him forth? Sitting here, he chants until the spring of the Jade Hall.

Heaven has revealed a wondrous sight for the spirit of poetry; through laborious toil, several evenings have been spent to reach the truth. In the Dream-Speaking Chamber, one constantly recalls dreams;
in the intoxication at Baling Pass, half the people were mistaken for others. Having been hidden for over a year, its white hue must now rest upon fine powder;
facing the rain, it shares a fragrance as if separated from the dust. One laughs at the withered *zhao* and peony trees; in the quiet chamber, the seductive flowers vie for beauty in spring.

Where the dark clouds and shadows fly, the spirit transmigrates; Secretly emitting solitary fragrance, it accords with its own true nature. Its reflection desires to peer into the water-mirror; Its slanting branches seem to lean toward those with affection.
How many clear mornings have passed over Hai-ning, Kui, and Xun? At Jin-gu and Tong-tuo, this single tree is but a speck of dust.
Why need one lament the passing of youth and the onset of twilight? With a head full of white hair, simply wear the blossoms of spring.
A single goblet offered to the God of the Chu River; Fragrant tidings, obscure and deep, seem destined for the True. All say it is heartless, yet it still possesses thought;
Suddenly I suspect it is a shadow, yet it is no mere man. The snow melts and clouds vanish like a dream; The moon sets, and the flute’s resentment toward the dust is hard to bear.
Most poignant is the traveler’s unsettled longing; I wrap my cloak and sit in perilous stillness, alone grieving for spring.
Riding side-by-side with cranes and herons, they descend from the Three Divine Mountains; though my sick eyes are dim, what I behold is yet true. One moon sinks slowly, casting its slanting shadow;

nine strains of music play as the *bǔxū* (void-traversing) immortals walk across the heavens. Cold powdered frost weeps tears upon the jade balustrades; the fragrance of orchids and musk wafts through the dust of white stockings.
It is like a scene upon a screen of rainbows and clouds; within the Warm Spring Palace, each displays its own springtime splendor.
Gazing upon the Victorious One, the divine spirit releases the grain; the multitude of immortals ride cranes as they truly court the Real.

Of what kind is this ethereal fragrance and peerless beauty? Only such a person transcends the mundane and enters the sacred. Old and weary, I am startled in secret by the passing years; in solitude, I gaze only upon ancient mists and dust.
I ask him, the one hidden among the tangerine trees—does he know? How many springs have passed since he transformed into a soaring dragon?

Amidst the blossoms, one catches a glimpse of the Forest Deity; he gazes coldly at the mist drifting across half his cheeks. With his hand, he plucks a tip of a branch, marking the crescent moon’s trace;

whether asleep or awake, the fragrance beyond the scent confounds the senses. Damp clouds remain motionless, concealing deep emerald depths; the last snow has just melted, filling the warm dust with vitality.
The myriad trees know of their own accord that Heaven cherishes them; they begin to vie for spring only after the Deity has passed from behind.
The incense from the imperial brazier permeates the Tai Luo deities; through the eternal night, the ladle is held aloft facing the Seven Sages. The fierce winds of vast eons open the spirit of Chu;

at the break of dawn, one crosses the Weak Water to reach the Immortal Star. The green-haired lord’s phoenix feathers flutter across the musical scores; the traces of the embryonic bird in the vermilion cauldron have transformed into dust.
Alone she charms the Dark Brilliance, forever ageless; the oaks and cedars of the sea know change, yet how many springs have passed?
The moonlight is faintly bright, yet I mistakenly perceive a divine transformation; upon the jade terrace, I apply powder, recording the true countenance of the past.
To know that the emerald feathers are but empty traces, one need not believe that the Jilin country ever transformed men. From afar, I gaze upon the solitary root, startled by the deepening dusk;
for my new poem and old dreams, I lament the former dust. A frozen dragon stands precariously, its scales and armor cold; though there be green coins, they cannot purchase spring.

The soaring spirit floats through the profound depths, displaying the divine essence of snow. On the empty river, misty waves seem truly sorrowful. Originally there was no smile that could captivate the world;

once, it quenched the thirst of those amidst the army. Exposed to warmth and brewing cold, it follows its traces through time; combing the wind and washing away the rain, its intent transcends the mundane.
Though the vital energy of mountains and rivers has not yet ceased, it alone brings a fine spring to these remaining years.

Exquisitely facing the myriad blossoms, she plays with her five spirits; amidst the void, she tirelessly delights in the True. How many concerns have there been for the heavens, flowers, earth, and moon?

Yet she is the sole mistress of the rivers, lands, streams, and mountains. She wishes to smile yet feels sorrow, ashamed to speak; appearing suddenly and vanishing in an instant like a drifting speck of dust.
Her fragrant form fears not to be worn away; even a single drop of its tenderness is as much springtime as this.
Powdered [snow] dissolves the divine spirit; it is not permitted that the exquisite *qiónghuā* should outvie its true nature.

A procession of pearl banners welcomes the feather-clad immortals; half the loom of ice-weaving halts the *jiāorén*. Transferred from the heavens, it travels through the celestial void; transformed before the wine-cup, it becomes a mote playing in the light.
Who shall join the Water Bureau to record this sequence of powder? Amidst the wind, it sheds tears for the spring of the *Tùyuán*.

With a body like a *chī* dragon and a tail like a *qiú* serpent, its aged form possesses a divine spirit. It unfurls living branches whose colors vie with the true. With a desire for snow, one would board a boat to travel to Shan;
the dew-dripping eaves surely resent the man who shoots the eagle. Suited to both sun and rain, its cold essence nourishes its resonance; harboring moods and emotions, it bathes in the dust at dawn.
A single branch of seasonal fragrance knows how to keep its appointment; what need is there for the *jiegǔ* drum to further clamor for spring?
Sitting in distress, I have no cause but to banish the god of sleep; suddenly, poetic inspiration arrives, desiring to ascend to the Truth.

Meeting you, my companion of dual purity amidst snow and moon, I, an old man, am moved by a hundred experiences of wind and frost. Knowing that this drifting life holds its sorrows, my heart and bowels are bitter and plain, secretly ashamed of the dust of the world.
Let the nature of things change with the passing years; as evening falls and the sky grows cold, I take no account of spring.
Ten thousand jade maidens surround the courtyard, illuminating the myriad deities; I gaze indolently at this short scroll, facing the horizontal portrait of the True One.
Reciting as I look upon the floating fragrance of Mount Yuling, I grow weary of the man who spits wine at Mount Bashi. In the moon palaces and frosty halls, they pity the shadows of dancers;
Upon icy cliffs and moss-covered walls, they block out the dust of seduction. Amidst the distance, one may see "rouge-snow"; The sentiment is the same, yet the springtime is of two kinds.
Not obstructing a single dewdrop on a leaf, the entire spirit is revealed; it seems one beholds the elegance of He Jizhen. Heaven has bestowed upon him poetic sentiment reaching back to antiquity;
with the moon and its clear reflection, there are exactly three persons. The cold mocks the snowy bank with its lingering whiteness; the pure spray from the icicle eaves remains untouched by dust.
Seeing only new inscriptions upon the eastern wall, they lean against the railing to linger and gaze at the spring shared by all.
Five exits, majestic and grand, they seize the spirits of the multitude; alone in a place of stillness, one beholds the solitary truth.

A natural air within the land of sandalwood; a jade-like person amidst the campaka groves. Though buried many times by winter snows, he does not die; a single drop of cold spring water, pure and free from dust.
How many rare treasures are there in this world? Who dares to vie for early spring upon a withered branch?
The divine spirit of the brush is locked deep within the green window. A sturdy stride brings him here; his shadow leaves the true form behind.

From of old I have admired his refined elegance; throughout my life I have delighted in him as a man of seclusion. The "Bamboo Servant" (Zhunuo) was once so fond of him he shared the honored seat before him;

the "Brother Alum" (Fandì) shares his lofty style, yet they remain two distinct entities. Suddenly he asks me, leaning on his staff, if I recognize the wine cup; one part is desolate, the other part is spring.
Pure cultivation does not serve as a deity of the five directions; beyond the smoke, who can unveil the half-ornamented true countenance?
Tearful eyes have not yet cleared, cold droplets like milk; white hair like snow, old age urges one on. The vast expanse of the long sky increases lingering regrets;
the distant waters are hazy, submerging all traces of dust. How could I ever hope to meet again at Tangchang? May swift whips drive my pursuing steeds toward the springtime of Yufeng Peak.

Though deep affection may exist, it does not disturb the spirit; one laughs at those peach and plum blossoms that appear so true after the rain. Verdant growth rises upon cold sleeves as sorrow enshrouds the moon;

jade-like beauty falls from tender clouds, drawing near to others with intensity. Three lines of verse conceal a hidden resonance; through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one enters the dust of emptiness.
Since Shouyang departed, her lingering grace has faded far away; I scratch my head in thought—this "Hanchang" flower is but a dream of spring.

The frosty forest is held fast by an eternal spirit; from the distant fragrant roots, the true essence of the flower emerges. Playing with the moon at the edge of the cliff, he startles the mountain ghosts;
welcoming the wind beyond the wall, he smiles at the passersby. Pure as jade and clear as ice, it is fit to be smeared with white pigment;

when the powder fades and the bones decay, it does not follow after the dust. As the nine-fold brilliance shoots through the crevices, radiance arises; Yuan Zhen’s prose is vibrant with the springtime.

Leaning thin against the sparse fence, half her spirit emerges; Snow and wind blow across her face, cold yet containing the True. In the glow of clear skies, whose jade is this fragrant purity? A haloed shadow upon the icicle eaves, she is like a certain person.
The holy bees have already seen her and come first to gather and explore; She would not consent to follow the dreaming butterfly as it long turns to dust.
In the chilly grove, all is hurried as the east grows white; Awakening from sorrow with a single ladle, heaven and earth are filled with spring.

At the ends of the earth, I remember the ancient deity; through village mists and rains, I have yet to meet the Real. The shifting patterns of "scattered" verse follow the cold of the south and the warmth of the north;
As the sun sets in the west and rises in the east, it pursues those who have gone before. Fortunately, the robe and bowl of Old Sō remain; In vain I pity the dust upon the eaves of He-jìng.
I recall the grounds where I once roamed at Jíyīng; Turning my head toward Cí'ēn, the spring air grows dim.
Above, there is no further form or vapor; what spirit is there? The power of the Way is firm and solid, forged true as iron. Enduring death and braving the cold, one pities this aged skeleton.

Turning the light back upon itself, one beholds the solitary person. Who can fathom the subtle appointment of the Weaver of Heaven? The pure bearing of the immortal guest refuses to be defiled by dust.
At midnight, a crane arrives from beyond the clouds; the Lord of Penglai Palace comes forth ahead of spring.
Gathering the lingering fragrance to offer to the inner deities, the numinous and true ones are faintly visible amidst the clouds. The Palace of Guǎnwá rises as the Phoenix City warms;
deep within the Verdant Pavilion, the people of Gènyuè dwell. Rich morning flesh flourishes beyond the lofty trees; the cold forms fade away from the azure dust of heaven.
Chéngzhāi has newly composed a poem based on the tale of the seductive spirit; startled, the springtime within the lines of the *Táofú* charm scatters.

The profound serenity and coolness naturally delight the spirit; meeting thus, one almost wishes to inquire of the immortals and sages. The ice-flakes settle in the clear morning like the Consort of the Xiang River;
the dew-wetted bamboo in the cold startles the people of Yue. Wind and moon form a summer covenant for a thousand years; the cool view of river and sky is a momentary dusting of the world.
Do not mistake the peach branches for emerald leaves; chant carefully with Changli Bai Juyi of "snow and spring."
How could these lines fail to move even ghosts and spirits? This exquisite melody of the solitary luan belongs to one seeking the truth.

At nightfall, the slender silhouette is especially suited to the moon; after the snow, its pure fragrance seems to permeate the soul. We come together at the Eastern Pavilion to compose verses in bitter earnest; yet the traces at West Lake must surely be covered in dust.
Do you know how those who have achieved their purpose season the cauldron of state? One must ensure that the universe is filled with the springtime of universal joy.
Flowers bloom at the end of winter; the awakened spirit is divine. A single kind of numinous root, utterly wondrous and true. In the fifth month they ripen into golden pellets;
in the three winters the stamens blossom like jade-towered immortals. Master Pang travels afar to investigate; Old Chang remains composed, untainted by dust.
Who can truly comprehend such a bitter heart? Would they be willing to share this snow-song with the "Yangchun"?
*The Hundred Verses on Plum Blossoms in Response to Píng Hǎisù*, by the Monk Zhōngfēng Huànzhù of Tiānmù (End of Volume).

This is a work composed by the Monk Zhōngfēng Huànzhù of Tiānmù. It breaks through the narrow views of scholastic learning (*yìxué*) and reveals the profound mysteries of the True Lineage (*zhèngzōng*).
Its expressions are rich and its principles are superior; it cites the ancients and draws parallels from the present.

All of this has its basis in fact. Formerly, our ancestor, the Great Master Bodhidharma, first came to China to reveal the profound essence of Vulture Peak and directly transmit it to those of superior capacity.
Thus, there arose the saying: "One flower opens into five petals; the fruiting occurs spontaneously.

From the founding patriarch down to Dajian (Huineng), the fragrance was linked and the flame continued; the lineages branched out and the branches divided, succeeding one another in an unbroken succession.

There is indeed a profound reason for this severance. Yet, it is not by abandoning words and speech, discarding names and signs, cutting off the paths of conceptual entanglements, or shattering the nests of the holy and the mundane that one can easily perceive even a semblance of its essence.

The Chan Master wields the sword of wisdom before the birth of Buddhas and sentient beings; he penetrates the source of all phenomena to the very bottom of the deep abyss of the ocean of awakening. His noble resolve...
In mountain retreats, his solitary style was beyond reach. Thus, when his writings appeared, they restored the sun of the Buddha’s teachings and blocked the surging tide of madness;

it was only fitting that they should serve as a banner of light for a hundred generations. Having already composed the song of the postscript, I, the old recluse Xiujū, could not refuse the request of his disciple, the Head Seat Wéizé, to provide a preface.
At this time, the twelfth month of the second year of Tàiding.
Written on the twenty-seventh day of the month by the recluse Qingmao of Fengtai in Jinling.
A single flower and five petals were transmitted from the original Bodhidharma; from the eight directions and four quarters, they have converged in this collection.
Zhongfeng, with the seeds of Bodhi, has made the interior of the realm transparently clear; with the medicine of Jīvaka, he removes the ailments and afflictions of the world. This is true vision.

Pine and cypress trees rise from the earth, while thorns and brambles are utterly forgotten as they reach toward the heavens. Such is the fragrance of this faculty of the tongue, which perfumes the universe and reaches the ears of all.
Furthermore, it causes the cool shade of these tree-seeds to provide shelter for future generations.
On the sixth day after the Lantern Festival of the year Taiding Bingyin, the old student Feng Zizhen, formerly a Court Attendant of the Bureau of Scholarly Worthies, prostrates himself in reverence.
The Shaolin "Direct Pointing" has no branches or leaves; it is but a self-proclaimed discourse that echoes sound and grasps at emptiness.

Old Zhongfeng has exerted his strength to sweep it away; citing the ancients to clarify the present is merely a leakage of the truth. I already know the end of its coming and going: the small boat appears and disappears amidst the cold mist and waves.
Lake Tai has terrified Li Babo; it does not permit other sons to poke their heads out to look. I intend to attain the state of Hanshan.
Several verses: A fierce wind in the void overturns the stone mortar; As it drifts down to the human world, who knows of it? The dew-pillar and the lantern open their smiling mouths.
The Patriarch’s Heart-Seal is inscribed as an inscription: "The most perilous within the perilous, the most level within the level.
What do you say to this one pivotal phrase? Touching the bridge of the nose, the two eyes open wide. I am originally without mind—who would wish to debate me? Return...
One must see for oneself the state of a Non-returner; Gautama’s compassionate heart reaches its ultimate depth. Ānanda, with his vast learning, employs skillful means;
I observe this "Chapter on Dwelling in Illusion" and sing of it as an illusion. Without moving my tongue, ten thousand mouths transmit it.

Though the single flower and five petals spread abroad in vain, it is but natural to extend one's hand into the marketplace. The livelihood of the Patriarchs can never be sold away; the pines and bamboos draw in the wind, leaving only emptiness.
How strange! It cannot help but weary that illusory body, repaying illusory debts within the light of illusion. A-he-he!
The Three Gorges flow backward and the Silver River pours forth. Binding straw mats and sitting upon the mouth of a lion, he seeks to test the old woman who once burned his hut.
A mirage and empty flowers; resting in the *cūṇa* (dust-mote) abode, he continues the postscript to the Long Song.

When the Master Zhongfeng of Tianmu finished his work titled *The Five Leaves of a Single Flower*, he composed this long verse himself as a postscript. His disciple—
Venerable Weize came forward to present this for inspection and requested a preface for it. Accordingly, I have composed verses following his rhyme:

On the full moon of the twelfth month in the second year of the Taiding era, I, the old recluse Qingmao of Fengtai in Jinling, declare that the essential meaning of the separate transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is like ten suns suspended in the great void, with not even a hair’s breadth of concealment. It is not something to be explained...

To reach such a consummate realization beyond mere scholastic tenets requires only those of great capacity; they must penetrate deeply, remaining utterly independent and transcending the emotional and intellectual measures of both sages and ordinary beings.
Only then, wielding the precious sword of the Vajra King, can one act with sovereign freedom in killing and giving life, and with effortless mastery in seizing and releasing.
With every step, there must be a path for self-exit; only then is one fit to continue the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. This is the Lion’s Rock.

Master Feng penetrated the very source and bottom of the Dharma; his realization was as vast and open as the great void. Countless hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings flowed forth in a surging tide from the ocean of his nature.
Naturally transcending the school and surpassing conventional categories, he shattered the delusions of fetal breath and transmitted the authentic, harmonious, and perfect teaching.

Having realized the intent of the Patriarchs, he opened the way for those who transcend the stream of scholastic interpretation. He maintained that [the teaching] begins with the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind), a point to which even the ancients had not previously discussed.

He modeled his work after the hundred poems of Hanshan and composed the "Discrimination of the Seven Investigations and Eight Returns" (*Qian zheng ba huan*) as well as the "Five Teachings on the Illusory Nature of Phenomena.
These collectively are titled "The One Flower and Five Petals," all of which serve to exalt the supreme, ultimate point of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, like a pearl resting upon a platter.
It does not move unless pushed; it is not for those who lack the great eye of wisdom and the hands of the great hammer that shatters [delusions] to easily enter its precincts and deliberate with it.
Written in the summer of the Gengshen year of the Yanyou era by Xiling of Jingshan.
The above collection of one flower with five petals was personally composed by National Preceptor Puyǒng during his lifetime; it was subsequently compiled and included in the *Gwangnok*.
There are two copies of this within our mountain monastery: one is a woodblock print from the Yuan dynasty, and the other is an ancient publication from our own country.
When compared, they are identical in every respect; it is clearly a re-engraved copy. This is the same as that which is recorded in the *Gwangnok*.
It is not without errors. A bookseller wished to carve new woodblocks and circulate it, yet he was unable to complete it quickly.
Therefore, he requested that I revise it based on the *Guǎnglù* (Extended Record) edition. Thus, I corrected those characters that were erroneous and marked those passages where the wording differed.
I have also supplemented the preface and colophon so that, should anyone in the world encounter this collected work, its volume sequence shall be as stated in the National Teacher’s own account.
Now, following the order established in the *Guanglu*, I have reorganized it into three volumes; therefore, I have annotated the original titles beneath each heading.
May readers grant their understanding of these matters.
Written respectfully by Gen'en of this mountain on a summer day in the sixth year of the Meiwajō era (the year of Jichū, i.e., 949).
